title: feat(vta): clear a context's DID with vta/contexts/update-did/1.1
body:
Serves `vta/contexts/update-did/1.1` (trust-tasks #684, released in `trust-tasks-rs` 0.24.6), where `did: null` clears a context's DID. 1.0 is still served.

**Why.** Once a context had a DID, it could only be replaced. 1.0 requires a non-empty `did`, and `vta/contexts/update` only ever sets one. The DID-delete blocker told the operator to reassign the DID first, so the only way to retire a context's last DID was to assign one they didn't want. The browser console already offered "none" and was refused with `"" is shorter than 1 character`.

**Behaviour:**
- 1.0 and 1.1 share one handler. 1.1 parses into the generated `update_did::v1_1::Payload`, and 1.0 still parses into `UpdateContextDidBody`.
- `update_context_did` takes `Option<String>`. `None` removes the DID, and the returned record omits `did`. Clearing an already-clear context succeeds, and only `updatedAt` changes. The log line says "cleared" or "updated".
- A 1.1 request with a missing `did`, `""`, `did:` or a non-DID string is refused `malformedRequest` by the dispatch spine's schema check, before serde could read a missing member as a clear.
- Deprecation table: 1.0 is superseded by 1.1, and legacy `PUT /contexts/{id}/did` names 1.1 as its successor. It still only sets a DID.
- 1.1 is added to the dispatch table, the conformance sweep, the `notFound` sweep, and `retry_safety` (RetrySafe).

**CLI** (pnm and cnm):
- `pnm contexts update-did <id> --clear`: the DID argument becomes optional and conflicts with `--clear`.
- `pnm contexts update <id> --clear-did`: conflicts with `--did`. The clear goes through update-did, and a name or description change still goes through `contexts/update`.

**DID-delete blocker** now offers both, and names update-did, which a context admin can run. The old `contexts update --did` needed super-admin.
```
context `{id}` acts as this DID — reassign it first: `pnm contexts update-did {id} <new-did>`, or leave the context with no DID: `pnm contexts update-did {id} --clear`
```

**SDK:** the public API is non-breaking. `update_context_did(id, did)` keeps its signature and now sends 1.1. `VtaClient::clear_context_did(id)` is new.

**Floor:** `trust-tasks-rs` and `trust-tasks-capability-client` go to 0.24.6. That is a correctness floor: below it `TASK_CONTEXTS_UPDATE_DID_1_1` doesn't compile, and the spine has no schema for `did: null`.

**Cuts over with** the browser console (`pnm-browser-plugin`), which sends `did: null` on 1.1. That PR follows this one.

**Checks run locally:**
- Before the rebase:
  - `cargo test -p vta-sdk -p vta-service -p vta-cli-common -p pnm-cli` against the released 0.24.6: 3168 passed, 0 failed.
  - `cargo test --workspace --exclude vtc-service --exclude vtc-client` with a local trust-tasks patch: 5156 passed.
  - `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` and `cargo fmt --check`: clean.
- After rebasing onto current main: `cargo check --all-targets` on the changed crates only.
- Not run locally: `vtc-service`/`vtc-client` and the reduced-feature clippy runs.

New tests:
- `clearing_a_context_did_removes_it_and_is_idempotent`
- `contexts_update_did_1_1_clears`, which also sends 1.0
- `contexts_update_did_1_1_refuses_a_non_did`
- 1.1 rows in the `notFound` and conformance sweeps

**Not done:** the offline `vta` binary's `contexts update --did` (`vta-service/src/main.rs`) has no clear option yet.

title: fix(vtc-service): config writes and admin invites need an unrestricted admin
body:
A security fix for a gap #1824 carried over from the REST handlers when it moved them to the spine.

**High.** `vtc/config/{patch,reload,restart}` and `vtc/config/import` asked only for an admin, as the old REST `AdminAuth` did. So an admin scoped to a single context could:
- lower `acl.unrestricted_admin_consent_threshold`, the APV-014 consent requirement;
- change `public_url` or `server.*`;
- restart the process repeatedly.

All four now require an **unrestricted** admin.

**Medium.** `vtc/admin/invites/{list,revoke}` were open to context admins, although an invite confers unrestricted authority. They now require an unrestricted admin. `create` refuses a context admin up front, including on the TTL-too-long path.

**Tests:**
- the context-admin refusal list in `tests/admin_verbs_spine.rs` now includes the config writes and invites;
- `tests/admin_config.rs::import_refuses_a_context_admin` covers import.

Checks: `admin_config` (36) and `admin_verbs_spine` (17) pass, and `cargo clippy -p vtc-service --all-targets -D warnings` and fmt are clean.

**Follow-ups, not in this PR:**
- An unrestricted admin can lower the consent threshold alone; lowering it should itself need consent at the current threshold.
- There is no restart cooldown.
- The per-signer rate-limit bucket for `/v1/trust-tasks` goes with #1827.
- Two tests pass without testing anything, because they point at the removed `GET /v1/admin/config`: `test_support_smoke::minted_admin_token_is_accepted` and the CORS preflight tests in `routing_cors.rs`.

title: Add the DTG credential context as v1, and the rules for contexts
body:
## Summary

Adds `contexts/v1.jsonld`, the JSON-LD 1.1 context the specification's *Base Structure* requires, and the GOVERNANCE.md rules that say who controls a context and when a new version is minted. Refs #4.

The IRIs are decided: [cred-spec #48](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/issues/48) records `https://registry.trustoverip.org/dtg/context/v1` for the context and the unversioned `https://registry.trustoverip.org/dtg/credentials#` for the type and property IRIs it defines, and cred-spec #64 applied both to the specification. The five follow-through points agreed on #48 are listed in [its closing comment](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/issues/48#issuecomment-5870055492); the ones that touch this repository are in this PR, the rest land in the companion spec PR.

## What `v1` defines

- `DTGCredential` and the seven concrete subtypes from the spec's taxonomy: `MembershipCredential`, `RelationshipCredential`, `DelegationCredential`, `InvitationCredential`, `PersonaCredential`, `StatementCredential`, `AuthorityCredential`.
- `issuerScope` (plain string), the correlation-scope declaration decided in [cred-spec #46](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/issues/46): one of `pairwise`, `directed` or `public`, validated by the specification and its schemas rather than by JSON-LD.
- `taskContext` (plain string) and `taskDigestMultibase` (multibase datatype, as VC 2.0 types `digestMultibase`).
- VSC: `predicate` as `@id`, `object` with `value` as `@json`, and `witnessContext` with `event`, `sessionId`, `method`. `object.id` and `object.digestMultibase` are inherited from VC 2.0.
- VDC: `delegation` with `scope` (set), `parent`, `maxDepth` (integer), `accepts`.
- VAC: `authority` with `scope` (IRI), `actions` (set), `parent`, `maxAttenuation` (integer).

Every term is `@protected` and written as a full IRI under `https://registry.trustoverip.org/dtg/credentials#`. `digestMultibase` is not redefined: VC 2.0 defines and protects it, and a redefinition is a fatal JSON-LD error.

## Also in this PR

- Both example credentials under `predicates/` carry `issuerScope`, since the specification makes it REQUIRED: `directed` on the member-issued endorsement, `public` on the witness service's attestation.
- PLAN.md no longer says the First Person context IRI "stays recognized by verifiers". The position agreed on #48 is that credentials issued before the Implementers Draft are not conformant whatever context IRI they list, so no legacy alias is carried forward.
- GOVERNANCE §3.1 states that a predicate profile's additional members (`witnessContext`, for example) live in the core context, so adding one is a new core version. Per-profile contexts are a `v2` question; objections here, please.

## Design choices to review

1. **Flat, not type-scoped.** A type-scoped context does not propagate into `credentialSubject`, so a term under a scoped `StatementCredential` would leave `predicate` undefined. That is the trap the WD02-era bundled file falls into.
2. **`scope` gets two IRIs.** The VDC's `delegation.scope` is a set of act strings; the VAC's `authority.scope` is one IRI. Same JSON key, different meanings, so they expand to `delegationScope` and `authorityScope` through property-scoped contexts. `parent` is the same kind of value in both and shares one IRI.
3. **`taskContext` is a plain string.** The Trust Tasks specification permits any unique string as a document `id` and recommends a bare UUID, so typing it as `@id` would turn a bare UUID into a relative IRI.
4. **`issuerScope` is a plain string.** Three fixed words compared exactly; IRI-valued terms named `public`, `pairwise` or `directed` would apply to any key of that name anywhere in a credential.
5. **Left out deliberately.** `PersonhoodCredential`, which the spec calls a non-authoritative hint rather than a type; `RelationshipCard`, which is a VDS; `SkillEndorsement`, `Person`, `endorsement`, which live inside an `@json` payload; and `nodeType` (cred-spec #53), held for `v2`.
6. **No prefixes.** Full IRIs throughout, so no CURIE can expand on the wire and no prefix can collide with a proof suite's context. `@version: 1.1` makes a JSON-LD 1.0 processor fail loudly on `@protected`.

## Digest

The content of `contexts/v1.jsonld` is final as of this revision. SHA-256 over the file's raw bytes (3636 bytes, trailing newline), which is also what the build publishes for `dtg/context/v1.jsonld` in `release.json`:

| Form | Value |
|---|---|
| hex | `3e1376acf401016a0162c1cdb31e44a85a7dd56749caed94a1dc0a0be6cbb448` |
| multihash, base58btc | `zQmSWyCagdx8oPfXn3piSUx6yqVy5MZ7ZG7nW1TC64QvKZh` |
| multihash, base64url | `uEiA-E3as9AEBagFiwc2zHkSoWn3VZ0nK7ZSh3AoL5su0SA` |

The companion spec PR pins one of these in *Base Structure* (#48 point 2). Any further byte change to the file before merge invalidates the pin, so the file does not change again without the spec PR being updated with it.

## Verification

- `docker compose run --rm check` passes against `origin/main`: validator, immutability, instance-values scan, 22 unit tests, build (2 predicate versions, 1 context valid).
- Ten example credentials, one or two per type, were expanded with jsonld.js 8 in safe mode against this context and a local copy of the VC 2.0 context, with no network. Every DTG member maps to its intended IRI, none falls through to VC 2.0's issuer-dependent vocabulary, `predicate` expands to the predicate IRI as a node reference, `object.value` becomes one `rdf:JSON` literal, and `delegation` and `authority` produce the expected typed quads.

## Landing

GOVERNANCE §3.1 says a context version lands together with the specification PR that makes the matching change to *Base Structure*. That is [cred-spec #68](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/pull/68) (`issuerScope`, the digest pin, and the other #48 follow-through); this PR merges after it, the same day.

## Not in this PR

- The build check that every example credential lists the context IRI in `@context`. Now unblocked; follows separately.

title: Name the correlation-scope declaration issuerScope and pin the v1 context
body:
## Summary

Names the property that carries a correlation-scope declaration, as decided in #46: a top-level `issuerScope` on every DTG credential, REQUIRED, exactly one of `pairwise`, `directed` or `public`, declaring the scope of that credential's `issuer` and nobody else's. Verifiers MUST reject a credential whose `issuerScope` is absent or invalid. The *Declaring scope* editor's note is gone, *Correlation Scope* no longer says the declaration has nowhere to live, and all sixteen examples carry the property, with the value following from who is issuing (community, witness service and governing party `public`; the reused member identifier `directed`; VRC peers `pairwise`).

Also lands the five follow-through points from the [#48 closing comment](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/issues/48#issuecomment-5870055492), in a new *Context Versions* subsection of *Base Structure*:

- the exact byte form of the context IRI and the required `@context` order (VC 2.0, then DTG `v1`, then proof, profile or community contexts);
- the `v1` digest, pinned normatively over the raw bytes of `contexts/v1.jsonld` as a base-58-btc Multihash (`zQmSWyCagdx8oPfXn3piSUx6yqVy5MZ7ZG7nW1TC64QvKZh`, hex `3e1376ac…b448`), with "verifiers SHOULD use a local copy matching this digest and SHOULD NOT dereference the IRI at verification time";
- the protected-terms warning for contexts listed after the DTG context;
- profile members live in the core context, so adding one is a new context version;
- credentials issued before the Implementers Draft are not conformant, whatever context IRI they list, with no legacy alias carried forward.

## Also

- The "context terms" editor's note in the VSC section now states what the published `v1` defines instead of predicting it.
- "DTG Predicate Vocabulary *(planned)*" becomes the [DTG VSC Predicate Registry](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-vsc-registry), which exists, in *Related Specifications* and the "where profiles live" note.
- The *Compatibility Rules* paragraph that said a versioned `@context` was not yet defined now describes the one that is.
- Document Status `0.5.0` → `0.6.0`: adding a REQUIRED property is a breaking change, released as a MINOR increment before ratification as *Compatibility Rules* allows. The version-history note no longer hard-codes a number that goes stale on every bump.
- A *Context integrity* item in Security Considerations; `issuerScope` in the two term definitions and in `CONTEXT.md`.

## Lands with

[dtgwg-vsc-registry#7](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-vsc-registry/pull/7), which publishes `contexts/v1.jsonld` with the `issuerScope` term. Per the registry's GOVERNANCE §3.1 the two land together; the digest above is over that PR's file at `a1768f7`, and any byte change there before merge invalidates the pin here.

## Test plan

- [x] All 17 JSON examples parse; every one that lists `@context` carries `issuerScope`
- [x] No dangling in-document anchors; `#context-versions` resolves
- [x] No remaining "not yet named", "not yet published", "DTG Predicate Vocabulary", `0.5.0` or `(planned)` for the registry in `spec/`
- [ ] Spec-Up-T render checked on the preview deployment

Closes #46.

title: Name the property and @context term that carry a correlation-scope declaration
body:
## Summary

WD02 says every identifier has a declared [correlation scope](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/blob/main/spec/body.md#correlation-scope) of `pairwise`, `directed` or `public`, and §Declaring scope settles *where* the declaration lives: in the credential, made by the issuer about its own identifier. What it does not settle is the property that carries it or the `@context` term for that property. The editor's note at the end of the subsection records that:

> The property that carries the declaration, and its `@context` term, are not yet named. Until they are, the requirements of this section bind a declaration that has been made and do not require one; the examples in this specification carry no declaration.

This issue tracks naming it. The decision was taken in #30's rebase (review item 4) and recorded in the #31 merge plan; neither is a place anyone will look once #31 closes.

## Why it matters

- **The section is normative in form and void in practice.** The reuse check, the ordering rule and the verifier rules all key off a declared value, and no conforming credential can carry one. An implementation today cannot declare a scope and cannot be non-conforming for failing to.
- **The examples are silent.** Every example in the specification omits the declaration, so none demonstrates the mechanism the section defines. The readability note in the introduction already says the reused member identifier is `directed`; once the property exists the examples should say so themselves.
- **Downstream text assumes it exists.** The witness `directed` minimum, the VDC delegator guidance (Privacy Consideration 10), the VMC acknowledgement item, and the common-control discussion in #9 all reason about declared scopes as if a verifier can read them.

## What has to be decided

1. **The property name**, and whether it sits at the top level of the credential or inside a structure alongside the issuer identifier. The declaration is a property of the identifier rather than of the credential (§Declaring scope, first consequence), which argues for a placement that reads that way.
2. **The `@context` term** under `https://firstperson.network/credentials/dtg/v1`.
3. **Whether the reciprocal credential in a bidirectional edge may restate the counterparty's scope** for readability, or whether each half carries only its issuer's own declaration, as the second consequence in §Declaring scope currently implies.
4. **Populate the examples** with computed declarations, and delete the editor's note.

Placement in the DID document is already ruled out and should not be reopened: `did:key` and `did:peer` numalgo-0 documents are derived from the identifier value, and those are the methods the specification recommends for the two narrow scopes.

## Migration note carried over from #30

#30's description records that Keyring Wallet fixtures (`ref-07-dtg-edge-semantics`) were built against the earlier four-value draft of #22 and declare `community`, a value that does not map onto one scope; each has to be re-decided as `pairwise` or `directed` per fixture. `rDid` is also a DIDComm wire field in the VRC reference implementation, so retiring it is a peer-compatibility change. #31 asked that the fixture owner be told before WD02 was cut. WD02 has since been cut (#44) and nothing records the outcome. Since the property named here is what those fixtures will declare, this is the natural place to confirm the fixtures have been re-decided, or to record that they have not.

title: feat(vtc-service)!: the administrator's operational verbs are signed Trust Tasks
body:
Built on #1818 (revoke-session authority, per-type size limits). First of a stack moving the admin-facing b1 verbs (inventory 2026-09-28) onto the Trust Task spine.

## What moves

The administrator's operational verbs are served by the spine (`trust_tasks::admin_tasks`) over TSP, DIDComm and HTTPS. Authority is the verified signer's ACL row, asking what the bearer extractor asked:

| task | authority |
|---|---|
| `vtc/registry/diagnostics/0.1` | Admin |
| `vtc/registry/sync-jobs/{list,retry,discard}/0.1` | Admin |
| `vtc/registry/records/list/0.1` | Admin |
| `audit/list/0.1`, `audit/verify/0.1` | unrestricted Admin (was `SuperAdminAuth`) |
| `config/{show,patch,reload,restart}/0.1` | Admin |
| `vtc/admin/invites/{list,revoke}/0.1` | Admin |
| `vtc/admin/invites/create/0.1` | unrestricted Admin; writing the invitee's unrestricted entry takes a passkey gesture bound to the document plus another admin's consent (was the session's step-up) |
| `auth/sessions/list/0.1` | own sessions, plus those of every subject the caller could withdraw (`caller_covers_target`) |
| `auth/revoke-session/0.2` | the same rule |

- `auth/sessions/list/0.1` now answers the published `{ sessions: [Session] }`, not a bare array. Note: the spec says a subject lists its own sessions; the admin view (subjects the caller covers) follows #1818's revoke authority.
- revoke-session 0.2 consumer item 7: a refused `subject` revocation is audited as the new `SessionRevocationRefused` event (producer + subject + reason). `vti-common`'s `AuditEvent` is non-exhaustive and variants land with their features, so no spec change was needed. `SessionRevoked` also records the `reason` now.
- `invites/create` answers `ttlSeconds > 86400` with its declared `ttlTooLong` rather than the schema's generic refusal.
- The console signs every one of these (dashboard, registry, audit, config, admin invites, sessions).
- Responses from the signed door are held to their `#response` schemas in the integration helper (`tests/common/signed.rs`), since the router's response-conformance layer keys on the `Trust-Task` header.

## git-ns console reads (`routes/mod.rs`)

Checked against `git-ns/view/0.5` (administrator scope), `namespace/list` and `repo/list`:

- `/v1/git-ns/drift`: covered. `view/0.5` `scope: administrator` carries `repos[].sync` (`state`, `checkedAt`, `drift`). The console reads it there; the route is removed.
- `/v1/git-ns/rights`: not covered. The view's `RightRecord` has no role-derived rows (`origin`) and no `subjectMember` / `granterDeparted`. Missing spec: a `git-ns/view` revision (or `git-ns/right/list`) carrying those.
- `/v1/git-ns/rights/issued-by-departed`: missing spec (`git-ns/right/issued-by-departed`, or a view filter).
- `/v1/git-ns/jobs`: missing spec (`git-ns/bridge/job/list`).
- `/v1/git-ns/projection`: missing spec (`git-ns/projection/show`).
- `/v1/git-ns/accounts`: view 0.5 returns only the caller's own accounts. Missing spec: `git-ns/account/list` for an administrator.
- `/v1/git-ns/activity`: missing spec (`git-ns/activity/list`, or an `audit/list` filter).

Those six routes stay.

## Routes

Removed: `GET /v1/health/diagnostics`, `GET /v1/registry/sync-jobs`, `POST /v1/registry/sync-jobs/{retry,discard}`, `GET /v1/registry/records`, `GET /v1/audit`, `GET`+`PATCH /v1/admin/config`, `POST /v1/admin/config/{reload,restart}`, `GET`+`POST /v1/admin/invites`, `DELETE /v1/admin/invites/{jti}`, `GET /v1/auth/sessions`, `DELETE /v1/auth/sessions[?did=]`, `DELETE /v1/auth/sessions/{id}`, `GET /v1/git-ns/drift`.

Kept: `GET /v1/audit/verify` (vtc-client `audit_verify`); `GET /v1/auth/whoami` (it describes the bearer session the request carries, which a document has none of, so it stays with the session surface).

## Tests

`tests/admin_verbs_spine.rs`: for every moved verb, a signed administrator is answered (signed reply, `#response` schema), an unsigned document is `proofRequired`, a signer the community doesn't know and a member are `permissionDenied`, a context admin is refused the unrestricted ones, and the bearer routes are gone. Sessions: published shape, context-admin visibility, member self-service, absent-equals-outside-authority, the audited refusal, `all`/`subject`/malformed forms. The existing suites (`admin_config`, `admin_invites`, `audit_list`, `diagnostics`, `registry_admin`, `config_identity`, `unrestricted_admin_consent`) are ported to the signed door; `session_revoke.rs` is replaced by the sessions module. Suites that used a removed route only as a sample authenticated route now use `audit/verify`.

## Found

`POST /v1/trust-tasks` sits behind the per-address unauth governor (burst 10, then one per 5 s). With the console's reads on the signed door this will throttle an operator clicking through pages. It needs a verified-signer bucket (like the VTA's anonymous-only limiter). Not changed here.

## Checks

Local results are in the comments below.

title: feat(vtc-service)!: the administrator's operational verbs are signed Trust Tasks (#1824)
body:
feat(vtc-service)!: the administrator's operational verbs are signed Trust Tasks (#1824)

The trust-registry reconciler, the audit log, the runtime configuration,
admin invites and the auth service's sessions are served by the spine
(trust_tasks::admin_tasks) on every transport, with the signer's ACL row
as authority: the role and scope questions the bearer extractors asked,
and an invite's step-up bound to the document.

auth/sessions/list/0.1 answers { sessions: [Session] } under the
revocation's authority (caller_covers_target); auth/revoke-session/0.2
is served on the spine, and a refused revocation by subject is audited
(SessionRevocationRefused). The console's drift read moves to
git-ns/view/0.5.

The bearer routes are removed, except GET /v1/audit/verify, which
vtc-client still calls.

The Identity panel offered "— none —" before the agent could honour it:
choosing it sent `did: ""` on update-did/1.0, whose schema requires a

"reassign it first" — got a validation error. trust-tasks'
update-did/1.1 (#684) makes `did` nullable, and the VTA clears on `null`.

  "Clear DID", and the panel says the DID itself is not deleted.
- task-surface.json re-synced from vta-sdk carrying update-did/1.1.
- @openvtc/trust-tasks floor ^0.21.13, the first release carrying
  update-did/1.1 — a correctness floor, since below it the import does
  not resolve.

The VTA and this cut over together: a VTA without 1.1 refuses it as an
unsupported task.

title: feat(vta/contexts/update-did): 1.1 — clear a context's DID with did: null
body:
Adds `vta/contexts/update-did/1.1`. In it `did` can be `null`, which leaves the context with no DID of its own. A string `did` must now be a valid DID.

**Why.** In 1.0 `did` has to be a non-empty string, and `vta/contexts/update` only ever sets a DID. So once a context has a DID, you can replace it but never remove it. The VTA refuses to delete a DID that a context acts as, and tells the operator to reassign it first. That leaves no way to retire a context's last DID except assigning another one they don't want. The browser console already offered "none" as a choice. It sent `did: ""`, and the schema refused it.

**Rules:**
- `null` removes the context's DID. The returned `ContextRecord` has no `did` member: absent, never `null` or `""`.
- Clearing a context that already has no DID succeeds, and only `updatedAt` changes.
- Clearing doesn't delete the DID. Its keys and log stay, so it can be assigned again or deleted.
- A context with no DID presents no identity. A consumer must refuse any operation that would sign as the context, rather than fall back to another DID it holds.
- A string `did` must match the DID Core §3.1 grammar. This is the same pattern `git-ns/_shared` uses: `^did:[a-z0-9]+:(?:(?:[A-Za-z0-9._-]|%[0-9A-Fa-f]{2})*:)*(?:[A-Za-z0-9._-]|%[0-9A-Fa-f]{2})+$`. 1.0's `minLength: 1` accepted `"did:"` and `"hello"`.

`did` is still **required**, so clearing is spelled `null`, never an omission. The pattern check tightens a constraint, which SPEC §5.2 allows as a MINOR bump on a `draft` spec. Any 1.0 request that carries a real DID is also a valid 1.1 request, and a 1.1 consumer must still accept 1.0. The response shape is unchanged. Includes `payload.invalid-examples.json`: a missing `did`, `""`, `did:`, `did:web:`, `did:Web:…`, `hello`, and a missing `id`.

**Implementations (companion branches, not yet opened):**
- VTA (`verifiable-trust-infrastructure`): serves 1.0 and 1.1 from one handler, and adds `pnm contexts update-did <id> --clear`. The DID-delete blocker now offers clearing.
- Browser console (`pnm-browser-plugin`): "none" sends `null` on 1.1.

Both need the release that carries this change.

**Checks run locally:** `npm run validate`, `npm run build`, `npm run check-bindings` (627 specs, all four languages agree), `cargo build --workspace --all-targets`, `cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs` (including `--all-features` `rejects_invalid_examples`), and the TS `npm test`. All pass. Not run locally: `go test` and `dart test`. The Rust, TS, Go and Dart bindings are regenerated in this PR.

title: Unwrap hard-wrapped prose to one line per paragraph
body:
## Summary

Joins the hard-wrapped prose in `spec/body.md` and `README.md` into one line per paragraph, matching the convention the rest of the spec already follows. No words change.

`spec/body.md` was mixed: most paragraphs were one line, but four regions were wrapped at ~80 columns by three PRs in the first week of September (#29, #30 and the ZKP dependency note): the whole *Correlation Scope* section, one block in *VMC*, the whole *VAC* section, and the *Zero-Knowledge and Selective Disclosure* editor's note. `README.md`'s new *Citing External Discussion* section was wrapped the same way while the rest of the README is not.

Rendering is unaffected either way. The reason to unwrap is editing: a change to one sentence in a wrapped paragraph rewraps every line after it, so the diff and `git blame` show the whole paragraph as changed. The companion spec PR for #46 rewrites *Declaring scope* and the *Correlation Scope* opener, both in the wrapped region, so this lands first to keep that diff readable.

## What was joined

Plain paragraphs, blockquote paragraphs (`> `), and list items whose continuation lines were indented. Fenced code, tables, headings and a bare `>` paragraph break are untouched.

## Test plan

- [x] Whitespace-normalized content of both files is byte-identical before and after (blockquote markers stripped)
- [x] Counts of code fences, headings, table rows and list items are unchanged in both files
- [x] No prose line remains that is 50–95 characters and followed by a continuation line

title: feat(sender-delegation): a signer names the one sender that may carry its documents
body:
Stacked on #642 (a consumer may require a proof over DIDComm). Draft: a spec to agree on before anyone implements it. Nothing here is released.

## Why

The VTA, the VTC (verifiable-trust-infrastructure #1739) and the did-hosting RP (affinidi-webvh-service #213) act on a DIDComm or TSP document only when its proven signer **is** the transport sender. That rule stays. It leaves no route for a signer that cannot send.

The case that needs one: a browser wallet signing in to an RP as a per-site persona. The persona's keys, key agreement included, are held by its VTA and never released. The VTA can sign as the persona (`vault/sign-trust-task`). It cannot be the DIDComm or TSP sender of the wallet's message. The wallet can send, but only as itself. Today the wallet refuses persona sign-in over DIDComm/TSP and uses REST (`vault/proxy-login`).

## What

`sender-delegation/0.1` is a signed Trust Task document that is never dispatched. The signer issues it to name:

- one delegate: the transport sender allowed to carry the documents;
- one consumer (`recipient`);
- the `id` of each covered document (1 to 16);
- a lifetime of at most 300 seconds (`expiresAt` is REQUIRED).

Its proof is `authentication`, by a key under the signer's `authentication`. It stands in for the transport authentication the signer cannot perform.

A consumer that accepts one:

- still verifies and authorizes each covered document as its own `issuer`. The delegate gains no authority;
- keys replay protection on the document's `issuer` and `id`;
- routes responses to the delegate;
- SHOULD decline delegation for approvals and consent decisions.

Signer requirements: the maintainer signs a delegation only behind the same gates as the covered documents, and only for a delegate the requester is entitled to name.

Privacy: a producer names a **pairwise** delegate for a pairwise signer. Delegating every persona to the wallet's long-lived DID would link the personas at every consumer.

Carriage:

| Binding | Where |
|---|---|
| DIDComm 0.2 §5.1 | a `sender-delegation` attachment on the envelope message |
| TSP 0.1 §5.5 | a `senderDelegation` member of the envelope. Refused in non-nested routed mode, where the authenticated sender is the last hop. |

Generated Rust, TypeScript, Go and Dart bindings are included.

## What an implementation would need (not in this PR)

- **VTI (VTA):**
  - `vault/sign-trust-task` must sign a persona's operational documents under `authentication`, with the persona key listed under `authentication`. It pins `assertionMethod` today, so the RP refuses a persona-signed `auth/authenticate` even before delegation comes into it. That means a `0.3` with a purpose, or the maintainer choosing it by type.
  - A way to sign a `sender-delegation/0.1` behind the same gates, restricted to a delegate the caller controls.
- **affinidi-webvh-service (and the VTA/VTC as consumers):** verify the delegation per the consumer requirements in `verify_sender_bound`, before accepting signer ≠ sender. Take it from the DIDComm attachment or the TSP envelope member. Route the reply to the delegate.
- **Wallet:** mint a pairwise transport identity per persona and RP, reachable through its mediator.

## Checks

- `npm run build`: 522 specs validated.
- `npm run check-bindings`: all agree.
- `cargo run -p trust-tasks-codegen && cargo fmt --all` and `npm run build-ts-bindings`: no drift.

title: feat(spec): a specification may declare its own document size bound
body:
Adds **Specification Requirements item 21 — Document size bound (where declared)**, and one sentence in **Parser Hardening** pointing at it.

## Why

Parser Hardening asks a consumer to bound the body it parses at "a body-size limit appropriate to the Trust Task specification's payload", and item 19 already observes that a transport-layer limit is the wrong place to choose a number — one figure covers every task a consumer implements. Nothing let a specification state its limit, so a consumer serving many tasks has had two choices, both wrong: a limit sized for the small tasks (which refuses a task legitimately carrying a JSON Schema, a DID log or a range of a file), or one sized for the largest (which opens every other task to bodies it has no use for).

The concrete case: a Verifiable Trust Community serves its whole Trust Task surface behind a 64 KiB cap. Registering a credential schema, and moving website content, do not fit it, and raising the cap for everything to fit them is the fix we want to avoid.

## What

- A specification **MAY** declare, per variant (request, response, or both), the largest serialized document — UTF-8 JSON as received, `proof` included, transport envelope excluded — a consumer serving the task is expected to accept; it **SHOULD** where its payload can carry bulk content.
- Two-sided: a consumer **MUST NOT** refuse a document within the bound on grounds of size alone, and **SHOULD** refuse a larger one with `malformedRequest` (no dedicated §8.3 code; the document does not conform to its specification), before parsing where it can learn the `type` first.
- Variants are independent. No declaration → Parser Hardening's consumer limit applies exactly as today. Additive: every existing specification and document is unaffected.
- A bound is not a licence for huge documents: content larger than a single document can carry moves by a chunked transfer whose chunk task declares its own bound.

## Registry half

trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf adds the `maxDocumentBytes` front-matter member, the generated `Payload::MAX_DOCUMENT_BYTES` / `schema_index::max_document_bytes_for` in Rust, and a check-bindings comparison (PR linked from there). It can merge ahead of this text: the member is optional and descriptive of what this item states.

title: vti-secrets: encrypted-at-rest file backend for hosts without an OS keychain
body:
## Problem

`vti-secrets` has no secure local option for a host without an OS credential store. On a headless Linux server with no Secret Service (no gnome-keyring, KWallet or KeePassXC, and no D-Bus session), the only local backend is `plaintext`, which keeps the secret in clear text. `vta-sdk::secure_store`'s `file` store is also plaintext at 0600.

Such a host must use a remote backend (Vault, Kubernetes, AWS, GCP or Azure) or a TEE. That is right for production, but a small single-host deployment has no secure option at all.

affinidi-webvh-service now takes every backend from `vti-secrets`, and refuses at setup on such a host with the list of secure backends. It does not implement its own crypto. This issue asks for the missing backend in `vti-secrets`, so every consumer (VTA, VTC, webvh, vti-message-bridge) gets it at once.

## Proposal: an encrypted-at-rest file backend (`encrypted_file`)

- The file holds an AEAD envelope: a versioned header, a KDF or sealing descriptor, a nonce, and ciphertext. Use XChaCha20-Poly1305 or AES-256-GCM, with the header as associated data. Write it at 0600 via `vti_common::secure_file`, and write it atomically.
- The key-encryption key comes from one of these, chosen explicitly:
  1. **TPM 2.0 sealed** (Linux, `tss-esapi`): a KEK sealed to the TPM, optionally bound to PCRs. This gives an unattended boot without a passphrase.
  2. **systemd-creds** / `CREDENTIALS_DIRECTORY`: the host encrypts the credential (TPM or host key), and the service reads the KEK from its credential directory. This is thin, and it is how systemd is meant to be used.
  3. **Passphrase via Argon2id**: store the salt and parameters in the header (m ≥ 64 MiB, t ≥ 3). The passphrase comes from a file or a systemd credential, never from an environment variable or the config.
  4. **Cloud KMS envelope** (optional): a data key wrapped by AWS, GCP or Azure KMS, for hosts that have KMS but not Secrets Manager.
- It fails closed: a wrong key, a bad tag or an unknown version is an error, never "no secret".
- `SecretBackend::EncryptedFile` is added to `SecretsConfig`, with the new fields documented. Implicit resolution never picks it. It is always explicit.
- Tests cover a round trip per KEK source that CI can run (passphrase, systemd-creds with a test key), tamper detection, and a wrong passphrase.

## Consumers

When it ships, webvh would make it the recommended backend for a headless host with no keychain, with the operator's explicit selection.

title: ci: run the pipeline in tiers, and split Feature combos into five parallel groups
body:
## What

Restructures `.github/workflows/ci.yml` into three tiers and splits the `Feature combos` job, which was the critical path, into five parallel groups. No step's command changes, and nothing new is cached.

### Tiers

| Tier | Jobs | Gate |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | Format, lockfile self-pins, lockfile resolves, cargo-deny, authorization-context types, `affects` | none |
| 1 | Check, Clippy, Test (workspace), Test (VTC), Test (VTC admin UI) | `needs:` all of tier 0 (the default `success()`), plus the existing `affects` filters |
| 2 | Feature combos (5 groups), Feature combos (all-features), Mobile build, Enclave build, Enclave proxy, MSRV | `needs:` every tier-1 job; `if: ${{ !cancelled() && !failure() && <affects gate> }}` |

The semver report and the release bump guard stay outside the tiers.

**Why tier 2 isn't on the default condition.** A job whose `if` has no status function gets an implicit `success()`, and that is false when *any* job it needs was **skipped**. Tier-1 jobs are skipped by their filters all the time (a vta-only PR skips both VTC jobs), so the default would quietly drop tier 2 as well. At job level, `failure()` is true if any **ancestor** failed. So a failed tier-0 job still stops tier 2, even though the tier-1 jobs in between were skipped rather than failed.

I checked all four cases against GitHub on a throwaway workflow, then deleted the branch:

| Case | Expected | Got |
|---|---|---|
| one tier-1 job ok, one skipped | runs | success |
| one tier-1 job failed | skipped | skipped |
| tier-0 ancestor failed, tier-1 job skipped because of it | skipped | skipped |
| control: default condition with a skipped need | skipped (the bug) | skipped |

### Feature combos groups

Expected times are the sum of each group's step times on recent PR runs. Each group also has about 0.5 min of setup.

| Job | Steps | Expected |
|---|---|---|
| `Feature combos (vta-service builds)` | tee+webvh, didcomm w/o webvh, rest only, tsp w/o didcomm, aws, azure, without tsp | ~11 min |
| `Feature combos (vta-service tests)` | setup wizard under extra backends, TEE Mode B carve-out | ~10.5 min |
| `Feature combos (vta-sdk, vta-tee)` | attest-verify, client+sealed-transfer, vetting, all-features (test), vta-tee tenant-overlay | ~10.5 min |
| `Feature combos (vti-rooms)` | member half (clippy), member half on wasm32, vti-rooms-wasm artifact | ~6.5 min |
| `Feature combos (mediator-backed)` | room-host didcomm+tsp, vta-service transport harness, VTC TSP receive, VTC registry round trip | ~9 min |

- Steps are grouped so that a group's steps share their dependency builds.
- Every step's name, `run`, `env` and comment is moved verbatim. I checked this mechanically: the multiset of old lines and the parsed `(name, run, env)` of all 21 steps are identical.
- Two comments pointed at a step that now lives in another group. Each gets a one-line bridging note.
- The shared preamble (system packages, toolchain, registry cache) is a local composite action, `.github/actions/feature-combos-setup`.
- All five groups share **one** registry cache key, `cargo-features-groups-`. The registry is content-addressed, so sharing it is safe, and it keeps the cache count the same as before. `-groups-` is not a prefix of `-all-`, so neither key restores the other's cache.

### Gates

- **Each group has its own `affects` output**, taken from its own `-p` flags. `scripts/ci-feature-combo-pkgs.sh <job-key>` reads one group and keeps the `--workspace` guard. `--list` enumerates the groups and applies the guard to each; `affects` runs it, so a group added later is guarded too.
- **MSRV** runs on a PR only when a manifest, the lockfile, `rust-toolchain`, `.cargo/` or ci.yml changes. This uses a new `ci-affects.sh --toolchain` mode that reuses the script's base resolution and fail-safes. Pushes to main and nightly still run everything.
  - The trade is written into the workflow: a PR whose *source* uses a feature newer than `rust-version` is no longer caught on the PR. The push to main reports it instead.

### Local validation

- `ruby -ryaml` parses the workflow; `check-workflow-action-pins.sh` passes.
- The union of the five groups' packages equals the old job's package set.
- I ran `ci-affects.sh` against temporary commits for these changes: docs only, vti-rooms source, vta-sdk source, vtc-service source, pnm-cli source, a member `Cargo.toml`, and `.cargo/`. Each group and MSRV answered as intended. For example, a vtc-service change runs only the mediator-backed group, and a pnm-cli `Cargo.toml` change runs MSRV and no feature group.

### Not done: dependency-artifact caching

This needs a third-party action (for example `Swatinem/rust-cache`), and installing one needs org approval, so this PR doesn't add it. The estimates below are for deciding whether to ask.

**What it would gain.** `rust-cache` caches `target/`, but strips workspace-member artifacts before saving. Only third-party dependencies are restored, so the #1133 stale path-dependency bug can't happen, and the key includes the toolchain and the job's rustc flags.

- Today every job compiles every dependency cold. That is most of the first cargo step in each job (for example vta-service tee+webvh at ~3.3 min), and likely a third to half of Test (workspace)'s ~16 min.
- My estimate is about 2-6 min saved per compile job, and about 5-8 min off the wall clock because it shortens both tier 1 and tier 2.

**What it would cost.** A deps-only `target/` with `line-tables-only` debuginfo is still about 0.5-1.5 GB compressed per feature set. There are about 12 compile jobs, and this PR splits Feature combos into five.

- One cache per job would be roughly 6-15 GB, against a 10 GB allowance that is already full with 32 registry caches.
- The allowance evicts least-recently-used entries, so the caches would evict each other and mostly miss. #891 is the one-oversized-cache case; this would be the same problem across every job.

**What might fit.** Cache dependency builds for the tier-1 critical path only: Test (workspace), Test (VTC) and Clippy.

- Save only from `main` (`save-if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'`), and let PRs restore only.
- Give the feature groups registry-only caches, as today, and drop per-job registry caches that duplicate one another.
- That is about 3-4 GB, and it needs the existing registry caches to shrink to make room.

title: feat(trust-tasks): advertise the acceptance window over trust-task-discovery 0.3 (VTI-TRN-047)
body:
Both VTI node types refuse a Trust Task document more than ten minutes (plus 60 s of skew) past its `issuedAt` (VTI-OPS-024). `trust-task-discovery/0.3` (trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#677, released in trust-tasks-rs 0.24.4) lets a responder state that window, so a producer holding a document knows when to issue a new attempt instead of delivering something that will be refused. This PR implements the responder half on both nodes (VTI-TRN-047) and routes the push engine's staleness decisions through the same value. It does **not** yet make the push engine read a recipient's advertised window (VTI-TRN-045). The reasons are set out below.

## What changes

- **Bump.** The trust-tasks-rs floor goes from 0.24.2 to 0.24.4, and trust-tasks-capability-client, pinned alongside it, goes to 0.24.4. Only those two lockfile entries move. No crate `version =` is edited.
- **One window value** (`vti_common::trust_task::acceptance`). `VTI_ACCEPTANCE_WINDOW` is `ACCEPTANCE_WINDOW` + `DEFAULT_SKEW`. The same value is:
  - applied by both consumers: `freshness_policy()` is now `VTI_ACCEPTANCE_WINDOW.freshness_policy().requiring_issued_at()`;
  - advertised by both responders: `advertised()` gives whole seconds, rounded **down** so the advertisement is never wider than what is applied. Where the schema cannot state the window it returns `None`;
  - read by the push engine: `past_max_age` for the SHOULD NOT bound and `refuses` for the MUST NOT bound.

  So VTI-TRN-047 holds by construction rather than by keeping two numbers equal by hand.
- **Shared responder** (`vti_common::trust_task::discovery`). It holds the pattern grammar (moved from the VTA) and the 0.1 and 0.3 response builders, so the VTA and the VTC answer the same way. The window goes at response level only. Each node applies one window to everything it dispatches, so repeating it on every entry would add nothing but fingerprint (discovery 0.3, *Correlation*).
- **VTA.** It serves `trust-task-discovery/0.3` alongside 0.1 and answers each in the version it was asked.
  - The 0.1 `frameworkVersion` changes from `"0.2"` to `"0.6"`. `"0.2"` was a stale copy of the framework crate's default, which is now 0.6.0. Without the change, one responder would name two framework releases.
- **VTC.** It serves `trust-task-discovery/0.3`; it did not serve discovery at all before.
  - Identified callers only, as on the VTA.
  - It lists the routing table itself: `DISPATCHED_URIS` plus the rooms and git-ns registrations.
  - The edits to `trust_tasks/mod.rs` are kept to four lines (`mod discovery;`, one match arm, one `DISPATCHED_URIS` entry, one census entry) to limit conflicts with #1809.
- **Registrations.**
  - `TASK_TRUST_TASK_DISCOVERY_0_3` in `vta_sdk::trust_tasks`, taken from the generated `TYPE_URI`, and added to its task list.
  - `ReadOnly` in `vta_sdk::retry_safety`.
  - The VTA dispatch table, plus a conformance witness whose response is produced by the real builder rather than written as a literal.
  - The VTC `DISPATCHED_URIS` and its declared-URI census.
  - A row in `trust-task-uri-registry.md`.
  - The URI is authenticated-only on both nodes, so it is not in `PUBLIC_URIS`.

## Why the push engine does not look up the recipient's window

VTI-TRN-045's first tier is "the recipient's window, from its authenticated discovery response". For the push engine that tier is disproportionate today:

- **No request/reply path.** A lookup is a request/reply exchange. Every push is one-way, and neither node gives the engine a way to match a reply to its request. The VTC has one for git-ns bridges, but it is tied to that client.
- **No recipient would answer.** The recipients are approvers' devices, members' wallets and requesters. None of them serves `trust-task-discovery`, so every lookup would time out and fall back to the constant anyway.
- **Wrong moment.** The window only matters for a document the engine is *holding* — the recipient is offline, or a mediator is refusing hops. That is exactly when a lookup cannot be answered.
- **No refusal signal.** The engine never sees an `expired` refusal. A REST attempt reports only its HTTP status, and a DIDComm or TSP reply goes to the node's inbound router. So 0.3's rule 7 (re-ask after an unexpected refusal) would have nothing to trigger it.

The engine therefore applies VTI-TRN-045's last tier, the documented constant, to every recipient. That constant is now the same value both nodes advertise. This is written up in the engine's module docs (*Which window*) and in `docs/05-design-notes/retry-and-idempotency.md` §5a. If a recipient ever advertises a window, the place to plug it in is the engine's two predicates.

## Tests

- `vti_trn_047_the_advertised_window_is_the_applied_window` (VTA and VTC): reads the window back out of the node's own discovery 0.3 answer and compares it with the spine's `freshness_policy()`.
- `vti_trn_047_a_document_at_the_advertised_edge_is_accepted_and_one_past_it_refused` (VTA and VTC): the same property checked at the boundary, so an advertisement that is too wide and one that is too narrow each fail.
- `vti_trn_047_discovery_0_3_advertises_the_window_the_vta_enforces` (VTA, `api_integration`): end to end over `/api/trust-tasks`. It checks that the answer comes back in 0.3, then sends documents just outside the advertised window (refused as `expired`) and just inside it (accepted).
- VTC: the answer lists every routed URI and is schema-valid; an unidentified caller is refused; more than 16 patterns is `malformedRequest`.
- vti-common:
  - the window is advertised exactly;
  - a fractional window is never advertised wider than it is;
  - a window the schema cannot state is not advertised;
  - `vti_trn_045_the_producer_predicates_agree_with_the_consumer_policy`;
  - both responses are schema-valid;
  - the pattern-grammar tests, moved from the VTA.

## Checks run locally

- `cargo fmt --all -- --check`: clean.
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`: clean.
- The three vta-service reduced-feature clippy runs (`rest`, `setup,keyring,rest,tsp,cli-synthesis`, `setup,keyring,rest,didcomm,cli-synthesis`): clean.

title: feat(trust-tasks): advertise the acceptance window over trust-task-discovery 0.3 (VTI-TRN-047) (#1817)
body:
feat(trust-tasks): advertise the acceptance window over trust-task-discovery 0.3 (VTI-TRN-047) (#1817)

Both VTI node types refuse a document more than ten minutes (plus 60 s of
skew) past its issuedAt (VTI-OPS-024). A sender holding a document before
delivery has to know that window to decide when to issue a new attempt
instead, and until now the only way to know it was to share the constant.
trust-task-discovery/0.3 (trust-tasks #677, trust-tasks-rs 0.24.4) lets a
responder state it.

- Raise the trust-tasks-rs floor to 0.24.4, the first release carrying
  discovery 0.3, and trust-tasks-capability-client with it. Only those two
  lockfile entries move.
- vti-common: `trust_task::acceptance::AcceptanceWindow` and
  `VTI_ACCEPTANCE_WINDOW` (ACCEPTANCE_WINDOW + DEFAULT_SKEW). This is the one
  value the consumers apply (`freshness_policy()`), the responders advertise
  (`advertised()`, rounded down so it is never wider, VTI-TRN-047), and the
  push engine judges staleness by (`past_max_age`, `refuses`).
  `trust_task::discovery` has the pattern grammar and the 0.1/0.3 response
  builders, so both nodes answer the same way.
- VTA: serves trust-task-discovery/0.3 next to 0.1, answering each in the
  version it was asked. The window goes at response level, since the VTA
  applies one window to everything it dispatches. The 0.1 frameworkVersion was
  "0.2", a stale copy of the framework crate's default. It is now "0.6",
  the MAJOR.MINOR of the 0.6.0 that 0.3 writes, so one responder no longer
  names two framework releases.
- VTC: serves trust-task-discovery/0.3 for the first time. It answers
  identified callers only, as the VTA does, and lists the routing table itself
  (DISPATCHED_URIS plus the rooms and git-ns registrations).
- Registrations: TASK_TRUST_TASK_DISCOVERY_0_3 in vta_sdk::trust_tasks and
  its task list, ReadOnly in retry_safety, the VTA dispatch table and its
  conformance witness (built from the real builder, not a literal), and the
  VTC DISPATCHED_URIS and its declared-URI census.
- Push engine (VTI-TRN-045): its two staleness predicates now read
  VTI_ACCEPTANCE_WINDOW, the same value the nodes advertise, where before
  they combined two separate constants. It still reads no advertised window.
  A lookup would be a request/reply exchange, and every push is one-way.
  None of the recipients (approvers' devices, wallets, requesters) serves
  discovery. The window only matters when the recipient cannot answer. The
  engine never sees an `expired` refusal, so 0.3's "re-ask after an
  unexpected refusal" would have no trigger. The module docs and
  docs/05-design-notes/retry-and-idempotency.md say so. What remains of the
  spec's divergence F.3 is the producer side only.

Tests: vti_trn_047_* on each node read the window back out of the node's own
discovery answer. They check it against the spine's freshness_policy, both by
value and at the boundary: accepted at the advertised edge, refused one
second past it. An end-to-end VTA test sends a 0.3 query over
/api/trust-tasks, then sends documents just outside and just inside the
advertised window and checks the service refuses (`expired`) or accepts
them. vti-common unit tests cover rounding, unstatable windows, schema
validity of both responses, and that the producer predicates agree with the
consumer policy at the boundary.

title: fix(vtc-service): session revocation and document size limits after #1808 review
body:
Follow-up to #1808 (squash-merged). These are fixes from its security review.

## Fixes

**1. Session revocation now takes authority over the subject, not just the admin role.** `auth/revoke-session/0.2` is on `DELETE /v1/auth/sessions[/{id}|?did=]`.
- **By session id.** `DELETE /auth/sessions/{id}` used to let any `admin` role revoke any session. That included a context admin revoking an unrestricted admin's session. It also answered 404 for an unknown id and 403 for someone else's session, which revealed whether a session existed. The 0.2 spec forbids both.
  - The VTC now asks the question `acl/revoke` asks, through `caller_covers_target`. You may always end your own sessions. An unrestricted admin may end anyone's. A context admin may end only the sessions of a subject whose every context it administers.
  - Three cases now get the same answer, `200 {revokedCount: 0}`, which is the spec's RECOMMENDED form and makes a retry succeed:
    - the session is absent;
    - it was already revoked;
    - it is outside the caller's authority.
- **By subject.** `DELETE /auth/sessions?did=` used to accept any overlapping context. So an admin of `a` could sign out an admin of `[a, b]`. It now uses the same rule and refuses with 403 when the caller lacks authority, whether or not the subject has sessions.
- The console's session revoke reads `revokedCount` and says "already gone" when it is 0.
- New tests are in `tests/session_revoke.rs`.

**2. Raised size limits apply only to types this node serves.** `policy/upsert/0.2` (192 KiB) and `did/register/0.1` (1 MiB) are in `DECLARED`, but neither is in `DISPATCHED_URIS`. The spine verifies the proof before it refuses an unrouted type. Verifying means canonicalising the whole document and resolving the signer's DID.
- So #1808 let an unauthenticated caller claim `policy/upsert` and have up to 1 MiB canonicalised and a DID resolved before the refusal. Before #1808 the limit was 64 KiB. Nothing was gained from the raise, because nothing served those types.
- A declared limit is now in force only while its type is dispatched. The HTTPS door's cap is `largest_max_document_bytes()`, taken over the served types, so it is 64 KiB today. Both rise on their own when those tasks land on the spine.

**3. The size refusal no longer echoes a huge `type` back.** A `type` longer than 256 characters is not named in the reason.

**Also:**
- Unit tests for a `type` placed late in the document, a nested `type`, and a duplicated `type`.
- A spine-level test showing that REST, DIDComm and TSP all meet the same refusal.
- The OpenAPI snapshot and `wire.ts` are regenerated.
- Two stale comments are fixed: in RegistryPreview, and on the ACL parity test.

## Review findings for #1808 that did not need a fix
- **Removed routes.** No caller is left in the console, vtc-client, cnm or the tests. Every signed replacement enforces the REST gate it replaced:
  - ACL: list, show and grant need manage; change-role and revoke need admin. Grant and promotion to admin need a bound gesture, and unrestricted also needs consent.
  - Profile and endorsement-type writes need an admin, because `resolve_auth_role` maps only `Admin`.
  - Purge needs a super-admin.
  - Self-remove, personhood and status are bound to the holder.
- **Admin grant and promotion.** The mark is keyed on `(actor DID, sha256(type, payload))`. It is single-use (removed before it is honoured) and has a TTL. Only the actor's own passkeys can record it.
  - An approval therefore covers only that operation, by that admin. It can't be reused on another grant.
  - Self-promotion is refused by the shared `change_role_inner`.
  - `postSignedWithStepUp` re-sends the byte-identical `ApiError.document`.
- **Dead code.** The submit, status and admin-manifest handlers and `routes/step_up_passkeys.rs` were never mounted on main. `join-requests/status/0.1` is served on the spine, bound to the holder.
- **Kept `credential-exchange/request`.** It is correct as it is. For the HTTPS binding to answer with the credential in its reply, `credential-exchange/request/0.1` would need a `#response` that carries the `issue` payload. Today the spec defines none, and SPEC §4.4.2 limits the reply to an empty courtesy ack. The alternative is an HTTPS binding rule that lets the next in-thread task be returned synchronously. Either one needs a spec change first. Report only.

## Left open
- `GET /auth/sessions` answers a bare array, which does not conform to `sessions/list/0.1` (already noted in #1808).
- revoke-session 0.2 item 7 asks for refusals of the `subject` form to be audited. They are logged, not audited, because that needs a new audit event.

## Local run
- `cargo test -p vtc-service` (lib and integration), `vtc-client`, `cnm-cli`: pass.
- admin-ui lint and vitest (498): pass.
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -D warnings` and `cargo fmt --check`: clean.

title: trust-tasks-rs-v0.24.5
body:
### Added

- **vtc/website**: Website content moves as a chunked Trust Task transfer ([#682](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/682))

Replaces the raw-byte REST routes (GET/PUT /website/files/{path}, POST /website/deploy) with Trust Tasks, modelled on backup/* and reusing vta/_shared/0.1/backup-transfer's chunk vocabulary:

  - vtc/website/upload/begin — commits the target (a file at a path, with optional ifMatch, or a whole-site bundle), total size, whole-content SHA-256 and every chunk digest before any byte moves.
  - vtc/website/upload/chunk — one chunk of up to 256 KiB, checked against the manifest on arrival; idempotent.
  - vtc/website/upload/commit — reassembles and verifies the SHA-256; writes a file target atomically, or stages a bundle.
  - vtc/website/upload/abort — discards an open or staged upload.
  - vtc/website/deploy — publishes a staged bundle (live replace, or a new managed generation with pruning).
  - vtc/website/files/show — ranged reads of up to 256 KiB with the whole-file etag.

  begin, chunk and files/show declare maxDocumentBytes (256 KiB, 352 KiB, 352 KiB response), so the community's 64 KiB default is not raised for every other task. Shared component vtc/_shared/0.1/website-transfer. Bindings regenerated for Rust, TypeScript, Go and Dart.

- **vtc**: Trust Tasks for the community's REST-only admin surfaces ([#680](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/680))

* feat(vtc): Trust Tasks for the community's REST-only admin surfaces

  Specifies, at 0.1, the VTC operations that existed only as REST routes, so each can be served as a sender-bound signed Trust Task over TSP, DIDComm or HTTPS:

  - auth/signing-key/{enroll,list,revoke} — delegated signing keys (the admin console's non-extractable browser key). Enrolment is signed by the key being enrolled (proof of possession) and names the identity it acts for; control of that identity is established by separate authority evidence, which the reference implementation takes as an operation-bound passkey step-up.
  - vtc/community/{branding,requested-attributes,join-discovery}/{show,update}
  - vtc/schemas/{register,list,show,delete} and vtc/schemas/accepts/{register,list,show,delete} — register and show declare maxDocumentBytes, since a credential schema exceeds the 64 KiB default.
  - vtc/vetting/vetters/grants/list, vtc/vetting/auto-grant/{show,update}, vtc/vetting/revocations/list
  - vtc/relationships/{suspend,restore} — the edge issuer's own proof replaces the REST pop authorization.
  - vtc/join-requests/vetting/show, and vtc/join-requests/query — its own task rather than credential-exchange/*, because an administrator instructs the verifier, which alone can author the query's challenge.
  - vtc/rooms/list — under vtc/, not rooms/, because it is authorized by host ACL and rooms invariant I5 forbids that for any rooms/* task.

  Shared components: auth/_shared/0.1/signing-key and vtc/_shared/0.1/{community-presentation,schema-registry,vetting-auto-grant,relationship-lifecycle}. Relationship persona attach/detach stays out, blocked on dtgwg-cred-spec#9. Bindings regenerated for Rust, TypeScript, Go and Dart.

- **spec-meta**: A specification declares its own maximum document size ([#679](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/679))

Adds an optional front-matter member, maxDocumentBytes { request?, response?, rationale }, stating the largest serialized Trust Task document (proof included, transport envelope excluded) of each variant that a consumer serving the task must not refuse on grounds of size alone, and should refuse beyond with malformedRequest.

  SPEC §12.4 already tells a consumer to bound what it parses at "a body-size limit appropriate to the Trust Task specification's payload", and §7.3 item 19 notes that a transport-layer limit is the wrong place to pick the number; until now no specification could say what it was. A consumer serving many tasks therefore applied one blanket cap sized for the small ones, and a task that legitimately carries a JSON Schema or a chunk of a file was refused. This lets the bound be stated, and enforced, per type.

  - specs/spec.meta.schema.json: the member (at least one variant, 1 KiB to 16 MiB; larger content belongs in a chunked transfer).
  - trust-tasks-codegen: reads it and emits Payload::MAX_DOCUMENT_BYTES on the request and response impls, plus schema_index::max_document_bytes_for(type_uri) for a dispatcher that learns the type before parsing. An absent variant never inherits the other's bound.
  - trust-tasks-rs: the trait constant, defaulting to None.
  - check-bindings: holds Rust's constants to the front matter, re-derived independently.
  - CONTRIBUTING-SPECS: when and how to declare it.

  Rust only for now, like ERROR_CODES; the TypeScript, Go and Dart generators do not emit it yet. The framework text (a §7.3 item) is proposed in the canonical specification repository; this is the registry's half.



### Specifications

- **webvh/witness/sign**: Let a witness sign the entry that deactivates a DID ([#681](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/681))

body:
The Release PR for every package in this repo. **Merging this is the release.**

| Package | Registry | Version | Bump |
|---|---|---|---|
| `trust-tasks` | crates.io | `0.24.4` → `0.24.5` | patch |
| `trust-tasks-capability-client` | crates.io | `0.24.4` → `0.24.5` | patch |
| `trust-tasks-didcomm` | crates.io | `0.24.4` → `0.24.5` | patch |
| `trust-tasks-didcomm-v1` | crates.io | `0.24.4` → `0.24.5` | patch |
| `trust-tasks-https` | crates.io | `0.24.4` → `0.24.5` | patch |
| `trust-tasks-proof` | crates.io | `0.24.4` → `0.24.5` | patch |
| `trust-tasks-rs` | crates.io | `0.24.4` → `0.24.5` | patch |
| `trust-tasks-tsp` | crates.io | `0.24.4` → `0.24.5` | patch |
| `@openvtc/trust-tasks` | npm | `0.21.11` → `0.21.12` | patch |
| `github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/trust-tasks-go` | Go (tag `trust-tasks-go/v0.3.12`) | `0.3.11` → `0.3.12` | patch |
| `trust_tasks` | pub.dev | `0.3.11` → `0.3.12` | patch |

What merging does, per registry (all in `publish.yml`, each keyed on "this
version is not published yet"):

- **crates.io** — `release-plz-release` tags `<crate>-v<version>`, publishes in
  dependency order and creates a GitHub Release per crate. Bump levels come from
  `cargo-semver-checks`.
- **npm** — `publish-npm` publishes with OIDC provenance and tags
  `<prefix>-v<version>`.
- **Go** — `publish-go` builds, vets and tests, then pushes the tag, which *is*
  the publication. **Irreversible**: proxy.golang.org never forgets a tag.
- **pub.dev** — `tag-dart` verifies against the *published* core and pushes the
  tag; `publish-dart.yml` publishes from it.

The npm, Go and Dart bumps are only as accurate as the commit subjects — nothing
checks their APIs the way `cargo-semver-checks` checks the crates. Look for a
missing `!` before merging.

This branch is regenerated from `main` on every push, so do not commit to it —
edits are force-pushed away. See RELEASING.md.

title: feat(vtc-service)!: the console's signed calls have no bearer twins
body:
Batch 1 of "VTC remote APIs are Trust Tasks only" (inventory `vtc-remote-api-inventory-2026-09-28`, class (a)). The admin console now signs every one of these verbs with its console key; the REST twins it and `vtc-client` no longer need are gone. Test deployments only: no compat shims.

## Removed REST routes (signed document only, at `POST /v1/trust-tasks` or any transport the VTC serves)

- `GET /v1/acl`, `POST /v1/acl`, `GET/PATCH/DELETE /v1/acl/{did}` (`acl/{list,grant,show,change-role,revoke}/0.1`)
- `PUT /v1/community/profile` (`vtc/community/profile/update/0.1`); the GET stays
- `DELETE /v1/members/{did}/purge` (`vtc/members/purge/0.1`)
- `DELETE /v1/members/me` (`vtc/members/self-remove/0.1`)
- `POST /v1/members/{did}/personhood/challenge`, `POST /v1/members/{did}/personhood` (`vtc/members/personhood/{challenge,assert}/0.1`); the revoke stays
- `POST /v1/endorsement-types`, `DELETE /v1/endorsement-types/{type_uri}` (`vtc/endorsement-types/{register,delete}/0.1`); the listing stays
- `POST /v1/vetting/vetters/list` (`vtc/vetting/vetters/list/0.1`)
- `GET /v1/join-requests/manifest`, the admin 0.2 read (`vtc/join-requests/manifest/0.2`)

## Kept, pending the vtc-client / cnm move (e2)

`vtc-client` still calls these over REST: as its fallback when it holds no signing key, or bearer-only. Each goes once the client sends it signed.

- `POST /v1/join-requests/{id}/decide` (`approve_join` / `reject_join`)
- `GET /v1/members/{did}/credentials` (`member_credentials`)
- `PATCH /v1/members/{did}` (`update_member_extensions`)
- `DELETE /v1/members/{did}` (`remove_member`)
- `POST /v1/vetting/vetters`, `POST /v1/vetting/vetters/show` (`grant_vetter`, `show_vetter`, used by cnm)
- `POST /v1/vetting/vetters/{memberDid}/resend` (`resend_vetter_grant`). The console also keeps this route: the signed `resend` is a vetter's request for their own credential, so an admin resending a member's grant has no signed twin yet.

Also kept: `POST /v1/credential-exchange/request`. It isn't really a twin. The spine answers `credential-exchange/request` by pushing the `issue` to the holder's messaging endpoint, so this HTTPS route is the only path for a holder with no messaging service (an invitee who scanned an offer). It can go once the spine answers that request inline over HTTPS.

## Admin console

- `signedOrBearer` is gone. Member credentials, update, admin-remove and purge, the endorsement-type writes, the join decision, the profile edit, naming a vetter, the vetter listing, the join manifest and the whole ACL (plugin, member promotion, name book) are signed documents. A browser that cannot sign is told to enable console signing.
- ACL grant and promotion to admin go through the operation-bound passkey gesture (`lib/signed-act.ts`): the operator confirms in a dialog, the gesture is recorded against that one act, and the identical signed document is sent again.
- The response types still come from the daemon. The signed-only verbs' schemas are published in the OpenAPI components (`routes::ApiDoc`), as the git-ns reads' already are.

## Bindings

- `DELETE /v1/auth/sessions?did=` was bound to `auth/sessions/list/0.1`. It is now `auth/revoke-session/0.2` (its `subject` form) and answers `{ revokedCount }`.
- `DELETE /v1/auth/sessions/{id}` is now `auth/revoke-session/0.2` too, and answers `{ revokedCount: 1 }`.
- `POST /v1/auth/sign-out` borrowed `revoke-session`. It ends the cookie session, which no task describes, so it now carries no binding.

## Dead code removed

- `routes/step_up_passkeys.rs`: not declared in `routes/mod.rs` and referenced nowhere.
- `routes/join_requests/submit.rs` (the whole module), the unmounted `status` handler and its REST holder-signature path, and the unmounted public `manifest` handler.

## Per-type document size limits

`trust_tasks::size`: each Trust Task type declares its largest document, with a default of 64 KiB. The spine checks it before anything is parsed, on every transport. A body over the default has only its top-level `type` read. A document over its type's limit is refused with the framework's `malformedRequest` `trust-task-error` and `details.maxBytes`. The HTTPS document endpoint's body cap is the largest any type declares; the rest of the unauthenticated chain keeps its 64 KiB cap.

Raised:
- `policy/upsert/0.2`: 192 KiB. That's 2 × the 64 KiB Rego source cap, for JSON escaping, plus 64 KiB for the envelope and proof.
- `did-management/did/register/0.1`: 1 MiB. A `did:webvh` log grows with the DID's age, and 1 MiB is what its HTTPS route accepts today.

Both are declared ahead of their spine wiring (the next batch of admin verbs).

## Found in passing

`GET /v1/auth/sessions` answers a bare array, not `auth/sessions/list/0.1`'s response. The response-conformance layer refuses it. Left for the batch that moves the session verbs onto the spine.

## Tests

- REST tests of the removed routes now send signed documents: `acl_canonical`, `community_profile`, `removal`, `members_crud`, `endorsements`, `personhood`, `unrestricted_admin_consent`, `vetting_journey`, and the audit suites' seeding.
- Session step-up promotion tests were dropped where `signed_step_up.rs` already drives the bound gesture end to end.
- New: `trust_task_size` (router-level size gate), `trust_tasks::size` unit tests, `signed_only_verbs_have_no_route`, `the_acl_has_no_rest_route`, and console `lib/acl.test.ts` (paging, step-up confirm and resend, decline).
- OpenAPI snapshot and admin-ui wire types regenerated; the `trust_task_manifest` allowlist was extended with the console's signed verbs.

title: feat(vtc/website): website content moves as a chunked Trust Task transfer
body:
Builds on #679 (merged: the `maxDocumentBytes` front-matter member and the `"variant": "response"` invalid-example fixtures). Rebased directly onto `main`; this PR is no longer stacked, and its diff is only its own commits. It is independent of #680.

Website content becomes a **chunked transfer**, not an exception to the Trust-Task-only rule, modelled on `backup/*`. It reuses the node-neutral `vta/_shared/0.1/backup-transfer` vocabulary (ChunkManifest, ChunkIndex, ChunkData, ExpectedSha256, ExpectedSizeBytes, ExpiresAt). It replaces `GET`/`PUT /website/files/{path}` and `POST /website/deploy`, which carry raw bytes.

## New Type URIs (all `0.1`, draft, framework 0.6.0)

| URI | Role | `maxDocumentBytes` |
|---|---|---|
| `vtc/website/upload/begin` | Commits the target (`file` + path + optional `ifMatch`, or `bundle`), total size, whole-content SHA-256, and every chunk digest | request 256 KiB (manifest: up to 4096 digests) |
| `vtc/website/upload/chunk` | Sends one chunk, checked against the manifest on arrival; idempotent | request 352 KiB (256 KiB chunk ≈ 349 526 base64url chars, plus envelope and proof) |
| `vtc/website/upload/commit` | Reassembles and verifies the SHA-256. A `file` is written atomically, honouring `ifMatch` (the PUT); a `bundle` is staged | — |
| `vtc/website/upload/abort` | Discards an open or staged upload; idempotent | — |
| `vtc/website/deploy` | Publishes a staged bundle: live replace, or a new managed generation plus pruning | — |
| `vtc/website/files/show` | Ranged read (≤ 256 KiB per range) with the whole-file etag; `ifMatch` makes multi-range reads consistent | response 352 KiB |

New shared component: `vtc/_shared/0.1/website-transfer`.

## Design decisions for review

1. **The chunk size is 256 KiB, `backup-transfer`'s ceiling.** It is the largest power of two whose document survives a 1 MiB mediator message after DIDComm encoding and two forward wrappers. The VTC's default limits are 10 MiB per file (40 chunks) and 50 MiB per bundle (200 chunks).
2. **Commit applies a file, but only stages a bundle; `deploy` is its own task.** Deploying replaces the whole site, and in managed mode prunes generations irreversibly, so it gets its own authorization and audit. It also lets a bundle be uploaded and verified before anyone decides to put it live. Today's REST handler does both in one request.
3. **Reads are ranged, not staged.** `files/show` takes an offset and length and needs no session: the file on disk and its hash already fix the terms. `backup/get-chunk` stages its data because a backup is produced once. Here, a changed file mid-read is answered `changed` instead.
4. **The path rules are checked at `begin` and again at `commit`.** They are the public read handler's rules: hidden files, blocklisted extensions, traversal. Managed mode refuses `file` targets (`singleFileWritesDisabled`), matching the PUT handler.
5. **An upload belongs to the identity that began it.** Another administrator's upload id is answered `notFound`.
6. **`abort` is included.** It isn't in the inventory, but it releases a large staged upload before expiry, matching `backup/abort`.
7. **Differences from REST:**
   - Empty files can't be uploaded: `ExpectedSizeBytes` is at least 1.
   - The audit actor is the signer's DID. REST writes the literal `"admin"`.
   - The etag is bare lowercase hex. REST's header value is quoted.

## Checks run locally (this branch)

All green: npm build / check-bindings / check-dart-packages; cargo fmt, test (workspace + `--features validate`, incl. the new invalid-example tests), doc, clippy `-D warnings` (default + all-features); TS tsc / test / smoke; Go build / vet / test / gofmt; Dart analyze / test.

title: vta-service-v0.45.1
body:
### Added

- **vta**: Re-invite an idle TSP relationship alongside the request, and stamp activity on every reply ([#1816](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1816))

The sender only learns that a peer lost its half of a TSP relationship when its
  reply window expires (§7.2.2 drops silently, and design note C2 rules out a
  signal back), so the first request after such a loss always cost a full 30s
  before D6 recovered it. The browser wallet timed out a DID creation at 30s while
  the VTA's recovered answer arrived at 30.07s.

- **vta**: List, reset and delete TSP relationships offline ([#1812](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1812))

TSP relationship state is per endpoint and persisted in the encrypted
  `relationships` keyspace, so neither restarting the VTA nor wiping the mediator
  clears it, and there was no way to clear this VTA's half. Adds:

    vta tsp-relationships list
    vta tsp-relationships reset  --peer <did> [--our <vid>]
    vta tsp-relationships delete --peer <did> [--our <vid>] | --all [--yes]

  Reset is the D4 stale-half reset (`None` plus cleared thread digests; the
  capability cache is kept), so the next send re-invites. Delete is the D5
  eviction's `forget`. `--all` also removes half-formed records, which D9's
  enumeration cannot see, and only reports without `--yes`. The keyspace is
  opened through `CliStore`, so it decrypts under hardened configuration. `reset`
  and `delete` are refused on a sealed VTA; `list` is not. Built only with the
  `tsp` feature. All reads and writes go through the SDK's
  `PersistentRelationshipStore`.



### Fixed

- **provision**: A setup DID granted without a hand-off is told to re-grant, not to shorten an expiry ([#1813](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1813))

Online `vtc setup` (and any setup whose ephemeral is the authenticated
  caller) rolls the setup DID over to a permanent long-term admin. That rollover
  is allowed only through the granter's one-time hand-off marker (VTI-ACL-054,
  `--admin-handoff` / `--handoff`), and every printed setup command carries it.
  When the entry was granted without it, provision-integration fell through to
  an ordinary grant and #1738's VTI-ACL-053 bound refused it with "your entry
  expires at …, so you cannot write a permanent one — give it an expiry no later
  than yours". That points the operator at the wrong remedy: the successor must
  be permanent, and what is missing is the marker, which can only be set when
  the entry is created (VTI-ACL-055).

  The refusal is now specific: it names the missing hand-off and prints the
  re-grant (`pnm acl delete --did <setup-did>` then `pnm acl create … --expires
  1h --handoff`, with the entry's own scope derived through `act_scope`). It
  refuses exactly what VTI-ACL-053 already refused, before anything is minted;
  nothing is newly allowed.

- **pnm**: The persona-holder hint prints a pnm acl update that runs ([#1811](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1811))

The persona refusal and `pnm persona --help` both told operators to run
  `pnm acl update --did <did> --capabilities persona-holder`. `acl update`
  takes the entry's DID as a positional argument and has no `--did` flag, so
  the command offered as the fix failed to parse.

  Both now print `pnm acl update <did> --capabilities persona-holder`. A new
  test parses that form and checks that the `--did` form is rejected, so a
  change to the arguments fails in CI rather than for an operator.

title: vta-sdk-v0.56.1
body:
### Fixed

- **provision-client**: Setup's authorization hint is a scoped grant, with the hand-off when setup rolls over ([#1815](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1815))

Two setup messages pointed operators at a grant that fails or over-grants:

  - The "not authorized on this VTA" diagnostic told the operator to run
    `pnm acl create --did <setup-did> --role admin` — no `--contexts`, which
    makes the setup DID an unrestricted admin, and no expiry or hand-off, so
    the operator had to add those by hand, and a hand-typed time-boxed grant
    without `--handoff` is refused at the last step (VTI-ACL-053). It now
    prints the scoped grant for the context being provisioned:
    `--contexts <ctx> --expires 1h --handoff` when setup rolls the setup DID
    over to a minted admin (VTI-ACL-054), a scoped permanent grant when it
    does not (AdminOnly).
  - The phase-1 guidance under the printed `pnm contexts create … --admin-expires
    1h --admin-handoff` described `--admin-handoff` as something that "lets" the
    hand-off, which reads as optional. It now says to keep it, that setup's
    last step is refused without it, and that it cannot be added afterwards.
