title: Store never flushes or bounds its journal: OOM becomes unrecoverable
body:
## Summary

`vti-common`'s `Store` opens fjall with default settings, never rotates a memtable, and does not flush on shutdown. The journal therefore grows until a memtable happens to exceed 64 MiB, and is replayed in full at startup. If the process is killed before that threshold is reached, each restart replays a larger journal than the last, and the service eventually cannot start at all.

The underlying trigger was an undersized container, which we are fixing on our side. We are filing this because the store's behavior turned a routine OOM kill into an unrecoverable one — that part is independent of the limit we set.

## What happened

A VTC instance (`vtc 0.11.58`, `ghcr.io/ic3software/vtc:0.11.58-e6f69c2f`, fjall 3.1.10) running with a 64Mi container limit accumulated 115 OOMKill restarts over 39 hours, with the interval between kills shortening from ~25 minutes to ~3 minutes.

On the data volume after those 39 hours:

- `data/0.jnl` — 16,044,581 bytes, still growing
- `data/keyspaces/*/tables/` — exactly one file across all 41 keyspaces: `keyspaces/0/tables/57`, 43KB, written at the last clean start
- nothing under `keyspaces/` modified since that start

Every write for 39 hours lived only in memtables and the journal. Replaying that journal put the process at ~53Mi of its 64Mi limit before it served a request, and `exit 137` can never flush, so the journal was never truncated. Each cycle replayed more than the last.

We also confirmed there is no flush on shutdown: scaling to zero delivered SIGTERM to a healthy process (`Created` 45s before `Killing`), after which the journal was unchanged at 16,048,994 bytes with no new table file.

## Why it cannot self-correct

The only per-write flush trigger is `src/keyspace/mod.rs:838` in fjall:

```rust
pub(crate) fn check_memtable_rotate(&self, size: u64) {
    if size > self.config.max_memtable_size {
        self.request_rotation();
    }
}
```

With defaults that threshold is 64 MiB per keyspace, the block cache is 32 MiB, `max_write_buffer_size` is `None`, and `max_journaling_size` is 512 MiB. In a container smaller than those values, no trigger is reachable and the journal grows without bound.

Both call sites take defaults:

- `vti-common/src/store/mod.rs:471` — `let db = fjall::Database::builder(&config.data_dir).open()?;`
- `vti-common/src/store/mod.rs:479` — `let keyspace = self.db.keyspace(name, KeyspaceCreateOptions::default)?;`

`rotate_memtable` / `rotate_memtable_and_wait` appear nowhere in the repository. `LocalStore::persist` (`mod.rs:498`) calls `db.persist(PersistMode::SyncAll)`, which fsyncs the journal but does not flush memtables — it makes the journal durable without bounding it.

`StoreConfig` (`vti-common/src/config.rs:22`) contains only `data_dir`, so none of this is reachable from a service's `config.toml` or from deployment manifests.

This is in `vti-common`, so it applies to every service using `Store`, including `vta-service`. VTC is just the one that writes enough to hit it first — a quiet instance of the same build had a 76KB journal over the same period.

## Suggested fix

The Affinidi mediator, which runs alongside these services on the same storage engine, already exposes this as operator-facing configuration, and we tune it in our deployments:

| Variable | Our value | What it controls |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `STORAGE_FJALL_BLOCK_CACHE` | 8 MiB | fjall read cache |
| `STORAGE_FJALL_WRITE_BUFFER` | 16 MiB | total memtable budget across keyspaces |
| `STORAGE_FJALL_MAX_JOURNAL` | 64 MiB | forced flush once the journal exceeds this |

Parity with that would resolve this completely. Concretely:

1. **Bound the journal.** Set `max_journaling_size` so a forced flush occurs on a known ceiling rather than at 512 MiB. This is the single change that prevents the failure, because it caps replay cost regardless of container size. Note fjall panics if this is set below 64 MiB, which implies a documented minimum container size.
2. **Set an explicit memory budget.** `cache_size` and `max_memtable_size` rather than inheriting 32 MiB and 64 MiB, ideally derived from the cgroup limit at startup.
3. **Flush on shutdown.** Rotate memtables in the SIGTERM path so planned restarts start from a near-empty journal.
4. **Document the minimum.** Nothing in the repo states what memory this service needs, which is how a 64Mi limit came to be set for it.

Alternatively, a periodic `rotate_memtable_and_wait()` achieves the same bound without new configuration, and would suit instances whose write volume never approaches any threshold.

## Question

`max_memtable_size` appears to be persisted per keyspace — written into the meta keyspace at creation and read back during recovery in `keyspace/options.rs`. If that is correct, a new value would only apply to newly created keyspaces and existing volumes would need a migration. Can you confirm whether a fix would take effect on an existing data directory?

## Notes

Figures above are measured from the running deployment and read from the fjall source at tag `3.1.10`. Happy to provide the full journal or raw pod events.

title: Bump GitHub Actions majors and marked to 18, combining Dependabot PRs
body:
Combines Dependabot PRs #9, #10, #11 and #12 into one signed-off change. The bot's own PRs cannot merge because their commits carry no DCO sign-off. Dependabot closes them itself once the new versions land on main.

## What changes

- **actions/checkout 6 → 7** (#9). The v7 breaking change blocks checking out a fork's PR under `pull_request_target` and `workflow_run`. No workflow here uses either trigger, so nothing changes for us.
- **actions/setup-node 6 → 7** (#10). Internal move to ESM plus new cache outputs. Inputs we use (`node-version`, `cache`) are unchanged.
- **actions/attest-build-provenance 3 → 4** (#11). Now a thin wrapper over `actions/attest`. The `subject-path` input is unchanged.
- **marked 15.0.12 → 18.0.14** (#12). Three majors: v16 drops the CommonJS build and Node 18, v17 changes list tokens for custom renderers, v18 trims trailing blank lines from block tokens. The build imports the ESM entry, runs on Node 24 and calls `marked.parse` with the default renderer, so none of these apply.

## Verification

Run inside the Docker tooling image after rebuilding it with the new lockfile (marked 18.0.14 confirmed in the image):

- `npm run check` passes: validate, immutability, instance-value check, 22 unit tests, build.
- The generated `dist/` is byte-identical to a build from the same tree with marked 15.0.12, apart from `builtAt` / `generatedAt` timestamps and the digests derived from them. The rendered profile pages, which are the only place marked is used, did not change.

The workflow bumps can only be exercised by CI on this PR.

title: feat(spec): check a proof's key against its proofPurpose, and sign for authentication
body:
## What

1. Adds **Proof Purpose and Verification Relationship** under Proof, with one sentence in Proof pointing to it.
2. Adds producer guidance: sign Trust Task documents with `proofPurpose` `authentication`. Use `assertionMethod` only when the governing specification defines the proof as an attestation.
3. Changes the three framework examples (Example 1, the error-response example, Appendix A) to `authentication`.

## Why

The Proof section requires the `verificationMethod` to resolve to material the `issuer` controls. It says nothing about what the key is authorized for, so as written any key in the issuer's DID document verifies, including one listed only under `keyAgreement`. A survey of the Rust verifiers in the ecosystem found none that checks the relationship against `proofPurpose`.

VC Data Integrity already requires the check through the Retrieve Verification Method algorithm of Controlled Identifiers v1.0 (§3.3, steps 10 and 11). The verification method's `controller` must equal the controller document's URL, and the method must be associated with the relationship the proof purpose names. Part 1 restates that rule for Trust Task documents. It is a conformance clarification.

Part 2 follows from Part 1. Once the relationship is checked, the purpose a producer picks decides which keys need which authority. A Trust Task document's proof shows that the party controlling the issuer identifier produced it, which is what `authentication` authorizes a key to show. `assertionMethod` authorizes attestations a third party relies on in its own right. Signing everyday requests and responses with `assertionMethod` would require every operational key to carry attestation authority.

## The rule (consumers)

1. `proofPurpose` names the relationship that is checked: `assertionMethod`, `authentication`, `capabilityInvocation` or `capabilityDelegation`. A proof is rejected if the value is `keyAgreement`, absent, or not recognized.
2. The resolved document's id must be the `issuer`, and the verification method's `controller` must be that same id.
3. The verification method must appear in the named relationship, either by reference or embedded. Relative references such as `#key-1` are resolved against the document id first. A reference names a method in the document's `verificationMethod` set, and is never resolved to a method embedded under a different relationship.
4. For DID methods with implicit relationships, the relationships the method defines are used. For did:key, the signing key is authorized for all four signing purposes and the derived X25519 key for `keyAgreement` only.
5. A failure is reported as `proofInvalid`.

## The guidance (producers)

- MUST use a purpose whose relationship lists the signing key.
- SHOULD use `authentication`.
- SHOULD NOT use `assertionMethod` unless the specification defines the proof as an attestation.
- A specification MAY require a particular purpose, and a consumer MAY enforce that requirement as policy.

## Compatibility

- The consumer check does not depend on which purpose the producer chose. An issuer that lists a key under both relationships keeps its old `assertionMethod` proofs and its new `authentication` proofs verifying. That is the shape VTC and VTA DID documents already publish (`#key-0` under both relationships).
- Producers that currently emit `assertionMethod` fall under a SHOULD NOT, not a MUST NOT. They remain conforming while they migrate.
- The new subsection is placed last under Proof, so no existing section number or anchor moves.
- There is no version header change. Releases here are their own commits.

## Downstream

- `SPEC.md` in `dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf` is generated from this repository.
- The verifier and signer change shipped as [`dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf` #637](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/637), released in **`trust-tasks-rs` 0.23.0**. The verifier is strict, and signing defaults to `authentication`. A follow-up in the same release restricts reference resolution to the top-level `verificationMethod` set only, never to a method embedded under another relationship — folded into this text's item 3 above.
- The same release updates the per-task examples to `authentication`, except where a task specification normatively requires `assertionMethod` — approver decisions stay `assertionMethod`, and `approve-response` 0.5 requires the proof. Those needed new task-spec versions.
- The equivalent check has also shipped in `verifiable-trust-infrastructure` (VTI #1752).

title: feat: serve push/* over TSP, through the same intake as DIDComm and HTTPS
body:
**Merges after #32.** This branch is based on `fix/didcomm-signed-controller-ops`; until #32 lands, the diff here includes its commits.

## What

TSP is the gateway's third transport, served on the same terms as DIDComm and HTTPS. Every remote API is a Trust Task, and it doesn't depend on the transport.

- **One listener, two protocols.** The mediator allows one websocket per DID. So the existing `affinidi-messaging-didcomm-service` listener now runs with `Protocols::BOTH` via `start_with_tsp`, and TSP frames come off the same socket (`tsp` feature on the service and on `affinidi-tdk` 0.18, as in VTI).
- **A thin adapter** (`src/tsp.rs`). It opens the [TSP binding](https://trusttasks.org/binding/tsp/0.1) envelope (`trust_tasks_tsp::ENVELOPE_TYPE`), hands the document to `intake::receive` and wraps the reply in the envelope. It adds no authorisation of its own.
- **The sender VID is a claim.** It is treated the same way as DIDComm's `from`: a VID that differs from the issuer the proof establishes gets `identityMismatch`.
- **Bare payloads are refused.** A Trust Task sent over TSP without the envelope is answered with `malformedRequest` and not executed. A payload that isn't a Trust Task at all gets no answer.
- **Relationships.** The gateway accepts a peer's relationship invite, which grants nothing. The service records control messages and answers §7.3 cancellations itself. Relationship state lives in memory, so after a restart a peer invites again.
- **Advertisement.** At startup the gateway resolves its own DID. It warns if the DID document has no `TSPTransport` service naming the mediator in its identity file, and the warning includes the entry to add. The `push-gateway` DID template in VTI doesn't emit this entry yet.

## Tests

- The document suite now runs over TSP as well as DIDComm and HTTPS: accepted, wrong issuer, unsigned, stale, `assertionMethod`, replay, and the no-DID gateway.
- Identity mismatch is tested on both transports that name a sender (TSP, DIDComm).
- A document accepted on any transport is a replay on every other.
- A bare TSP payload is refused.
- Unit tests cover reading `TSPTransport` from a DID document.

`cargo test --workspace`, `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings`, `cargo fmt --check` and `cargo deny check` pass locally.

title: feat!: authorise provision and wake by the document's proof on every transport
body:
## What changes

`push/provision` and `push/wake` are Trust Tasks, and they are now authorised by the document's own proof on **every transport the gateway serves** (DIDComm and HTTPS), with one set of rules. Each transport adapter only unpacks and hands the document to one intake (`src/intake.rs`). No transport's claim about its sender authorises anything.

This matches what the VTA now sends (VTI #1740; delivered by the durable push engine, VTI #1767): the VTA signs `push/provision` / `push/wake` as its own operational documents. They carry an `authentication` proof, `issuer` = the VTA, `recipient` = the gateway, `issuedAt` and a unique `id`. The push engine reaches the gateway over whichever transport the gateway's DID advertises (TSP > DIDComm > `TrustTaskHTTPS`), so the gateway has to authorise the same way on each.

### The proof (`src/proof.rs`)

The caller is the document's `issuer`, and only when:
1. the proof is `eddsa-jcs-2022` and its `proofPurpose`, parsed as a trust-tasks-proof `ProofPurpose`, is `authentication`. `assertionMethod` or any other purpose is refused (VTI-KEY-106);
2. the DID of `proof.verificationMethod` == `issuer`, by exact match;
3. the issuer's DID document lists that method, its `controller` == `issuer`, it is referenced or embedded under `authentication`, and it is neither `revoked` nor past `expires`. A resolved document over 64 KiB is refused;
4. the signature verifies over the raw document with `proof` removed.

Steps 3–4 run through trust-tasks-proof 0.23's proof-purpose API. The gateway's `IssuerKeys` implements `ProofPurposeResolver`, and verification goes through `PurposeBound::new(&keys, ProofPurpose::Authentication)`. A key is therefore released only for the relationship the proof declares. The hand-rolled `PinnedKey` resolver is gone.

### One delivery, once (`src/intake.rs`, `src/replay.rs`)

An `authentication` proof has no challenge, so the document itself binds it to one delivery (VTI-KEY-107):
- `recipient` is required and must be this gateway's DID. Otherwise the answer is `wrongRecipient`, or `malformedRequest` if `recipient` is missing.
- `issuedAt` is required and may be at most 5 min old and at most 60 s in the future (VTI-OPS-024). Otherwise the answer is `expired` or `malformedRequest`.
- `expiresAt` must not have passed.
- Replay protection (VTI-OPS-026):
  - **Keyed** on (**proven issuer**, document `id`). The issuer is the one the proof established, never a transport claim.
  - **Bounded**: 8192 records per issuer, 512 per handle, and a 65536 soft bound shared fairly with a hard cap at twice that.
  - **Fail-closed**: at any bound, or if the guard errors, the record refuses the document. It never evicts.
  - **Claimed only after** rate limiting and authorisation, so a refused caller leaves nothing.
  - **Shared by the transports**: a document accepted over DIDComm is a replay over HTTPS.
  - A duplicate gets the first response back and nothing is re-executed. A different document under a used `id` gets `idConflict`. A transient push failure releases the claim.

### Controllers served (`GATEWAY_ALLOWED_CONTROLLERS`)

Only listed controller VTA DIDs are served (exact match, no patterns):
- A registration naming any other controller is refused.
- A provision by a controller that has since been delisted is refused.
- Unset or empty means nothing is served.
- `*` is an explicit open mode.

`push/provision` also requires the proven issuer to be the handle's `controllerVtaDid`. `push/wake` requires it to be on the handle's allowlist.

## Transports

- **DIDComm**: served when `GATEWAY_IDENTITY_FILE` is set. The adapter passes the envelope `from` to the intake only as a claim. If it is present and differs from the proven issuer, the answer is `identityMismatch`.
- **HTTPS** (`POST /trust-tasks`): now authorised by the document proof exactly as on DIDComm. This matches how the VTA push engine's REST transport posts, which is the bare signed document. The old `X-TT-Did` / `X-TT-Signature` body-signature scheme (`src/auth.rs`) is **removed**, not kept alongside: it was did:key-only and had no recipient binding, freshness or replay protection.
- **TSP**: not served yet. Adding it means one more adapter, a TSP listener under the gateway's identity advertised as `TSPTransport` in its DID document, that hands unpacked documents to `intake::receive`. Authorisation would not change.
- A gateway **without an identity** has no DID for a document to name as `recipient`, so it accepts no signed document on any transport and serves `push/register` only. Startup warns about this.

## Dependencies

- trust-tasks-rs 0.23.2 (was 0.21/0.22)
- **trust-tasks-proof 0.23.2** (new), for `ProofPurpose` / `ProofPurposeResolver` / `PurposeBound`
- affinidi-tdk 0.18, affinidi-messaging-didcomm-service 0.13, which bring in affinidi-messaging-sdk 0.28.1
- affinidi-secrets-resolver 0.5.12
- ed25519-dalek is now a dev-dependency only
- vta-sdk is not a dependency of the gateway

## Deploy

1. **Set `GATEWAY_ALLOWED_CONTROLLERS`** to the DID(s) of the VTA(s) this gateway serves. Without it every registration is refused.
2. **Set `GATEWAY_IDENTITY_FILE`**. Without a DID the gateway accepts no provision or wake on any transport.
3. Recreate test deployments from scratch. There is no migration.

The `test-wake*` helpers now sign their documents with an `authentication` proof, addressed to the gateway DID taken from the register response. They need a gateway with an identity, running in open mode.

## Breaking changes

- Unsigned provision/wake is refused (`proofRequired`) on every transport.
- An `assertionMethod` proof is refused (`proofInvalid`).
- HTTPS header signatures are ignored.
- A gateway without an identity serves register only.

The VTA side is already in place: VTI #1740 signs these documents, and VTI #1767 delivers them through the push engine.

## Tests

`cargo test --workspace`: 133 passed (77 unit, 25 `tests/api.rs`, 31 `tests/document_auth.rs`). `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`, `cargo fmt --check` and `cargo deny check` are clean.

- `tests/document_auth.rs` (was `didcomm_auth.rs`) drives the transport-neutral intake. New `every_transport_*` tests run the same documents through the DIDComm handoff and through the real HTTPS router:
  - signed by a listed controller: provision and wake accepted and delivered;
  - wrong issuer, either a signed non-controller (`permissionDenied`) or a controller's DID signed by another key (`proofInvalid`): refused;
  - unsigned: `proofRequired`;
  - stale `issuedAt`: `expired`;
  - signed for `assertionMethod`: `proofInvalid`;
  - replayed: first answer returned, nothing sent again;
  - none of the refusals touch the allowlist.
- Also new:
  - a replay across transports is still a replay;
  - a gateway without a DID accepts no signed document.
- The earlier suite still passes: envelope-only sender, tampering, `identityMismatch`, `wrongRecipient`, missing `recipient`, the time window, `idConflict`, the refuse-not-evict and fair-share budgets, and allowlist admission.
- `tests/api.rs` now signs provisions and wakes with document proofs. New tests:
  - `tampered_signed_document_is_refused`;
  - `header_identity_authorises_nothing`: a retired `X-TT-*` header is ignored and the answer is `proofRequired`.
- Unit tests:
  - `src/proof.rs`: VM controller, `authentication` membership (an `assertionMethod`-only key is refused), revoked/expired, oversized document, unlisted VM;
  - `src/intake.rs`: retention outlives acceptance, expired document, missing `issuedAt`;
  - `src/replay.rs`: keying and budgets.

## Scope notes

- The replay record is in memory and per process. Per VTI-OPS-027 it would need to be shared across replicas; the gateway runs as one process. A restart forgets it, which the acceptance window makes safe.
- The 64 KiB DID-document cap applies after resolution. The resolver's own network timeout bounds the download.

## Pre-merge checklist

```
- [x] No new reqwest::Client::new() / bare fetch(); all clients have finite timeouts (R1.2) — proof resolver uses the tuned resolver timeout (test-wake helper is a dev CLI)
- [x] No lock held across a network await (R1.3)
- [x] No local state committed before its remote effect, or the flow is resumable with an idempotency key (R2.1) — replay claim released on a transient failure
- [x] Every retry is bounded + backed off; non-idempotent ops are not blind-retried (R1.4) — n/a
- [x] Accept/poll/listen loops survive transient errors (R1.5) — a failed resolve refuses the one document
- [x] Acks/deletes happen only after durable handoff (R1.6) — n/a
- [x] New/changed wire types: camelCase, deny_unknown_fields where security-relevant, schema registered, all consumers (incl. JS) updated (R3.*) — no new wire types; VTA already signs (VTI #1740)
- [x] Config absence = most restrictive; fail-closed if enforcement can't start (R5.*) — no controllers listed = none served; no identity = no signed documents; resolver build failure stops startup
- [x] Logs/status claim only what was verified; background-job failures are surfaced (R6.*)
- [x] "Process dies on the next line" answered for every mutation touched (R2.1)
- [x] Deviations from this guide flagged explicitly with rule numbers — none
```

title: feat: serve push/* over TSP, through the same intake as DIDComm and HTTPS
body:
feat: serve push/* over TSP, through the same intake as DIDComm and HTTPS

The gateway's mediator listener now multiplexes TSP with DIDComm on its one
websocket (affinidi-messaging-didcomm-service `tsp`, Protocols::BOTH). A new
TSP adapter (src/tsp.rs) opens the TSP binding envelope, hands the document
to intake::receive with the authenticated sender VID as the transport's
claim, and returns the reply in the envelope. It adds no authorisation: a
sender VID that differs from the proven issuer is identityMismatch, as a
DIDComm `from` is. Relationship invites are accepted; they grant nothing.

At startup the gateway resolves its own DID and warns when the document has
no TSPTransport service naming its mediator.

The document suite now runs over TSP too (accepted, wrong issuer, unsigned,
stale, assertionMethod, replay), a document accepted on any transport is a
replay on every other, and a bare TSP payload is refused with
malformedRequest.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

title: trust-tasks-rs-v0.23.3
body:
### Added

- **vta/services**: Report, and update 1.1 with a mediator drain window ([#656](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/656))

* feat(vta/services): report, and update 1.1 with a DIDComm drain window

  Two gaps that keep the VTA's service management on bespoke REST routes, found
  moving the SDK onto the Trust Task spine.

  - `vta/services/report/0.1` — per-mediator inbound counts and each sender's
    last-seen mediator over a window, so an operator can tell who is still on the
    old route before ending a drain. Today it exists only as a bearer-token REST
    route (`GET /mediators/report`). Operator-only, with a REQUIRED request proof:
    the response is a contact log of other parties' DIDs, which the recipient may
    release only to a signer it has decided is the agent's operator.
  - `vta/services/update/1.1` — adds an optional `drainTtlSecs` for `didcomm`.
    Replacing the mediator drains the old one, and 1.0 gave the operator no say in
    how long, so the agent could only apply its default. The REST route and the
    CLI (`services didcomm update --drain-ttl`) carry an operator-chosen window;
    without it here, moving the CLI to the Trust Task would silently drop the
    option. A 1.0 request is a valid 1.1 request; a value below the recipient's
    floor may be raised to it, and must be over a DIDComm-carried request.

  (`services/report` was pushed to #654 after it merged, so it did not ship there.)

  Rust, TypeScript, Go and Dart bindings regenerated; `npm run build` (strict
  Security & Privacy), `check-bindings` and the Rust tests (903) pass.

title: vta-service-v0.44.0
body:
### Added

- **credential-exchange**: Every step is a signed Trust Task on the spine, over any transport ([#1771](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1771))

Every credential-exchange step — offer, request, issue, query, present — and
  the VTC's `vtc/members/request-vmc` and `join-requests/submit-receipt` pushes
  were bare DIDComm messages typed as their task URI, served beside the binding
  envelope. `bindings/didcomm/0.2` §2 requires a consumer to refuse that
  carriage; it skipped the spine's proof, freshness, recipient and replay checks;
  and no transport but DIDComm could carry it. They were never missing a TSP
  binding. Each is a signed Trust Task now.

  VTC
  - Pushes `offer`, `issue`, `query`, `request-vmc` and `submit-receipt` through
    the durable push engine (TSP > DIDComm > REST, escalating on no delivery
    evidence) as documents signed with its operational key under
    `authentication` — `credentials::delivery::push_document`, the one outbound
    funnel. `AppState::send_to_member` and `push_to_holder` are gone.
  - Serves `credential-exchange/request` and `present` on the dispatcher, from
    every transport. None of the five steps defines a response, so what goes
    back on the carrying transport is the SPEC §4.4.2 empty `#response`
    acknowledgement; the answer is the next step, pushed on the thread (`issue`
    after `request`, threaded on the offer; `submit-receipt` after `present`,
    threaded on the query, to whoever sent it).
  - The bare `request`/`present` arms are deleted; typed as themselves they are
    refused naming the envelope.
  - The git-ns break-glass notice ([#1745](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1745)) was the last caller of the removed
    DIDComm-only send; it now goes through the push engine too, signed with the
    operational key under `authentication` like the removal notice it copies.

  VTA (holder)
  - Serves `offer`, `issue` and `query` on the spine and pushes `request` and
    `present` back. They are counterparty tasks: an issuer or verifier holds no
    ACL entry here, so they dispatch on a zero-authority claim beside the
    ceremony carve-out (`is_counterparty_task`), and each handler acts with the
    VTA's own authority under the gate it always had — an offer only with a
    configured `credential_holder_did`, a presentation only to a trusted verifier
    or after operator approval.
  - This restores `query`, whose bare arm #1739 deleted, leaving a holder that
    could not answer a verifier. A deferred query is answered with silence (an
    acknowledgement would claim a task not yet performed); `pending-approve` now
    also pushes the `present` to the verifier on the query's thread.
  - The bare `offer`/`issue` arms are deleted. The helpers only the TEE
    attestation arms still use are gated on `tee` until those arms go.

  Breaking (wire): a holder or wallet must read the pushed documents and send
  `request`/`present` as signed documents with `threadId`. openvtc #392 is the
  companion and is merged.

  Not fixed here, found on the way: the push engine carries one signed document
  for the whole delivery window, while a receiving VTA refuses an `issuedAt`
  older than ten minutes, so a holder offline when its credential is pushed gets
  it `expired` (removal notices share this). And a counterparty's `issue` or
  deferred `query` still costs this VTA a durable write from any sender, as the
  bare handlers did; a floor like the ceremony one is a follow-up.

- **vta**: Device pushes go through the durable Trust Task push engine ([#1767](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1767))

* feat(vtc): push to a member over TSP once it has spoken TSP here, when its DID document says nothing

  A member whose DID document advertises no transport — a `did:key` wallet,
  which cannot carry services — was always pushed to over DIDComm, even when it
  was demonstrably listening on TSP. The VTA already solved this for device
  push by learning from inbound (`tsp_reach`): a verified TSP frame proves the
  sender is on TSP now. The VTC had no equivalent.

  - `TspReachability` moves from vta-service to `vti_common::tsp_reach` so both
    nodes share one. The VTA re-exports it at its old path, unchanged.
  - The shared push engine (`vti_common::trust_task_push`) takes it through
    `PushContext::learned_tsp`. A recipient whose document advertises nothing
    is tried over TSP first while fresh, with DIDComm behind it. A peer that
    switched back gives no error on TSP, only silence, and escalation on
    missing evidence is what recovers. What a document does advertise still
    wins: learning only fills in for one that says nothing.
  - The VTC records the verified sender of every inbound TSP frame
    (`handle_tsp`) in `AppState::tsp_reach`, and `member_push` passes it to the
    engine.



### Security

- **acl**: No principal widens its own entry, and no grant exceeds its granter (VTI-ACL-052, VTI-ACL-053) ([#1738](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1738))

* security(acl)!: no principal widens its own entry, and no grant exceeds its granter (VTI-ACL-052, VTI-ACL-053)

  A context-scoped admin, such as a companion service's credential
  (`--role admin --contexts vgi-bridge`), could raise its own authority.
  `update_acl` had no self check and no test either way. Tests written
  against main confirm every case below. Adding a foreign context or
  raising the role was already refused. What went through was clearing
  any narrowing on the caller's own entry, and minting a sibling entry
  that carried none of it:

  - Self-update to clear its capability narrowing, drop its key filter,
    or extend its expiry. All three succeeded.
  - A create for another DID it controls, in the same context, with none
    of its own narrowing: full capabilities, no key filter, no expiry.
  - An update that cleared another entry's narrowing past what the caller
    itself held.
  - Self role change (`acl/change-role`).
  - Rotation (`acl/swap-key`) rebuilt the entry field by field. It dropped
    `expires_at`, `allowed_keys`, `approve_scope` and the step-up fields,
    so a one-hour bootstrap grant became permanent. It also dropped
    `created_by`. This violated VTI-CLT-029.
  - An initiator could grant approve authority it did not hold
    (VTI-ACL-042).
  - A context admin could update or delete an entry that also acts in a
    context it does not administer, because overlap was enough.

  VTA (`operations/acl.rs`, the choke point for REST, DIDComm, TSP and the
  Trust Task spine):

  - update and change-role refuse the caller's own entry (VTI-ACL-052).
    Delete already did.
  - create, update and change-role measure the resulting entry against
    the caller's stored entry (`validate_within_caller`, VTI-ACL-053). The
    entry must not exceed the caller's effective capabilities (additive
    ones stay under VTI-ACL-033), key filter, expiry, or confer authority
    (VTI-ACL-042). A caller with no live entry writes nothing.
  - update, change-role and delete require the caller to cover every
    context the entry acts or approves in, not just overlap
    (VTI-ACL-050 as tightened).
  - update re-runs the role and act-scope checks on the patched entry, so
    a role change alone cannot turn "nowhere" into "everywhere".
  - swap-key copies the entry exactly and only moves the subject. It
    refuses an expired entry (VTI-CLT-029).

  VTC (`routes/acl.rs`, `routes/admin/invites.rs`,
  `routes/members/update.rs`):

  - An `acl/grant` rewrite of your own entry is refused. Before, a re-grant
    with no `expiresAt` made a time-boxed admin permanent.
  - `acl/change-role` refuses your own entry in either direction; the
    ceremony already refused self-promotion.
  - `vtc/members/update` refuses a role or label change on your own entry.
  - Rewrite, change-role and revoke (including scoped revoke) require
    full coverage for every role, not only admin targets.
  - A grant cannot outlive the granter's expiry, and a granter with no
    live entry is refused.
  - `vtc/admin/invites/create` requires an unrestricted admin. It writes
    a community-wide admin entry, and a context admin could previously
    invite a DID it controls into one.

| `trust_tasks` | pub.dev | `0.3.2` → `0.3.3` | patch |

What merging does, per registry (all in `publish.yml`, each keyed on "this
version is not published yet"):

- **crates.io** — `release-plz-release` tags `<crate>-v<version>`, publishes in
  dependency order and creates a GitHub Release per crate. Bump levels come from
  `cargo-semver-checks`.
- **npm** — `publish-npm` publishes with OIDC provenance and tags
  `<prefix>-v<version>`.
- **Go** — `publish-go` builds, vets and tests, then pushes the tag, which *is*
  the publication. **Irreversible**: proxy.golang.org never forgets a tag.
- **pub.dev** — `tag-dart` verifies against the *published* core and pushes the
  tag; `publish-dart.yml` publishes from it.

The npm, Go and Dart bumps are only as accurate as the commit subjects — nothing
checks their APIs the way `cargo-semver-checks` checks the crates. Look for a
missing `!` before merging.

This branch is regenerated from `main` on every push, so do not commit to it —
edits are force-pushed away. See RELEASING.md.

title: security(vta-mobile-core)!: sign every request under authentication and verify every reply
body:
Brings the mobile engine in line with main's signing rules. Merged with main, which now carries:

- #1739: the VTA and the VTC accept a Trust Task over DIDComm or TSP only when its Data Integrity proof verifies as its `issuer`, and that issuer is the transport sender.
- #1740: every VTA and VTC response, errors included, is signed with the operational key under `proofPurpose: authentication`, and so are the approval requests the VTA pushes.
- #1752 (VTI-KEY-022): a proof's key must be listed under the relationship its `proofPurpose` names.
- #1757: the VTA requires `assertionMethod` on an approver's decision.
- #1766 and #1767: a consent request must be signed under `authentication`, and VTA device pushes go through the durable push engine.
- trust-tasks 0.23.

Before this PR the engine had three gaps:

- It signed its requests under `assertionMethod`.
- It announced TSP reachability with an unsigned `messaging/ping/0.1`, which #1739 refuses with `proofRequired`.
- It returned the VTA's replies without checking who signed them.

## Outbound: every request is signed

- `attach_did_signed_proof` now signs under `authentication` (VTI-KEY-106). It refuses a document if:
  - the document does not name the signer as `issuer`;
  - it lacks a `recipient`, an `issuedAt` or an `id`;
  - it already carries a proof.
- `MediatorSession::send_trust_task`, `send_trust_task_one_way` and `TspMediatorSession::send_trust_task` refuse, before sending, a document that is unsigned or is not issued by the session's holder to its peer.
- `build_approve_response_webauthn` takes a `Signer` and signs the document. The passkey assertion is still the step-up gate.
- New `build_messaging_ping` builds a signed ping. `TspMediatorSession::announce`, which sent the unsigned ping, is removed.

## Inbound: every reply is verified

New export `verify_trust_task_reply(request, reply, expected_signer)`. A reply is accepted only when all of these hold:

| Check | Rule |
|---|---|
| `type` | the request's `type` + `#response`, or a `trust-task-error` |
| `threadId` | `request.threadId ?? request.id` |
| `issuer` / `recipient` | the expected peer / the request's `issuer` |
| proof | `eddsa-jcs-2022`, `proofPurpose: authentication`, verification method of the expected peer, **listed under `authentication` in its DID document** |
| signature | verifies over the reply without `proof` |

Error replies are held to the same rule. Failures return the new `FfiError::UnverifiedReply`.

The checks work on the documents, not the transport:

- **DIDComm:** `MediatorSession::send_trust_task` verifies the reply before it returns it.
- **TSP:** the reply arrives on the inbox, so the native reply router calls the export after correlating the reply.

## Pushed approval requests are operational messages

The step-up approve-request, consent request and task-consent request the VTA pushes to a device are the VTA's own operational messages, signed with its operational key under `authentication` (#1740). `verify_signed_request` requires `proofPurpose: authentication` **and** the verification method listed under `authentication` in the issuer's DID document. A pushed request signed under `assertionMethod`, or by a key the issuer lists only under `assertionMethod`, is refused before it prompts.

The exception on the device side is the human approver's own decisions: the step-up `approve-response` (webauthn and DID-signed approvals, and the denial) and the `task-consent/decision` (approve and deny). Their proof is the approver's evidence, not an operational request, so they are signed under `assertionMethod` via the new `attach_approval_proof`. This matches the trust-task spec, #1757, affinidi-webvh-service #213 (`verify_approval`) and the browser wallet (OpenVTC/vta-browser-plugin#279).

`attach_approval_proof` refuses to sign unless the approver's DID document, resolved locally through `affinidi-did-common` (a new dependency), lists the signing key under `assertionMethod`. Every other document the device sends stays under `authentication`.

## Verification reuses vta-sdk

The merge with main switched the signature check in `proof.rs` to `PurposeBound` fixed to `assertionMethod`, which would have refused every `authentication` request and reply. Signature verification for both pushed requests and replies now goes through vta-sdk's `verify_trust_task_proof_with`:

- It binds the key to the purpose the proof declares (VTI-KEY-022), so the crate's own relationship lookup on the verify path is gone.
- It re-resolves a cached DID document once before failing (VTI-KEY-134), so a peer that rotated a key in place is not refused on stale material.

The device still pins the purpose and the `eddsa-jcs-2022` suite before it verifies. It also checks the enrolled-issuer allowlist before any DID resolution, so an unenrolled DID causes no network I/O. `trust-tasks-proof` is no longer a direct dependency.

`ConsentRequest::verify` is not used. It takes a single expected issuer and the approver's DID, and validates the payload strictly. The mobile FFI takes an allowlist of enrolled executors and reads the payload leniently for display. Adopting it would change the FFI with no gain in the checks.

## Breaking changes

Test deployments only; nothing is kept for compatibility.

- `FfiError::UnverifiedReply` is added.
- `build_approve_response_webauthn` gains a `signer` argument.
- `TspMediatorSession::announce` is removed. Use `send_trust_task` with `build_messaging_ping`.
- New exports: `verify_trust_task_reply`, `build_messaging_ping`.
- Request proofs change from `assertionMethod` to `authentication`, except the step-up `approve-response` and the `task-consent/decision`, which are `assertionMethod`.
- Pushed approval requests must be signed under `authentication`, with a key listed there.
- Unsigned or wrongly signed replies are refused.

The unsigned REST-only builders (`build_auth_challenge`, `build_refresh`) and the gateway `push/register` are unchanged. The app does not send them to the VTA over DIDComm or TSP, and the new send guard would refuse them if it tried.

## Tests

- `reply::tests::reply_verification`:
  - accepted: a VTA-signed success, and a VTA-signed error;
  - refused: unsigned (success and error), `assertionMethod` purpose, signed by another DID, another DID claiming the issuer, wrong or missing `threadId`, misaddressed, wrong `type`, tampered payload;
  - accepted: a request that carried its own `threadId`, answered on that thread.
- `reply::tests::only_signed_requests_from_the_holder_to_the_peer_are_sent`.
- Signed-ping and issuer-mismatch tests in `session` and `stepup`. `stepup` asserts every approve-response is signed under `assertionMethod`.
- `task::tests::refuses_a_pushed_request_signed_under_assertion_method` (step-up and consent prompts) and `consent::tests::refuses_a_request_signed_under_assertion_method`.
- `proof::tests::a_pushed_request_by_a_key_not_listed_under_authentication_is_refused`: the same key, listed under `authentication` in one `did:peer` and only under `assertionMethod` in another. The first verifies and the second is refused.
- `proof::tests::a_method_counts_only_under_the_relationship_that_lists_it`, and `proof::tests::an_approval_key_must_be_listed_under_assertion_method`.
- `consent` tests assert that both the approve and deny decisions are signed under `assertionMethod`.
- After the merge: `cargo test -p vta-mobile-core` gives 74 passed and 4 ignored (live network). `cargo clippy -p vta-mobile-core --all-targets -- -D warnings` and `cargo fmt --check` are clean.
- The Swift bindings generate cleanly from this branch with `uniffi-bindgen generate --library`, as `scripts/package-ios.sh` does. They are build artifacts and are not committed here.
- Not run: the live `--ignored` tests against a deployed VTA.

## Release

This PR changes the UniFFI surface. OpenVTC/vta-mobile-agent-ios#29 needs a `vta-mobile-core` release built from this PR, followed by a `Package.swift` bump to that release's xcframework URL and checksum.

title: security(vta-mobile-core)!: sign every request under authentication and verify every reply (#1744)
body:
security(vta-mobile-core)!: sign every request under authentication and verify every reply (#1744)

* security(vta-mobile-core)!: sign every request under authentication and verify every reply

The VTA and the VTC now accept a Trust Task over DIDComm or TSP only when its
Data Integrity proof verifies as its issuer and that issuer is the transport
sender (#1739), and sign every response, errors included, with their
operational key under proofPurpose authentication (#1740, VTI-KEY-106). The
mobile engine signed most of its requests, but under assertionMethod, sent an
unsigned ping to announce TSP reachability, and returned replies without
checking who had signed them.

Outbound:

- attach_did_signed_proof signs under authentication, and refuses a document
  that does not name the signer as issuer, lacks a recipient, an issuedAt or
  an id, or already carries a proof.
- MediatorSession::send_trust_task, send_trust_task_one_way and
  TspMediatorSession::send_trust_task refuse a document that is unsigned, or
  not issued by the session's holder and addressed to its peer.
- build_approve_response_webauthn takes a Signer and signs the document; the
  assertion stays the step-up gate.
- New build_messaging_ping: a signed messaging/ping/0.1.
  TspMediatorSession::announce, which sent the unsigned ping, is removed.

Inbound:

- New verify_trust_task_reply(request, reply, expected_signer). A reply is
  accepted only when all of these hold:
  - its type answers the request (#response or trust-task-error);
  - its threadId is the request's thread;
  - it is issued by the expected peer to the request's issuer;
  - its eddsa-jcs-2022 proof is under authentication, by the peer, with a key
    the peer lists under authentication;
  - the signature verifies.
  Error replies must pass too. Failures are the new FfiError::UnverifiedReply.
- MediatorSession::send_trust_task verifies the reply before returning it.
  Over TSP the reply arrives on the inbox, and the native layer calls the
  export once it has correlated the reply.
- verify_signed_request, used for VTA-pushed approval requests, also requires
  the proof's key to be listed under assertionMethod in the issuer's DID
  document. It used to accept a key listed under either relationship.

Breaking FFI changes (test deployments only; no compatibility kept):

- FfiError gains UnverifiedReply.
- build_approve_response_webauthn gains a signer argument.
- TspMediatorSession::announce is removed.
- Request proofs change from assertionMethod to authentication.
- Replies without a verifying VTA proof are refused.

The app side of this change is OpenVTC/vta-mobile-agent-ios.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* fix(vta-mobile-core)!: verify pushed approval requests under authentication

The VTA signs the step-up approve-request, consent and task-consent requests
it pushes to a device with its operational key under proofPurpose
authentication (#1740, VTI-KEY-106). The engine required assertionMethod on
those, so it would refuse every prompt from an upgraded VTA.

- Pushed requests must carry proofPurpose authentication, and the proof's
  verification method must be listed under authentication in the issuer's
  DID document. One signed under assertionMethod is refused before it
  prompts.
- The device's own step-up approve-response is the one exception: its proof
  is the human approver's evidence, not an operational request, so it is
  signed under assertionMethod (attach_approval_proof). Every other request
  the device sends stays under authentication.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* fix(vta-mobile-core)!: sign the approver's task-consent decision under assertionMethod

The task-consent decision, approve or deny, is the human approver's own
attestation, like the step-up approve-response. The did-hosting RP
(affinidi-webvh-service #213, verify_approval) refuses one signed for
authentication or with a key not listed under assertionMethod, and the
trust-task spec and the browser wallet sign it the same way.

- build_task_consent_decision_did_signed and build_task_consent_decision_denied
  sign under assertionMethod (attach_approval_proof).
- attach_approval_proof refuses to sign unless the approver's DID document,
  resolved locally, lists the signing key under assertionMethod. The
  device's did:key does.
- Every other document the device sends stays under authentication, and a
  pushed request signed under assertionMethod is still refused.

The VTA's decision handler (main and #1740) verifies the proof and binds the
signer but does not check the purpose, so it accepts these decisions.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* fix(vta-mobile-core): verify pushed requests and replies through vta-sdk's purpose-bound verifier

The merge with main left verify_signature binding every proof to
`assertionMethod`, which would refuse the `authentication` proofs the VTA now
signs its pushed approval requests and replies with. Verify through vta-sdk's
`verify_trust_task_proof_with` instead: it binds the key to the purpose the
proof declares (VTI-KEY-022), so the hand-rolled relationship lookup goes, and
it re-resolves a cached DID document once before failing (VTI-KEY-134). The
purpose and eddsa-jcs-2022 suite stay pinned before it runs.

trust-tasks-proof is no longer a direct dependency.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

---------

title: vta-keyspaces-v0.3.4
body:
### Added

- **vta**: Device pushes go through the durable Trust Task push engine ([#1767](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1767))

* feat(vtc): push to a member over TSP once it has spoken TSP here, when its DID document says nothing

  A member whose DID document advertises no transport — a `did:key` wallet,
  which cannot carry services — was always pushed to over DIDComm, even when it
  was demonstrably listening on TSP. The VTA already solved this for device
  push by learning from inbound (`tsp_reach`): a verified TSP frame proves the
  sender is on TSP now. The VTC had no equivalent.

  - `TspReachability` moves from vta-service to `vti_common::tsp_reach` so both
    nodes share one. The VTA re-exports it at its old path, unchanged.
  - The shared push engine (`vti_common::trust_task_push`) takes it through
    `PushContext::learned_tsp`. A recipient whose document advertises nothing
    is tried over TSP first while fresh, with DIDComm behind it. A peer that
    switched back gives no error on TSP, only silence, and escalation on
    missing evidence is what recovers. What a document does advertise still
    wins: learning only fills in for one that says nothing.
  - The VTC records the verified sender of every inbound TSP frame
    (`handle_tsp`) in `AppState::tsp_reach`, and `member_push` passes it to the
    engine.

title: pnm-cli-v0.25.0
body:
### Security

- **acl**: No principal widens its own entry, and no grant exceeds its granter (VTI-ACL-052, VTI-ACL-053) ([#1738](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1738))

* security(acl)!: no principal widens its own entry, and no grant exceeds its granter (VTI-ACL-052, VTI-ACL-053)

  A context-scoped admin, such as a companion service's credential
  (`--role admin --contexts vgi-bridge`), could raise its own authority.
  `update_acl` had no self check and no test either way. Tests written
  against main confirm every case below. Adding a foreign context or
  raising the role was already refused. What went through was clearing
  any narrowing on the caller's own entry, and minting a sibling entry
  that carried none of it:

  - Self-update to clear its capability narrowing, drop its key filter,
    or extend its expiry. All three succeeded.
  - A create for another DID it controls, in the same context, with none
    of its own narrowing: full capabilities, no key filter, no expiry.
  - An update that cleared another entry's narrowing past what the caller
    itself held.
  - Self role change (`acl/change-role`).
  - Rotation (`acl/swap-key`) rebuilt the entry field by field. It dropped
    `expires_at`, `allowed_keys`, `approve_scope` and the step-up fields,
    so a one-hour bootstrap grant became permanent. It also dropped
    `created_by`. This violated VTI-CLT-029.
  - An initiator could grant approve authority it did not hold
    (VTI-ACL-042).
  - A context admin could update or delete an entry that also acts in a
    context it does not administer, because overlap was enough.

  VTA (`operations/acl.rs`, the choke point for REST, DIDComm, TSP and the
  Trust Task spine):

  - update and change-role refuse the caller's own entry (VTI-ACL-052).
    Delete already did.
  - create, update and change-role measure the resulting entry against
    the caller's stored entry (`validate_within_caller`, VTI-ACL-053). The
    entry must not exceed the caller's effective capabilities (additive
    ones stay under VTI-ACL-033), key filter, expiry, or confer authority
    (VTI-ACL-042). A caller with no live entry writes nothing.
  - update, change-role and delete require the caller to cover every
    context the entry acts or approves in, not just overlap
    (VTI-ACL-050 as tightened).
  - update re-runs the role and act-scope checks on the patched entry, so
    a role change alone cannot turn "nowhere" into "everywhere".
  - swap-key copies the entry exactly and only moves the subject. It
    refuses an expired entry (VTI-CLT-029).

  VTC (`routes/acl.rs`, `routes/admin/invites.rs`,
  `routes/members/update.rs`):

  - An `acl/grant` rewrite of your own entry is refused. Before, a re-grant
    with no `expiresAt` made a time-boxed admin permanent.
  - `acl/change-role` refuses your own entry in either direction; the
    ceremony already refused self-promotion.
  - `vtc/members/update` refuses a role or label change on your own entry.
  - Rewrite, change-role and revoke (including scoped revoke) require
    full coverage for every role, not only admin targets.
  - A grant cannot outlive the granter's expiry, and a granter with no
    live entry is refused.
  - `vtc/admin/invites/create` requires an unrestricted admin. It writes
    a community-wide admin entry, and a context admin could previously
    invite a DID it controls into one.

title: fix(vtc-service)!: a community backup travels only over DIDComm or TSP
body:
## Summary

A community backup now travels only over a channel that is confidential end to end: DIDComm or TSP. It is never sent over REST or HTTPS.

The backup request carries its password, and the backup itself carries the community's signing key bundle. Over REST, both exist in plaintext wherever TLS terminates. Whoever holds that point could sign as the community.

The VTA side of the same change is #1733. The spec is trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#646, published in trust-tasks 0.23. It covers `vtc/backup/{export,import}` 0.1 and the node-neutral `backup/*` 0.1 family. Every type and URI here comes from the generated 0.23 bindings.

Export and import are the backup Trust Tasks, dispatched by the spine. Refusing HTTPS is the spec's confidentiality policy, applied on the same Trust Task. There is no other backup API. The two bearer routes remain only as 403 stubs.

## Changes

### VTC

- **Bearer routes:** `POST /v1/backup/export` and `POST /v1/backup/import` always answer 403, and the message names the fix. Their request-body types and the 64 MiB import body cap are removed.
- **Trust Tasks:** these tasks are refused on the REST binding with `permissionDenied`:
  - `vtc/backup/export/0.1`
  - `backup/initiate-export/0.1`
  - `backup/initiate-import/0.1`
  - `backup/finalize-import/0.1`

  The check runs after the super-admin check, and before any state is serialized, a slot is opened or the password is used. `get-chunk`, `put-chunk`, `complete-export` and `abort` carry only ciphertext or handles, so they are unaffected.
- **Authority:** unchanged. Every verb still requires an unrestricted administrator, read from the signer's ACL row.
- **Audit before release:** `export_inner` writes the `BackupExported` row before returning the envelope, and refuses the export if the write fails. It now also refuses when the VTC has no audit trail at all. Before, it released the backup unrecorded. This covers `vtc/backup/export` and `backup/initiate-export`.
- The boot message for an interrupted import no longer points at the retired REST route.

### vtc-client

- `export_backup` runs `backup/initiate-export`, then `get-chunk` for every chunk, then `complete-export`, over the client's DIDComm or TSP session. It checks every chunk against the manifest, and the whole against the committed SHA-256 and size.
- `import_backup` runs `initiate-import`, then `put-chunk` for every chunk, then `finalize-import`, which carries the password. A committed import now reports `status: committed`.
- Both refuse without a session (`VtcError::Session`), before anything is sent.
- **New `VtcClient::shutdown`:** it closes a DIDComm or TSP session. Before this, a session client could not release its mediator connection.
- The hand-written `task::BACKUP_EXPORT` and `task::BACKUP_IMPORT` URIs are removed.
- New dependencies: `sha2` and `base64` (workspace).

### vta-sdk

- **DIDComm Trust Task replies:** the client's DIDComm arm required the binding envelope type on every reply. The VTC types its reply as the reply document itself, so every `VtcClient` admin document over DIDComm failed. The new `DIDCommSession::send_and_wait_trust_task` accepts either carriage. A document-typed reply is accepted only when its body is that document, and it is either `<request type>#response` or a `trust-task-error`. Correlation, authcrypt and reply-proof verification are unchanged.

### cnm

- `cnm backup export` and `cnm backup import` connect with `vtc::connect_end_to_end`. It uses TSP when the VTC advertises it, falls back to DIDComm if TSP fails, and uses DIDComm when TSP is not advertised. There is no REST fallback.
- Both close the session on every path out.
- `cnm` now builds `vtc-client` with `tsp`, which includes `didcomm`.

### Test harness

- `MockVtcDidcomm` now signs replies with the VTC did:peer's own Ed25519 key, not a key its DID document does not list. A client that verifies reply proofs can then check them.

- `docs/03-vtc/backup-restore.md` describes the channel rule, the chunked transfer and the limits. The bearer-route and REST rate-limit text is removed.

- `POST /v1/backup/{export,import}` always answer 403.
- The backup Trust Tasks are refused over `POST /v1/trust-tasks`.

- `vtc-client::import_backup` returns the `finalize-import` reply, whose commit status is `committed` rather than `imported`.
- `vtc_client::task::{BACKUP_EXPORT, BACKUP_IMPORT}` are removed.

## Tests

- **New:** `a_backup_round_trips_over_didcomm` (`tests/backup_didcomm.rs`, `--features didcomm-harness`). It drives the real `vtc-client` through a mediator to the production DIDComm listener:
  - an export that spans several chunks, audited before release;
  - an import preview of the same backup;
  - a wrong password, refused.

  This is the end-to-end test that was missing. It found the vta-sdk reply-type fault, the harness signing key and the leaked session above.
- `an_export_over_rest_is_refused`
- `an_export_with_no_audit_trail_is_refused`
- `the_password_bearing_verbs_are_refused_over_rest` (`backup/*`)
- `backup_export_and_import_are_refused_over_rest` (bearer routes, integration)
- `a_backup_needs_a_session`
- `backup_chunks_encode_and_digest_consistently` (vtc-client)
- The existing `backup/*` round-trip and `vtc/backup/export` tests now run over DIDComm.
- The bearer-route error-code tests are removed. Their codes are covered on the Trust Task door.

title: fix(vtc-service)!: a community backup travels only over DIDComm or TSP (#1755)
body:
fix(vtc-service)!: a community backup travels only over DIDComm or TSP (#1755)

* fix(vtc-service)!: a community backup travels only over DIDComm or TSP

The backup request carries its password, and the backup carries the
community's signing key bundle. Over REST both exist in plaintext wherever
TLS terminates.

- POST /v1/backup/export and /v1/backup/import always answer 403.
- vtc/backup/export and backup/initiate-export, initiate-import and
  finalize-import are refused on the REST binding, after the super-admin
  check and before any state is serialized, a slot is opened or the
  password is used. The chunks are ciphertext and are unaffected.
- The export audit row is still written before the envelope is returned,
  and a VTC with no audit trail now refuses to export instead of releasing
  the backup unrecorded.
- vtc-client export_backup and import_backup use the backup/* chunked
  transfer over a DIDComm or TSP session, verifying every chunk and the
  whole, and refuse without a session.
- cnm backup connects to the VTC over TSP, or DIDComm when the VTC
  advertises no TSP, and has no REST fallback.

Implements trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#646.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* fix(vtc-service): prove the backup round trip over a live DIDComm session

Merging main and driving vtc-client's backup against the production
DIDComm listener through a mediator (new tests/backup_didcomm.rs) found
three faults the per-side tests could not:

- vta-sdk demanded the binding envelope type on every Trust Task reply,
  but the VTC types its reply as the reply document itself. Every
  VtcClient admin document over DIDComm failed. The SDK's DIDComm arm now
  accepts either carriage, and a document-typed reply only when its body
  is that document answering this request.
- The DIDComm harness signed replies with a key the VTC's did:peer does
  not list, so a client that verifies reply proofs refused them. It now
  signs as the DID's own Ed25519 key.
- VtcClient had no way to close its session, so cnm backup leaked it.
  VtcClient::shutdown closes it, and cnm backup calls it on every path.

Also: drop vtc-client's hand-written vtc/backup URIs (unused) and name
the bearer stubs' URIs from the generated specs; the 403 stubs lose the
64 MiB body cap; the boot message and backup docs no longer point at the
retired REST routes.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* test(vtc-service): witness backup/export's declared code end to end; drop the unbound import witnesses

vtc/backup/import/0.1 is no longer bound, so its conformance witness and its
decryptionFailed census witness go. The export's passwordTooShort witness is
back in tests/backup.rs: a super-admin sends a too-short password through the
spine over each end-to-end transport the harness offers (DIDComm and TSP) and
the reply carries the declared code.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* test(vtc-service): cnm backup over REST is refused with the transport named

A community backup moves only over an end-to-end transport, so the live cnm test now checks the REST connection is refused before anything is exported. The export and import round trip is held in tests/backup.rs over each end-to-end transport.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

  Implements two follow-ups to the configurable bridge role map (VGI #84),

    anyone asking. A repository leaves `stale` when a projectRoles job
    queued after the report succeeds.

    whose role is the observed one. A revert weighs as revoking own when
    the role is at or above the one own projects to. Without a report the
    default map is assumed. A namespace admin gets no forge role under any
    map.

### Security

- **acl**: No principal widens its own entry, and no grant exceeds its granter (VTI-ACL-052, VTI-ACL-053) ([#1738](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1738))

* security(acl)!: no principal widens its own entry, and no grant exceeds its granter (VTI-ACL-052, VTI-ACL-053)

  A context-scoped admin, such as a companion service's credential
  (`--role admin --contexts vgi-bridge`), could raise its own authority.
  `update_acl` had no self check and no test either way. Tests written
  against main confirm every case below. Adding a foreign context or
  raising the role was already refused. What went through was clearing
  any narrowing on the caller's own entry, and minting a sibling entry
  that carried none of it:

  - Self-update to clear its capability narrowing, drop its key filter,
    or extend its expiry. All three succeeded.
  - A create for another DID it controls, in the same context, with none
    of its own narrowing: full capabilities, no key filter, no expiry.
  - An update that cleared another entry's narrowing past what the caller
    itself held.
  - Self role change (`acl/change-role`).
  - Rotation (`acl/swap-key`) rebuilt the entry field by field. It dropped
    `expires_at`, `allowed_keys`, `approve_scope` and the step-up fields,
    so a one-hour bootstrap grant became permanent. It also dropped
    `created_by`. This violated VTI-CLT-029.
  - An initiator could grant approve authority it did not hold
    (VTI-ACL-042).
  - A context admin could update or delete an entry that also acts in a
    context it does not administer, because overlap was enough.

  VTA (`operations/acl.rs`, the choke point for REST, DIDComm, TSP and the
  Trust Task spine):

  - update and change-role refuse the caller's own entry (VTI-ACL-052).
    Delete already did.
  - create, update and change-role measure the resulting entry against
    the caller's stored entry (`validate_within_caller`, VTI-ACL-053). The
    entry must not exceed the caller's effective capabilities (additive
    ones stay under VTI-ACL-033), key filter, expiry, or confer authority
    (VTI-ACL-042). A caller with no live entry writes nothing.
  - update, change-role and delete require the caller to cover every
    context the entry acts or approves in, not just overlap
    (VTI-ACL-050 as tightened).
  - update re-runs the role and act-scope checks on the patched entry, so
    a role change alone cannot turn "nowhere" into "everywhere".
  - swap-key copies the entry exactly and only moves the subject. It
    refuses an expired entry (VTI-CLT-029).

  VTC (`routes/acl.rs`, `routes/admin/invites.rs`,
  `routes/members/update.rs`):

  - An `acl/grant` rewrite of your own entry is refused. Before, a re-grant
    with no `expiresAt` made a time-boxed admin permanent.
  - `acl/change-role` refuses your own entry in either direction; the
    ceremony already refused self-promotion.
  - `vtc/members/update` refuses a role or label change on your own entry.
  - Rewrite, change-role and revoke (including scoped revoke) require
    full coverage for every role, not only admin targets.
  - A grant cannot outlive the granter's expiry, and a granter with no
    live entry is refused.
  - `vtc/admin/invites/create` requires an unrestricted admin. It writes
    a community-wide admin entry, and a context admin could previously
    invite a DID it controls into one.

title: feat(vtc)!: serve acl/{show,list,update,revoke} as Trust Tasks on the spine
body:
## Why

The VTC served only `acl/grant` and `acl/change-role` as Trust Tasks. Listing the ACL, showing an entry and revoking one existed only as bearer REST routes. So the VTI-ACL-050 full-cover check on revoke (#1738) lived on one door, and a community could not take authority away with a signed document on any transport.

## Change

### Server (`vtc-service`)

- `acl/show`, `acl/list`, `acl/update` and `acl/revoke` are dispatched by the spine (`trust_tasks/acl_tasks.rs`).
  - Authority is the verified signer's ACL row, read when the document runs.
  - Payloads are validated against the generated `trust-tasks-rs` 0.23 schemas.
- **One code path.** The operations are `routes::acl::{list_entries, show_entry, revoke_entry, plan_update}`. `GET /v1/acl`, `GET /v1/acl/{did}` and `DELETE /v1/acl/{did}` are thin adapters over them, with no REST-only behaviour.
- **`acl/update`** is planned by `plan_grant` with the role held fixed. It therefore inherits every check #1738 added to grant:
  - VTI-ACL-052: no self-modification.
  - VTI-ACL-050: full cover of the entry.
  - VTI-ACL-053: bounded by the granter.

  It also refuses:
  - a missing entry (`acl/update:notFound`);
  - a narrowing (`acl/update:narrowingNotPermitted`; use revoke);
  - a role (`acl/update:roleChangeNotPermitted`);
  - the VTA-only members `allowedKeys`, `approve` and `stepUp`.

  Widening an admin needs the passkey gesture bound to the document, and community-wide authority also needs another admin's consent. Both go through the gate `acl/grant` uses, now shared as `settle_signed_gate`. There is no bearer route for update.
- **`acl/revoke`**:
  - Emits `acl/revoke:subjectNotPresent` and `acl/revoke:lastAuthorityProtected`.
  - Keeps full cover, the self-revoke refusal, the member-row guard and the attrition lock.
  - Now also revokes the subject's live sessions on a full removal.
- **`acl/list`** gains `direction` (`acting-in`, `subtree`, `any`).
- **`acl/grant` hardening**, found while sharing the planner:
  - Restating an admin with a later expiry, or none, counts as widening and needs the gesture.
  - A rewrite that reduces authority revokes the subject's sessions.
  - The audit row names the actor who made the write, not the entry's original creator. An update is audited as `AclUpdated`.
- Proof-REQUIRED census: 46 → 48. Design notes are updated.
- `admin_consent.rs` is untouched.

### Clients

- **`vtc-client`**: `acl_{list, list_all, show, grant, update, change_role, revoke}`.
  - Requests are built and schema-checked from the generated types, then sent as signed documents on whatever transport the client holds.
  - Replies are decoded into the generated `Response` types.
- **`cnm`**: `cnm access {list,show,grant,update,change-role,revoke}` administers the community's own (VTC) ACL. `cnm acl` stays the VTA's.

## Breaking (test deployments only)

- `DELETE /v1/acl/{did}` now answers **200** with the canonical `acl/revoke#response` (`{"entry": null | AclEntry}`) instead of 204.
- `?scopes=` naming no scope is refused with 400. It used to be read as a full removal.
- `admin-ui/openapi.json` and `wire.ts` are regenerated, and `tsc` is clean.

## Tests

- **`trust_tasks::acl_tasks`** (16): each task through the spine with each transport's context, allowed and refused:
  - self-modification;
  - full cover;
  - granter bound (contexts and expiry);
  - narrowing, role and not-found codes;
  - the gesture for widening an admin;
  - `lastAuthorityProtected`;
  - a relayed document;
  - unsigned documents refused with `proofRequired`.
- **`acl_canonical`**: parity between REST and signed documents for show, list, revoke (reduce, remove, refusals, and the declared code) and update ≡ grant. Also covers the empty-scopes refusal.
- **`acl_trust_tasks`** (new, `tsp,didcomm-harness`): each task end to end over a live mediator and HTTPS, with the answers compared across transports. `TestTspPeer` gains `request_tsp` for this.
- **`vtc-client`** unit tests cover payload validation. **`cnm`** parse tests cover `access`.

Results of the final local run follow in a comment.

  (acl/update:notFound), a narrowing (acl/update:narrowingNotPermitted),
  a role (acl/update:roleChangeNotPermitted), and the VTA-only members
  allowedKeys/approve/stepUp. Widening an admin needs the bound passkey
  gesture, and community-wide authority another admin's consent, through
  the same gate acl/grant uses (settle_signed_gate).
- acl/revoke emits acl/revoke:subjectNotPresent and
  acl/revoke:lastAuthorityProtected, and now revokes the subject's live
  sessions on a full removal too.
- acl/list gains `direction` (acting-in, subtree, any).
- acl/grant: restating an admin with a later or no expiry now counts as
  widening (needs the gesture); a rewrite that reduces authority revokes
  the subject's sessions; the audit row names the actual actor rather
  than the entry's original creator, and an update is audited as
  AclUpdated.

BREAKING: DELETE /v1/acl/{did} answers 200 with the canonical
acl/revoke#response ({"entry": null | AclEntry}) instead of 204, and
`?scopes=` naming no scope is refused (400) rather than read as a full
removal. openapi.json and wire.ts are regenerated.

Clients
- vtc-client: acl_{list,list_all,show,grant,update,change_role,revoke},
  sent as signed documents over the session or HTTPS, decoded into the
  generated response types. acl_update has no bearer fallback.
- cnm: `cnm access {list,show,grant,update,change-role,revoke}` for the
  community's own (VTC) ACL.

Tests: each task through the spine as REST, DIDComm and TSP hand it over,
allowed and refused; REST/document parity in acl_canonical; unsigned
documents refused; and a live-mediator test (acl_trust_tasks) driving
each task over DIDComm, TSP and HTTPS. The proof-REQUIRED census moves
from 46 to 48.

* test(vtc): form the TSP relationship once per peer; not-found reason is not_found

title: vtc-client-v0.7.7
body:
### Added

- **vtc**: Git-ns/account/unlink and cnm git unlink ([#1746](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1746))

* fix(vtc): one forge account per member, and only current members' accounts count

  - Link uniqueness (git-ns/account/link item 4) was already enforced under
    the git-ns store lock. The check and the recording are now one step
    under the member-row lock too, and a regression test pins it: a
    second member completing a link to an already-linked forge id ends
    `failed` and the account stays with the first.
  - A departed member who held no git right kept their linked accounts for
    good: the link deletion sat after sweep_departures' early return for
    "no departed member held a right". It is now its own pass in the
    lifecycle sweep (git-ns/account/link, Consent/purpose: MUST delete it
    when the member leaves).
  - linked_accounts, which the role projection and drift adoption read,
    now holds only current members' accounts. A member whose access lapsed
    but who has not left keeps the account, so nobody else can link it,
    but it projects no role.
  - GET /v1/git-ns/accounts gains memberCurrent, and the console's Repos
    plugin no longer offers adoption for an account whose member is not
    current. The daemon already refused that adoption.

- **vtc/git-ns**: Separation of duties and break-glass for elevated git rights ([#1745](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1745))

* feat(vtc-service): re-project git roles, and use the bridge's reported role map

  Implements two follow-ups to the configurable bridge role map (VGI #84),
  spec-first in trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#639.

  git-ns/bridge/event 0.3 (roleMapReported)
  - Served beside 0.1 and 0.2; all three are read as 0.3 by one handler.
  - The report is refused malformedRequest when a map is unordered
    (own >= maintain >= commit, commit <= write) or lists a repository
    twice, and permissionDenied when a repos/stale resource lies outside
    the namespace. Otherwise it is kept on the namespace (git_ns::role_map),
    and only while the same bridge DID serves it.
  - Each stale active or orphaned repository has its roles digest
    forgotten, so the projector re-sends its complete desiredRoles without
    anyone asking. A repository leaves `stale` when a projectRoles job
    queued after the report succeeds.
  - drift/resolve adopt derives the right from the map: the lowest right
    whose role is the observed one. A revert weighs as revoking own when
    the role is at or above the one own projects to. Without a report the
    default map is assumed. A namespace admin gets no forge role under any
    map.

  git-ns/roles/reproject 0.1
  - Open to a community administrator, or to git.ns.admin on the namespace
    by explicit record. A repository owner is refused. Covers a namespace
    (every active or orphaned repository) or one repository. Normal consent
    class, policy action roles.reproject, audited as
    gitNs.roles.reprojected. Refused with manualMode or noForgeAccess.
  - `cnm git reproject <resource> [--reason]` and
    vtc-client git_ns_reproject.

  - The namespace and repository rows carry the effective role map
    (roleMap, roleMapSource, roleMapStale).
  - The people tables show each person's effective forge role, and "no
    forge role" for a namespace admin.

    repository's map. rightForForgeRole is removed.

    header gain a "Re-project roles" button.

  (or above) now weighs as revoking own, because write is the role own
  projects to there. Before, it weighed as revoking maintain.

    header gain a "Re-project roles" button.

  (or above) now weighs as revoking own, because write is the role own
  projects to there. Before, it weighed as revoking maintain.



### Security

- **acl**: No principal widens its own entry, and no grant exceeds its granter (VTI-ACL-052, VTI-ACL-053) ([#1738](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1738))

* security(acl)!: no principal widens its own entry, and no grant exceeds its granter (VTI-ACL-052, VTI-ACL-053)

  A context-scoped admin, such as a companion service's credential
  (`--role admin --contexts vgi-bridge`), could raise its own authority.
  `update_acl` had no self check and no test either way. Tests written
  against main confirm every case below. Adding a foreign context or
  raising the role was already refused. What went through was clearing
  any narrowing on the caller's own entry, and minting a sibling entry
  that carried none of it:

  - Self-update to clear its capability narrowing, drop its key filter,
    or extend its expiry. All three succeeded.
  - A create for another DID it controls, in the same context, with none
    of its own narrowing: full capabilities, no key filter, no expiry.
  - An update that cleared another entry's narrowing past what the caller
    itself held.
  - Self role change (`acl/change-role`).
  - Rotation (`acl/swap-key`) rebuilt the entry field by field. It dropped
    `expires_at`, `allowed_keys`, `approve_scope` and the step-up fields,
    so a one-hour bootstrap grant became permanent. It also dropped
    `created_by`. This violated VTI-CLT-029.
  - An initiator could grant approve authority it did not hold
    (VTI-ACL-042).
  - A context admin could update or delete an entry that also acts in a
    context it does not administer, because overlap was enough.

  VTA (`operations/acl.rs`, the choke point for REST, DIDComm, TSP and the
  Trust Task spine):

  - update and change-role refuse the caller's own entry (VTI-ACL-052).
    Delete already did.
  - create, update and change-role measure the resulting entry against
    the caller's stored entry (`validate_within_caller`, VTI-ACL-053). The
    entry must not exceed the caller's effective capabilities (additive
    ones stay under VTI-ACL-033), key filter, expiry, or confer authority
    (VTI-ACL-042). A caller with no live entry writes nothing.
  - update, change-role and delete require the caller to cover every
    context the entry acts or approves in, not just overlap
    (VTI-ACL-050 as tightened).
  - update re-runs the role and act-scope checks on the patched entry, so
    a role change alone cannot turn "nowhere" into "everywhere".
  - swap-key copies the entry exactly and only moves the subject. It
    refuses an expired entry (VTI-CLT-029).

  VTC (`routes/acl.rs`, `routes/admin/invites.rs`,
  `routes/members/update.rs`):

  - An `acl/grant` rewrite of your own entry is refused. Before, a re-grant
    with no `expiresAt` made a time-boxed admin permanent.
  - `acl/change-role` refuses your own entry in either direction; the
    ceremony already refused self-promotion.
  - `vtc/members/update` refuses a role or label change on your own entry.
  - Rewrite, change-role and revoke (including scoped revoke) require
    full coverage for every role, not only admin targets.
  - A grant cannot outlive the granter's expiry, and a granter with no
    live entry is refused.
  - `vtc/admin/invites/create` requires an unrestricted admin. It writes
    a community-wide admin entry, and a context admin could previously
    invite a DID it controls into one.
