title: Close the admin-promotion entry in the divergence register
body:
One of the three entries #35 recorded in Appendix F.2 has been resolved. It
leaves the table and is recorded in **F.5 Closed**, which is what the register
says it does with a divergence that has been closed ("An entry leaves the tables
above when the divergence is closed, and is recorded here so that a reader can
tell a register that is being worked from one that has been abandoned"). No new
marker is introduced: F.5's row form is `| Requirement | Closed by |`, and the
requirement column of a closed row carries no `*(observed)*` qualifier, so the
`*(observed)*` on the F.2 row does not travel with it.

The change that closed it is OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#1658
(merged 22 September 2026), which closes
OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#1645. **Those numbers are in the commit
message rather than in the row**, because every other row in F.5 names the
behaviour and not a change in one implementation's history, and F.6 says why:
"it does not need the implementation to be named — the register describes
behaviour so that it is useful to every implementer facing the same question."
Say the word if the working group would rather the rows cited the change, and
I will add it to this one and to the four already there in the same form.

## What the entry required, and what was verified against the code

The entry's resolution had four parts. Each was checked in the merged tree,
not taken from the change's own description.

- **The step-up is a rule the decision point applies, not a check in a
  handler.** `role_change_via_pipeline` took a `step_up: bool` from its caller,
  which made the handler the gate. It now resolves the elevation itself from
  the caller's live session (`acl::elevation::verified`, which reads the
  session row rather than the bearer token), and `ceremony::decide` applies the
  host invariants after the policy and unconditionally — `StepUpForAdmin`
  (VTI-OPS-051) and `SelfPromotion` (VTI-OPS-050). There is no configuration in
  which they lapse and no policy edit that reaches them.
- **`acl/grant` is gated too**, on the *widening* rather than on the write
  (`elevation::widens_admin_authority`), because a grant writes an entry rather
  than moving one and so has no transition to hang an invariant on. Re-stating
  an entry at the role and scopes it already holds — how the console edits a
  label — confers nothing; re-stating it across more contexts, or across all of
  them, confers authority without the role ever changing, and demands the
  elevation.
- **Nothing was lost in the move.** Self-promotion refusal became the
  invariant; the promote lock moved from the update handler into
  `ceremony::orchestrate`, where the window it closes actually lives; the
  already-an-administrator re-check generalised into a compare-and-swap re-read
  under that lock, so a racing role write is a `409` rather than an overwrite;
  the role-change policy and the role-credential re-mint run on every caller of
  the pipeline.
- **The console promotes through `acl/change-role`** (`PATCH /v1/acl/{did}`
  with `fromRole`/`toRole`), stepping the session up first, and
  **`vtc/members/update` answers `adminRoleForbidden`** — now a *witnessed*
  code in the node's error-code census rather than a declared-but-untested one,
  with the census's unwitnessed count lowered accordingly.

**The related escalation was also fixed, and the closed row records it**,
because it is the part a reader of the register learns most from. The
role-change route never ran `validate_acl_modification`, and the guard it did
run only fired on a subject that was *already* administrative. An entry's
context list means *nowhere* under a non-administrative role and *everywhere*
under an administrative one, so an administrator of one context could take a
member scoped nowhere to the administrative role and land a community-wide
administrator without ever naming a context they do not hold. It is checked
now, decoded through the act-scope reading rather than by testing the list for
emptiness.

## The other two entries are untouched, deliberately

- **The bearer-token entry** (VTI-OPS-020/021/024/093, the 47 tasks served over
  a bearer route with no operation document) is only partly addressed. The
  document dispatcher now enforces, but the routes themselves have not moved.
- **The dispatcher-leniency entry** (VTI-OPS-021/024) was addressed by
  OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#1659, and I checked whether it is now
  closed. It is not, quite, and the difference matters:
  - The **acceptance window and the required time of issue are closed
    unconditionally** — a 10-minute window with 60s skew, `issuedAt` required,
    no flag, every binding that reaches the dispatcher.
  - The **proof requirement is enforced unconditionally on the HTTP binding**,
    where there is no transport-authenticated sender to stand in.
  - On the messaging transports it is enforced only when `[trust_tasks]
    require_declared_proof` is set, and that **defaults to false**, because
    `openvtc-core` does not yet sign its documents (OpenVTC/openvtc-core#371).
    While it is off, a proofless document for a task whose definition requires
    a proof is still accepted on those transports from a transport-
    authenticated sender, narrowed to exactly the tasks the entry lists and
    logged at `warn` naming VTI-OPS-021 each time.

  So the divergence is narrowed, bounded and has a stated removal point, but
  the behaviour the entry describes is still reachable in the shipped default.
  That is a different claim from "closed", and the register is only worth
  reading if the two are kept apart — so I have left the entry alone rather
  than closing it, or half-closing it with a qualifier the register does not
  have. It should close when the flag's default flips, and that is one line
  then.

## Render

`npm run render` completes and `docs/index.html` carries the moved row under
F.5 with no trace of it in F.2. No other file changes.

title: Close the admin-promotion entry in the divergence register (#37)
body:
Close the admin-promotion entry in the divergence register (#37)

The entry recorded by #35 leaves F.2 and is recorded in F.5, which is
what the register does with a divergence that has been closed.

Promotion to the administrative role now runs through `acl/change-role`,
and the step-up is a host invariant the decision pipeline applies around
the policy rather than a check in a handler. The elevation is resolved
at the decision point from the caller's live session, so it is a fact
about the caller rather than an assertion by whichever route asked, and
every path onto the same entry is gated by the same one. Self-promotion
is refused by a second invariant. `acl/grant` of the administrative role
checks the same predicate one layer out, on the widening rather than on
the write. The serialisation and the role-change policy moved with the
promotion, the already-administrative re-check generalised into a
compare-and-swap under the same lock, the console was pointed at the
role-change operation, and `vtc/members/update` refuses `role: admin`
with `adminRoleForbidden`, witnessed by the node's error-code census.

Closing it also closed an escalation the entry did not record: the
role-change path never checked the resulting entry against the caller's
own scope, and a context list means nowhere under a non-administrative
role and everywhere under an administrative one, so an administrator of
one context could promote a subject scoped nowhere and land a
community-wide administrator without naming a context they do not hold.
The closed entry carries that, because a reader of the register should
learn what the change turned out to be about.

Closed by OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#1658, which closes
OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#1645. The row itself names
behaviour rather than a change in one implementation's history, as every
other row in F.5 does: the register is written to be useful to every
implementer facing the same question.

The other two entries #35 recorded stay where they are. The bearer-token
entry is only partly addressed, and the dispatcher-leniency entry is
addressed on one binding and behind a flag that defaults to off on the
others, which is not the same as closed.

title: fix(consent): an Approve can no longer be settled as a Deny by its own window closing (VTI-40)
body:
Reported, with a patch, by the Keyring team as **VTI-40**. Thank you: the diagnosis was exact and their `decide()` patch is the core of the popup half below.

## The defect

`confirm.tsx`'s `decide()` sent `RUNTIME_CONSENT_RESULT` without awaiting it and called `window.close()` in the same tick. The background treats the consent window's removal as a denial (`settle(false, …)` from `windows.onRemoved`). Chrome does not order the two events at the service worker, so when the removal arrived first an **Approve was settled as a Deny**, and the result then reached an already-settled consent and was dropped. No error was shown. Every consent surface uses `decide()`: site consent, task consent, the WebAuthn approver, and persona disclosure.

Related: `raiseDisclosureConsent` registered no `onRemoved` at all, so closing a disclosure window left the request pending forever.

## The fix, in two layers

1. **The popup sends, waits for the ack, then closes.** `consent-result.ts` `consentResultSender` awaits the send, swallows errors, then closes. This is Keyring's `Promise.resolve(sendMessage(...)).catch(...).finally(close)`, plus handling for a synchronous throw. It also reports one decision only, because the window now stays up for the round trip and a second click must not send a contradicting answer.
2. **The background acknowledges only after settling.** The result handler calls `deliverConsentResult`, then `sendResponse({ ok: true, matched })`, so the popup's await resolves once the decision has landed.
3. **Close-means-deny waits a grace period (defence in depth).** `consent-window.ts` `openConsentWindow` now owns the create, fail-deny and close-deny lifecycle for all three raisers. On removal it waits `CLOSE_GRACE_MS` (1s) before denying. A microtask or zero timeout would not be enough, because the result is a separate task on the worker's queue. `settle` is idempotent, so a decision that arrives within the grace wins. The grace can only turn a would-be denial into the decision the operator actually sent. Only a result carrying `approved: true` ever approves.
4. **Disclosure consent now settles as a denial on close**, because it goes through the same helper.
5. **Access pane:** the subject DID placeholder now reads `did:key:z6Mk… or did:peer:2…`.

CLAUDE.md gains a short section on the invariant and what breaks it.

## Tests

`tests/consent-window-race.test.mts` (12 tests) uses an in-memory `chrome.windows` stand-in with stepped timers:
- removal before an approve result → **approved**; result then removal → approved
- closed with no decision → **denied** after the grace (pending entry and listener released); a late result cannot overturn it
- **disclosure window closed → denied**
- window creation failure → denied immediately; an unrelated window closing does nothing
- source guard: all three raisers call `openConsentWindow`, `background.ts` has no raw `chrome.windows.create(` or `chrome.windows.onRemoved`, and the result handler calls `sendResponse`
- popup: closes only after the ack, still closes when the send rejects or throws, and sends one decision on a double click

`npm run lint`, `npm test` (777 pass) and `npm run build` in `packages/extension` are all green. There is no version bump because the change is extension-only.

## Pre-merge checklist

- [x] No new reqwest::Client::new() / bare fetch(); all clients have finite timeouts (R1.2) (n/a, no network)
- [x] No lock held across a network await (R1.3)
- [x] No local state committed before its remote effect, or the flow is resumable with an idempotency key (R2.1)
- [x] Every retry is bounded + backed off; non-idempotent ops are not blind-retried (R1.4) (n/a)
- [x] Accept/poll/listen loops survive transient errors (R1.5) (n/a)
- [x] Acks/deletes happen only after durable handoff (R1.6): the consent ack is sent only after settle
- [x] New/changed wire types: camelCase, deny_unknown_fields where security-relevant, schema registered, all consumers (incl. JS) updated (R3.*): the `RUNTIME_CONSENT_RESULT` response is internal to the extension and has one consumer
- [x] Config absence = most restrictive; fail-closed if enforcement can't start (R5.*): a window that could not be opened, or was closed with no decision, still denies
- [x] Logs/status claim only what was verified; background-job failures are surfaced (R6.*)
- [x] "Process dies on the next line" answered for every mutation touched (R2.1): if the worker dies during the grace, the in-memory consent dies with it and the caller's promise dies too, as it did before
- [x] Deviations from this guide flagged explicitly with rule numbers: none; this closes an R7.2 gap (a lost consent decision)

title: trust-tasks-rs-v0.22.1
body:
### Added

- **persona**: Attribute/get — read one attribute, by identifier ([#616](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/616))

The family had no narrow read, and the shape of the workaround is the
  argument for the task. A client revealing one value called
  `persona/attribute/list` with a `typePrefix` and `includeValues`, then
  filtered to the id it already held — so showing one email address
  decrypted and returned every email address the holder has, and the audit
  trail recorded a listing of the pool rather than a decision about one
  fact.

  - Values are withheld unless asked for, and a `sensitivity: high` value
    needs a second flag, on the same two-step as `attribute/list`. A
    withheld value is stated (`valueWithheld`), never left to inference: a
    consumer reading an absent value as "there is none" shows the holder an
    empty field where their passport number is.
  - `version` reads a retained earlier version, which is what makes "what
    did I show them in March" answerable — a disclosure record and a pinned
    entry both name one. A purged version is `versionPurged`, never a
    silent fall back to the current value.
  - `retainedVersions` names the versions still held, so a holder deciding
    whether to purge can see what purging would take away rather than being
    asked to make an irreversible decision blind.

  One identifier, never a list: a maintainer that accepted several would
  recreate the enumeration the task exists to avoid, one call later.

title: security(persona)!: holder authority is granted, never inherited from a role
body:
Closes question 1 of §7 in `docs/05-design-notes/persona-context-first.md`, and records the answers to the other three.

### The defect

`persona-holder` exists because **no role** carries authority over the holder's pool. Super-admin carried it anyway — `authorize` skipped the ACL read for an unrestricted admin and `decide` returned `Ok` unconditionally — which left the capability's premise true only of the roles nobody automates with. The unrestricted admin credential is the one most likely to be sitting in a script, and it read the attribute pool, the faces over it and the disclosure history with no ACL entry saying so.

### The change

The grant is now the only way in, for every role. A super-admin can still grant itself the capability — it is the same credential that grants — so this is not a boundary it cannot cross. It is the difference between crossing it and crossing it **deliberately**: the grant is an ACL write, audited and revocable on its own, where the inherited form left no trace.

The refusal names the fix, per the workspace's error-suggests-the-command rule:

> It requires an ACL entry granted the `persona-holder` capability, and no role carries it — not even super-admin … Grant it deliberately: `pnm acl update --did <did> --capabilities persona-holder`.

### For operators upgrading

`pnm acl update --did <did> --capabilities persona-holder`, or `pnm contexts create --admin-holder` when provisioning a client that is the holder's own. The provisioning paths already carry an existing grant across a credential rollover, and `create_acl` already refuses a context-scoped admin from minting one — neither needed changing.

### Tests

The 30 integration tests that broke were the defect on display: the fixture authenticated as an unrestricted admin and reached the pool. It now grants the capability explicitly, `authed` alone is what an ungranted caller looks like, and `the_grant_reaches_the_pool_and_nothing_else_does` holds both halves — including that the refusal names the capability.

One test needed a second identity (`OTHER_SEED`): it needs a granted holder and an ungranted caller *at the same moment*, and a grant is keyed by DID. SPEC §7.2 item 6 refuses a document whose issuer disagrees with the transport identity, so the second caller signs with its own seed rather than borrowing the holder's.

### Also

§7 of the design note is rewritten from four open questions into four decisions with their reasoning — including that ratifying the agent-scoped correlation index surfaced a live probe oracle on `persona/local/profile/put`, closed in dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#609.

CI set run locally: fmt, clippy `-D warnings`, workspace tests (4819), `-p vtc-service -p vtc-client` (1865).

title: security(vtc)!: a declared proof is required by default
body:
#1659 made the Trust Task dispatcher enforce what a specification declares, but
gated one refusal — a document carrying **no** `proof` for a task whose
specification declares one REQUIRED — behind `[trust_tasks]
require_declared_proof`, default `false`. That switch had exactly one reason,
written into its own rustdoc: `openvtc-core` built
`join-requests/{submit,status}`, `members/{self-remove,vmc}` and
`members/personhood/assert` with a deliberate "no `proof` is attached", so
enforcing would have refused every join on a community serving that client.

The same rustdoc carried the removal condition, and it was exact: *"when
`openvtc-core` signs the five documents above, the default flips and this field
goes with it."* openvtc#371 is merged and all five now sign, via
`trust_task_doc::build_signed_value`. So the default flips and the field is
gone. Divergence 2 of the VTI specification's Appendix F.2 closes rather than
merely being visible.

Refs #1641, openvtc#371. Follows #1659.

## What changed

- **`narrow_for_transitional_allowance` is deleted.** #1659 implemented the
  relaxation by *narrowing the policy value* rather than skipping the call, so
  removing it is a deletion of the narrowing, not of the enforcement:
  `spec_policy_for(..).enforce(&doc)` now runs against the registry's own
  policy, with `recipient`-REQUIRED, `issuedAt`-REQUIRED and audience binding
  untouched.
- **`TrustTasksConfig::require_declared_proof` is retired**, and the dispatcher
  no longer reads config for anything but `vtc_did`.
- A comment at the enforcement site records that nothing may reintroduce a
  per-deployment relaxation: VTI-OPS-093 forbids a binding weakening a document
  requirement on the strength of a transport property, and a switch that lets an
  operator do it is the same weakening reached by a longer path.

## A config that still carries the key

Retired, not ignored — and the two values are answered differently, because they
are different intents:

| in `config.toml` | behaviour |
|---|---|
| `require_declared_proof = true` | **warning at load**, then a normal start |
| `require_declared_proof = false` | **fails to load**, with an error naming openvtc#371 and saying the client must be upgraded |
| absent | nothing; this is the state to arrive at |

The workspace's precedent for a retired key (`[auth.step_up]`,
`[[policy.require_consent]]`) is a hard failure, and `= false` gets that: it is
an intent that can no longer be honoured at all, and starting anyway would
enforce the opposite of what the operator's file says — they would learn it from
their clients' refusals instead of from their own config. `= true` is the other
case the precedent does not cover: it asked for what the service now does
unconditionally, so the operator's intent survives intact and the only stale
thing is the line itself. Refusing to boot over a request that has already been
granted is not the proportionate answer, so it warns.

The refusal lives in the deserializer, so it holds on every path that parses an
`AppConfig`. The warning lives in `AppConfig::load` and goes to stderr rather
than `warn!`, because config is loaded *before* `init_tracing` and a `warn!`
with no subscriber installed is exactly the silence this is meant to avoid.
The key is `skip_serializing`, so a config this service writes back never hands
it to the operator again.

## Rollout — read this if you run `openvtc`

A deployment running an `openvtc` build **older than openvtc#371** sends those
five documents unsigned. After this change its **joins, status polls,
self-removals, VMC collection and personhood assertions are refused** with
`proofRequired` — correctly, but abruptly, and there is no longer a setting that
will accept them.

**The fix is to upgrade the client.**

A deployment that already sets `require_declared_proof = true` has been running
this behaviour since #1659, is unaffected by this change, and has one line to
delete.

## Tests

The `vti_ops_021_*` pair that pinned the relaxed path had its premise removed, so
it was rewritten rather than deleted — the pattern #1659 itself used when it
replaced `a_transport_authenticated_task_declares_a_proof_it_does_not_carry`.
Each rewrite says in the code why its conclusion changed.

- `vti_ops_021_a_missing_proof_is_refused_on_every_transport` replaces three
  tests (the REST refusal, the DIDComm allowance, and the DIDComm refusal with
  the flag on). One unsigned document is now driven over REST, DIDComm **and**
  TSP and must be refused on each. The old tests each asserted about a single
  transport, so between them they could have agreed with VTI-OPS-021 on two and
  disagreed on the third with nothing noticing.
- `vti_ops_021_the_same_document_signed_is_accepted_on_every_transport` is new
  and is the control: without it the test above would pass equally on a spine
  that refused every DIDComm and TSP document outright, which satisfies "the
  same requirements on every transport" by taking the community offline.
- Four config tests cover the retired key: `= false` fails to load and the error
  names what replaced it; `= true` still parses; absence is silent; and the key
  is never written back.

### The fixtures that relied on an unsigned document

**Two, and the larger one is the DIDComm/TSP harness itself.**
`TestJoinClient` built every document through `wrap_trust_task`, whose comment
read "over DIDComm the authcrypt sender authenticates the holder, so the
document carries no `proof`" — this repository's rule, not the specification's,
and exactly the one being removed. With enforcement unconditional the harness
produced a wire shape no client produces, and `join_didcomm` / `join_tsp`
stopped at `proofRequired` before reaching any of the behaviour they exist to
test (3 of 4 and 2 of 4; the pre-fix run and CI agreed on the set).

The client now signs with its own `did:peer` Ed25519 authentication key
(`<did:peer>#key-1`, resolved locally — `did:peer` needs no I/O), so the
document's `issuer` and the authcrypt sender stay the same party. That matters
beyond tidiness: the spine binds the proof to the in-band `issuer` (SPEC §4.7)
and every assertion in these tests names the applicant by its `did:peer`. One
`document()` method now serves all three senders — task-typed DIDComm,
enveloped DIDComm, TSP — so they cannot disagree about what a producer sends.
`wrap_trust_task` stays for `proof`-OPTIONAL tasks and for cases that are
*about* a missing proof; its doc says which is which.

The second:
`trust_tasks::tests::personhood::one_member_cannot_assert_personhood_for_another`
sent an unsigned `vtc/members/personhood/assert/0.1` over DIDComm and reached
its handler only through the allowance. Left alone it would now stop at
`proofRequired` and keep passing for a reason that has nothing to do with
subject binding — green, and asserting nothing. It now signs, with a real
`did:key`, so the caller identity lands where the handler reads it
(`verified_signer`, bound to the document's own `issuer`) and the refusal under
test is still the one produced.

The module's other four fixtures are unchanged and stay unsigned, which is
correct rather than lenient: `vtc/members/personhood/challenge/0.1` declares
`proof` OPTIONAL, so the transport-authenticated sender genuinely is the whole
of the caller's identity there. The helper's rustdoc now says so, instead of
pointing at the retired flag.

## Docs

`docs/05-design-notes/vtc-trust-task-proof-enforcement.md` §3, §4, §6 and §7 are
rewritten: the gate section records what it was and how its stated condition was
met, and gains the config-migration table and the rollout note above. `docs/README.md`'s
summary of the note follows. No operator doc or example config carried the key.

title: feat(persona): attribute/get — read one attribute, by identifier
body:
The persona family has no narrow read of a single attribute, and the shape of the workaround is the argument for the task.

A client revealing one value calls `persona/attribute/list` with a `typePrefix` and `includeValues`, then filters the result to the identifier it already holds. So revealing one email address decrypts and returns **every** email address the holder has, across the wire, into a client that wanted one of them — and the audit row records a listing of the pool rather than a decision about one fact. (`openvtc-core`'s `pool::reveal` is exactly this, with a comment saying the SDK has no by-id read.)

### The shape

| Member | Why |
|---|---|
| `attributeId` | One identifier, never a list — accepting several recreates the enumeration this task exists to avoid |
| `includeValue` (default false) | The disclosing path is the one a producer names, as on `attribute/list`. The audit row can then answer "did plaintext leave?" |
| `includeSensitive` (default false) | A `sensitivity: high` value needs both flags. Masking a value already received defends a screen; not sending it keeps a passport number out of a log |
| `version` | Read a retained earlier version — what makes "what did I show them in March" answerable, since a disclosure record and a pinned entry both name one |

Response is the attribute, plus:

- **`valueWithheld`** — stated, never left to inference. A consumer reading an absent `value` as "this attribute has none" shows the holder an empty field where their passport number is and concludes the record is broken.
- **`retainedVersions`** — the versions still held, names only. A holder deciding whether to purge cannot otherwise see what purging would take away, which is a live gap: the openvtc purge prompt currently has to say "any face that pins an old version" because it cannot count them.

A purged `version` is `persona/attribute/get:versionPurged` rather than `notFound` — the attribute is still there — and never a silent fall back to the current value, which would answer a question about the past with a fact about the present.

### Checks

`npm run validate` (478 specs, invalid-examples all rejected as required), `npm run check-bindings`, all four generators, `cargo fmt --all -- --check`, `cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs`, `dart analyze --fatal-infos`, the language-floor `dart format` check, and the TypeScript build.

title: fix(console): a face made in a context claims no provenance
body:
"Make a face here" in the console has never worked. It sent `provenance: "selfAsserted"` on a context-local inline entry; the schema has no such member and sets `additionalProperties: false`, so the agent refused the whole write:

> Additional properties are not allowed ('provenance' was unexpected)

**The member's absence is a rule, not a gap.** A `credentialBacked` provenance names a `credentialId` and a `claimPath`, and a value authored inside a context has nowhere to put either — so a context-local value is self-asserted by construction. Carrying the member would let a context assert that a value is attested when no credential was ever checked, over a value the issuer never saw. The spec calls it "a privilege escalation dressed as a convenience".

**Why TypeScript did not catch it.** Excess-property checking applies to an object literal assigned to a typed target; it does not reach through the inferred return type of a `.map()`, and the payload was built in a map. The generated type is correct and was no help.

So the guard is a test that reads what was actually sent. `packages/core/tests/persona.local.mjs` is new and covers all three local tasks — `local/profile/put`, `local/binding/set`, `local/profile/delete` — which had no test at all. Each absence is paired with a positive claim, per that suite's own rule that a file of "does not send X" assertions would pass an implementation that sent `{}`.

Found while writing the equivalent test on the agent side; the same defect exists in `vta-sdk` (its hand-written `InlineValue` makes `provenance` required, so *no* local write it built could conform) and in openvtc, both being fixed separately.

Ran locally: `npm run lint`, `npm run build`, `npm test` (674), and the dist guards.

body:
feat(persona): attribute/get — read one attribute, by identifier (#616)

The family had no narrow read, and the shape of the workaround is the
argument for the task. A client revealing one value called
`persona/attribute/list` with a `typePrefix` and `includeValues`, then
filtered to the id it already held — so showing one email address
decrypted and returned every email address the holder has, and the audit
trail recorded a listing of the pool rather than a decision about one
fact.

  needs a second flag, on the same two-step as `attribute/list`. A
  withheld value is stated (`valueWithheld`), never left to inference: a
  consumer reading an absent value as "there is none" shows the holder an
  empty field where their passport number is.
- `version` reads a retained earlier version, which is what makes "what
  did I show them in March" answerable — a disclosure record and a pinned
  entry both name one. A purged version is `versionPurged`, never a
  silent fall back to the current value.

  whether to purge can see what purging would take away rather than being
  asked to make an irreversible decision blind.

title: fix(consent): an Approve can no longer be settled as a Deny by its own window closing
body:
fix(consent): an Approve can no longer be settled as a Deny by its own window closing

Keyring VTI-40. The consent popup sent RUNTIME_CONSENT_RESULT without awaiting
it and called window.close() in the same tick. The background reads the
window's removal as a denial, and Chrome does not order the two events at the
service worker, so a removal that arrived first settled an Approve as a Deny;
the result then reached a settled consent and was dropped. Every consent
surface was exposed: site consent, task consent, the WebAuthn approver and
persona disclosure.

- confirm.tsx: decide() goes through consentResultSender, which awaits the
  send (errors swallowed), then closes, and reports one decision only.
- background.ts: the result handler settles, then sendResponse({ ok: true }),
  so the popup's await resolves only once the decision has landed.
- consent-window.ts: openConsentWindow owns the create / fail-deny /
  close-deny lifecycle for all three raisers; close-means-deny now waits
  CLOSE_GRACE_MS so a result already in flight still wins.
- Disclosure consent registered no onRemoved, so a closed disclosure window
  left the request pending forever; it now settles as a denial.
- Access pane: the subject DID placeholder says did:peer:2 is accepted too.

Reported with a patch by the Keyring team (VTI-40).

title: ci(release): one Release PR for every package
body:
Releases used to arrive as up to thirteen Release PRs: release-plz's for the
crates, plus one per npm package, Go module and Dart package. Merging any of
them is a push to main, and every push regenerated every other Release PR from
the new main and restarted its CI - so cutting a release meant merge, wait for
CI on the rest, merge the next, wait again.

Now `release-pr` in publish.yml runs scripts/release-pr.sh, which builds ONE
Release PR on the `release` branch:

- the crates via `release-plz update` - the same bumps, changelogs,
  cargo-semver-checks levels and `core` version group release-plz's own PR
  carried, minus the PR-opening half;
- the npm, Go and Dart packages via scripts/release-bump-{ts,go,dart}.sh
  (renamed from release-*-pr.sh, now working-tree only);
- committed once, signed off, authored as the release token's owner.

Publishing is unchanged: every publish job already keys on "this version is not
published yet", so merging the one PR releases everything in it. `release-pr`
runs after all of them and not after a failed one.

Also fixes a latent mis-scored bump in all three bump scripts: `git log | grep
-q` under pipefail reported failure whenever grep exited before git log
finished writing, silently scoring a breaking change as a patch. It downgraded
#610's `feat(persona)!` for the npm package in a dry run of this change.

check-dart-packages now reads DART_PACKAGES from release-pr.sh in place of the
removed release-dart-pr matrix.

## Cutover
After this merges, the new `release-pr` job opens the combined PR on the `release` branch. Then close #611–#614 and delete their `release-*` / `release-plz-*` branches — nothing updates them any more.

## Verified
- Dry run of `scripts/release-pr.sh` in an isolated clone (gh stubbed): one signed-off commit covering the same 11 packages as #611–#614.
- `npm run check-dart-packages` passes, and fails when a package is dropped from `DART_PACKAGES`.
- The npm bump for #610 now scores `breaking` (0.20.0) on 5/5 runs.

Not updated: comments in `trust-tasks-go/**/version.go` and `trust-tasks-dart/lib/src/runtime/version.dart` still name the old script names; editing them would trigger patch releases of four packages for a comment change.

title: trust-tasks-rs-v0.22.0
body:
### Added

- **persona**: An arrangement of faces is a world, not a facet ([#610](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/610))

`face` and `facet` share a stem and name different things — a projection
  of the pool, and an arrangement of those projections. Every consumer's UI
  had already resolved it by saying "world" on screen while the wire said
  facet, which leaves the collision in place for anyone reading both.

  - `persona/world/{put,list,delete}/1.0` — the same tasks, with `facetId`
    as `worldId`. `persona/facet/*` is retired, `supersededBy` the new
    slug, so documents already issued stay verifiable.
  - `persona/correlation/analyze/1.1` — `facetId`, `facetIds` and
    `crossesFacets` become `worldId`, `worldIds` and `crossesWorlds`. A
    breaking rename carried as a MINOR increment, which SPEC §5.2 permits
    for a `draft`. 1.0 is retired in its favour.
  - `_shared/0.1` gains `WorldColour`, the same eight colours.
    `FacetColour` stays because a retired specification's schema is frozen
    and still references it.

  Nothing else moves: same members, same semantics, same error codes.
  `facet` survives elsewhere in the registry in its ordinary English sense
  (a facet of a trust record, of an account) and is left alone.



### Fixed

- **persona**: Local/profile/put answers the correlation index only to the holder ([#609](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/609))

`correlation.matchesPoolValue` is a yes/no on "does the holder hold this
  exact value anywhere", computed from the agent-wide index — and the task
  is context-scoped, so the response handed that answer to any caller
  authorized in one context.

  A caller that can write is a caller that can guess: one value per write,
  unbounded, each answer confirming or eliminating one. No value crosses
  the boundary and none needs to — for a name, an address or a date of
  birth, confirmation is disclosure, and the guesser is inside a single
  context learning about all of them.

  So `correlation` becomes conditional: a maintainer MUST include it only
  for a caller authorized to read across the holder's contexts, and MUST
  omit the member entirely otherwise. Omit rather than soften — a coarser
  signal is still an oracle, only a slower one. The holder is still owed
  the warning that a throwaway is reusing a real value, through an audit
  entry or the holder-reach correlation task.

  The schema's own description said the index is answerable "only to the
  holder" while this response answered it to anyone in the context. The
  prose and the conformance rules now say what that means for this member.

title: feat(persona)!: an arrangement of faces is a world, not a facet
body:
`face` and `facet` share a stem and name different things: a face is a projection of the holder's pool, a facet is an arrangement of those projections. `Facet.faceIds` reads as though one contains the other.

Every consumer had already resolved it in the only place it could — pnm, the openvtc TUI and the browser console all say **world** on screen — which leaves the collision live for anyone who reads the wire as well as the screen. This makes the wire agree.

### What changes

| Was | Is | Note |
|---|---|---|
| `persona/facet/{put,list,delete}/1.0` | `persona/world/{put,list,delete}/1.0` | `facetId` → `worldId`; everything else identical |
| `persona/correlation/analyze/1.0` | `persona/correlation/analyze/1.1` | `facetId`/`facetIds`/`crossesFacets` → `worldId`/`worldIds`/`crossesWorlds` |
| — | `_shared/0.1#/$defs/WorldColour` | the same eight colours |

The predecessors are **retired with `supersededBy`**, not deleted: a retired specification stays readable and its documents stay verifiable, which is the alias window consumers migrate across. `FacetColour` stays in `_shared` for the same reason — a retired schema is frozen, so what it references has to remain.

`analyze` 1.0 → 1.1 is a breaking rename carried as a MINOR increment, which [SPEC §5.2](https://trusttasks.org/SPEC#52-compatibility-rules) permits while a specification is `draft`.

### What does not change

Same members, same semantics, same error codes (`persona/world/put:faceAlreadyPlaced` keeps its name — a face is still a face). `facet` survives elsewhere in the registry in its ordinary English sense — a facet of a trust record, a facet of an account — and is untouched.

### Checks

`npm run validate` (477 specs), `npm run check-bindings`, all four binding generators regenerated, `cargo fmt --all -- --check`, `cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs`, `dart analyze --fatal-infos`, the language-floor `dart format` check, and the TypeScript build.

title: fix: use shared_tdk_config for unified DID resolution (#1661)
body:
fix: use shared_tdk_config for unified DID resolution (#1661)

Signed-off-by: Robert Kwolek <robert.k@affinidi.com>
author: robert-affinidi

title: fix(sdk): VTA_ALLOW_PRIVATE_ENDPOINTS on the login handshake and session hub
body:
## Problem

`challenge_response` and `SessionHub::new` built their TDK from
`TDKConfig::builder()` with no resolver. The TDK then constructs its own
`DIDCacheClient` from `DIDCacheConfigBuilder::default()`, whose host policy is
`PublicOnly` and which knows nothing about `VTA_ALLOW_PRIVATE_ENDPOINTS`.

Every other resolution in vta-sdk goes through `resolver::webvh_host_policy`, so
an operator running a VTA on a loopback host could opt in everywhere **except**
the one place that packs the authenticate message. Since vta-sdk 0.42
introduced the policy, `did-git-sign` against a local
`did:webvh:…:localhost%3A8100` VTA failed every login, even with the opt-in set:

```
DIDComm pack failed: … Failed to resolve recipient DID: …
BlockedHost: localhost is not a public host (HostPolicy::PublicOnly)
```

## Fix

One crate-private `session_hub::shared_tdk_config()` hands the TDK the
process-shared resolver from `resolver::shared_did_resolver(None)`. Both the
REST authenticate handshake and `SessionHub::new` use it.

- The host policy is now the crate's: `PublicOnly` unless the operator opted in.
- The VTA DID that `resolve_vta_endpoint` fetched a moment earlier answers from
  cache instead of being fetched again.

### Why local mode, not `PNM_RESOLVER_URL`

The keys this resolver finds are the ones messages are encrypted to, and both
paths have always verified the `did:webvh` log in-process rather than on a
sidecar's word. This is the same call, for the same reason, as `didcomm_light`.
Consumers that want a sidecar build their own `TDKConfig` and use
`SessionHub::with_configs`.

## Compatibility

- No public API changes.
- Without the env var, behaviour is unchanged apart from the shared cache
  (300 s, successes only), which the `didcomm_light` auth path already lives with.
- With the env var, these two paths now agree with the rest of the SDK.

## Tests

`session_hub::tests`:

- `shared_tdk_config_carries_the_shared_resolver` — the config never leaves the
  TDK to build its own resolver.
- `opt_in_lets_the_tdk_dial_a_loopback_webvh_host` — re-runs the test binary as
  a child with `VTA_ALLOW_PRIVATE_ENDPOINTS=1` and asserts the TDK's resolver
  dials a loopback `did:webvh` host (counting listener) and does not fail with
  `BlockedHost`. The child runs out of process because the opt-in is read from
  the environment and the shared resolver is cached per policy, so setting it
  in-process would leak into `resolver::tests`, which pin the strict default.

## Verification

```sh
cargo clippy -p vta-sdk --lib --features session -- -D warnings   # clean
cargo test -p vta-sdk --lib --features session session_hub::tests # 8 passed, 1 ignored by design
cargo test -p vta-sdk --lib --features session resolver::tests    # 11 passed
```
author: robert-affinidi

title: security: sign the five documents whose specs declare a proof REQUIRED
body:
Step 1 of OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#1641, and the removal condition #1659 named for its own escape hatch.

## Why

Five verbs here send Trust Task documents whose specifications declare `proof` **REQUIRED**, unsigned:

| Task | |
|---|---|
| `vtc/join-requests/submit/0.2` | the application itself |
| `vtc/join-requests/status/0.1` | the background poll that chases it |
| `vtc/members/self-remove/0.1` | leaving |
| `vtc/members/vmc/0.1` | the member's half of the membership pair |
| `vtc/members/personhood/assert/0.1` | the evidence |

They relied on the authcrypt sender or the TSP sender VID instead. **That is a different claim:** transport attribution says who *handed the document over*; the proof says who *wrote it*. Same party here, but only one of them survives being relayed, and `issuer` is what a community reads downstream.

The consequence was not local. VTI #1659 made the VTC enforce what a specification declares — and then had to add `[trust_tasks] require_declared_proof`, **defaulting to false**, because this client did not sign. One client's five documents kept the rule off for every task and every sender. `pnm-browser-plugin`, `vtc-client` and `vta-sdk` all sign already.

**With this merged, that flag's removal condition is met:** VTI can flip the default and delete the field.

## What changed

Signing is one function — `trust_task_doc::build_signed_value` — beside the envelope builder, for the reason that module exists at all: three copies of the envelope logic had already drifted apart, and a verb signing its own way is the same failure in a new place.

Where each key comes from:

- **submit** — the persona's keys, fetched at the submit.
- **status poll** — resolved per poll as the poll list is built.
- **self-remove** — carried on the job, exactly as `IssueVmc` already carried one.
- **vmc** — the signing secret already in hand for the credential.
- **personhood/assert** — the key that already signed the presentation inside it.

**Two paths now fail closed.** A persona whose signing key cannot be read cannot leave a community, and is not polled — said locally, rather than sending a document the far side will refuse.

**`community/profile/show` is deliberately left alone**: it declares `proof` RECOMMENDED, not REQUIRED, and nothing gates on it.

## Two things worth a reviewer's eye

**A test asserted the old premise.** `join_submit_body_is_a_trust_task_document_the_vtc_can_parse` had `assert!(doc.proof.is_none(), "DIDComm submit is unsigned (authcrypt)")`. I inverted it rather than deleting it, so the file records that the shape changed and why.

**Clippy's argument limit, answered with structure not an allow.** The extra parameter pushed three functions to 8 arguments. `submit_member_vmc` now takes the `Delivery` route that already existed; the two join verbs take a new `join::Applicant`. That is what `Delivery`'s own comment argues for — "a sixth positional `&str` is how one call ends up with two of them swapped" — and a route that carries the signing key means a verb cannot forget to sign.

## Tests

`a_signed_document_carries_a_proof_by_its_issuer` — the proof is `eddsa-jcs-2022`, its `verificationMethod` is under the document's **own** `issuer` (SPEC §4.7: a proof by some other party establishes only that somebody signed something), and signing leaves the envelope intact. The submit's shape test now asserts the proof as part of that shape.

`cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`: clean. `cargo test --workspace --lib --bins`: 1398 passed, 0 failed.

title: fix(ci): attribute a failed semver baseline to the package that broke
body:
## The published crate is not broken

`vta-service` 0.39.0 builds and documents cleanly from crates.io. Both repros run
green today:

```sh
# the issue's repro — default features
cargo new --lib x && cd x && echo '[workspace]' >> Cargo.toml
cargo add vta-service && cargo build        # Finished in 1m32s, exit 0

# the semver baseline's own feature set, from the tool's reproduce hint
cargo add vta-service@=0.39.0 --features aws-secrets,azure-secrets,bbs,\
cli-synthesis,config-seed,default,didcomm,gcp-secrets,k8s-secrets,keyring,rest,\
setup,tee,test-support,transport-harness,tsp,vault-secrets,vsock-store,webvh
cargo check                                          # exit 0
RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings" cargo doc --no-deps -p vta-service   # exit 0
```

No packaging slip either — the whole graph resolves and compiles from the
registry copy.

## What actually failed, and it was a compile error, not rustdoc

From the failing job on #1664
([log](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/actions/runs/35785322853)):

```
    Building vta-service v0.39.0 (current)
       Built [ 190.388s] (current)      <-- our source compiles and documents
    Building vta-service v0.39.0 (baseline)
    Checking affinidi-messaging-mediator v0.28.33
error[E0027]: pattern does not mention field `verbatim`
   --> …/affinidi-messaging-mediator-0.28.33/src/tasks/websocket_streaming.rs:510:13
error[E0063]: missing field `verbatim` in initializer of `PubSubRecord`
error: could not compile `affinidi-messaging-mediator` (lib) due to 2 previous errors
error: failed to build rustdoc for crate vta-service v0.39.0
```

Three things this pins down:

- **rustc, not rustdoc.** `E0027`/`E0063` are ordinary compile errors. rustdoc
  never got to run; cargo-semver-checks reports the failed `cargo doc` invocation
  either way, which is what made it read as a doc problem.
- **Not our code.** The `(current)` build — the same source — succeeded 190 s
  earlier. Only the `(baseline)` build failed, and it failed inside a dependency.
- **Upstream, and reproducible on its own.** A scratch crate depending on nothing
  but `affinidi-messaging-mediator@=0.28.33` fails identically.
  `affinidi-messaging-mediator-common` added `verbatim` to the exhaustive public
  struct `PubSubRecord` in a semver-compatible release, so the mediator's own
  caret requirement broke it — the exact class CLAUDE.md flags ("a new struct
  field in a published crate IS breaking").

Timeline: 0.28.33 published 20:16Z, the job resolved it at 21:36Z, 0.28.34 fixed
it at 21:32Z, and the next run (#1669, 22:40Z) resolved 0.28.35 and reported
`coverage: all 9 expected crates were checked / all baselines built`. The report
has been green since.

Why our own CI never saw it: `Cargo.lock` pinned a working mediator. The semver
**baseline** resolves without a lockfile, so it takes the newest
semver-compatible release of everything — which is precisely what makes it the
only check in the repo that sees what a consumer's fresh `cargo add` sees, and
also what exposes it to somebody else's bad release. The mediator reaches
`vta-service` only through the optional `transport-harness` feature (it carries
`MockVta::start_with_transports`), which is why the default-feature reproduction
the report printed did not reach it.

## The fix

The lasting defect is the attribution, so that is what changes. A misattributed
red costs the next reader the entire diagnosis again — which is the failure mode
this job's own name was chosen to avoid.

`scripts/semver-build-failure.py` replaces the grep in `semver-report.sh`. It
pairs each failure with the `Building <crate> (current|baseline)` line that
opened it, collects the packages rustc actually gave up on, and pins their
versions from the registry paths in the diagnostics. Three verdicts instead of
one:

- **dependency** — names the package and version, says the baseline resolves
  without a lockfile and that our builds stay green because `Cargo.lock` pins
  below it, and says the fix is upstream or a raised floor, *not* a change here.
- **published crate** — unchanged for the case it was written for, and now
  carries cargo-semver-checks' own reproduction command with the feature flags
  on it, rather than a bare `cargo add` that may not reach the failure.
- **workspace copy** — an ordinary red build in the branch; not a registry
  problem.

Run against the real #1664 log it now prints:

> `::error::BUILD FAILED IN A DEPENDENCY, NOT IN vta-service: rustdoc for
> vta-service v0.39.0 (baseline) could not be built because
> affinidi-messaging-mediator 0.28.33 does not compile. …The fix is upstream — a
> corrected release of the named package, or a raised floor on it — NOT a change
> to this workspace.`

It still exits non-zero: the report genuinely could not check that crate.

## Catching it earlier

A CI doc build would **not** have caught this — it resolves through `Cargo.lock`
and would never see the broken release. Only a lockfile-free resolution does, and
the semver job already is that. What it lacked was a correct verdict, so the guard
added is on the classifier itself: fixtures (the #1667 log among them) and a
`--self-test`, wired into the `authorization-context types` job, which finishes in
seconds rather than inside the 45-minute report it serves. If cargo-semver-checks
rewords its output, the fixtures break rather than the next incident's diagnosis.

## Release

Nothing here needs a release to take effect — the fix is CI tooling, and the
published `vta-service` 0.39.0 was never broken. No `version =` field is touched.

## Verification

- `python3 scripts/semver-build-failure.py --self-test` — pass
- classifier run against the real failing CI log — correct dependency verdict
- classifier run against a healthy log — silent, exit 0
- `bash -n scripts/semver-report.sh`, `ci.yml` YAML parse — pass
- `cargo fmt --all -- --check` — pass
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` — pass
- no Rust source changed, so the two test jobs are unaffected by this diff

Closes #1667 — the premise ("the published crate does not build") turned out to be
false, the report has been green since 0.28.34, and what remained fixable here is
fixed. Nothing waits on a release: no `version =` field is touched and the
published artifact was never broken.

title: vta-service 0.39.0 on crates.io does not build: the semver baseline fails rustdoc
body:
Noticed while merging #1664, whose semver job failed for this reason and not for anything in that PR.

## What

The semver report aborts with:

```
error: aborting due to failure to build rustdoc for crate vta-service v0.39.0
PUBLISHED CRATE DOES NOT BUILD: vta-service -- the semver baseline is the published
crate as a consumer receives it, so a baseline that fails to build means consumers
cannot build it either.
```

The job's own message says how to reproduce it:

```sh
cargo new --lib x && cd x && echo '[workspace]' >> Cargo.toml
cargo add vta-service && cargo build
```

## Why it matters

This is not "the check could not run". The baseline is the crate exactly as a consumer receives it from crates.io, so if rustdoc cannot build it there, a consumer adding `vta-service` to a fresh project has the same problem. Every other crate in the sweep passed (`vti-common` 196/196, `vti-rooms`, `vti-rooms-dtg`, `vti-secrets` all "no semver update required"), so this is specific to `vta-service` as published, not a workspace-wide breakage.

It also means the semver report stays red for every PR until it is fixed, which is the failure mode where a permanently-red informational check stops being read. That is the second cost, and the reason to fix it rather than note it.

## Worth checking first

- Whether the published 0.39.0 is missing a file or a feature the manifest implies (a `include`/`exclude` slip, or a path dependency that resolved locally but not from the registry).
- Whether it builds but only *rustdoc* fails — the error names rustdoc specifically, and a doc-only failure (an intra-doc link to something behind a disabled feature, say) is a different fix from a compile failure.

Unowned; filed so the red report has a home rather than being re-diagnosed on the next PR.

title: fix(persona): local/profile/put answers the correlation index only to the holder
body:
`persona/local/profile/put` is **context-scoped**, and its response carries:

```json
"correlation": { "severity": "high", "matchesPoolValue": true }
```

`matchesPoolValue` is computed from the holder's **agent-wide** blinded index: does any attribute in the pool hold this exact value. So a caller authorized in one context — including an application — can write a local face with a guessed value and read back whether the holder holds it anywhere, one guess per write, unbounded.

No value crosses the boundary in either direction, and it does not need to. For a name, an address or a date of birth, confirming a guess **is** disclosure, and the guesser is inside a single context learning about all of them. The schema's own description said the index "is above the boundary, is keyed by a hash, and only the holder can query it" — while this response answered it to anyone in the context.

### The change

`correlation` becomes conditional. A maintainer **MUST** include it only for a caller authorized to read across the holder's contexts, and **MUST** omit the member entirely otherwise.

Omit rather than soften: a coarser signal is still an oracle, only a slower one.

The holder loses nothing. A maintainer **SHOULD** still record the assessment where the holder can read it — an audit entry, or the holder-reach correlation task — because the warning that a throwaway identity is reusing a real value is the reason this task is indexed at all. What changes is who is told, not whether it is noticed.

### Scope

Description and prose only — no member added, removed or retyped, so no consumer breaks. The four generated bindings are regenerated for the changed descriptions.

Checks run locally: `npm run validate`, `npm run check-bindings`, `cargo fmt --all -- --check`, `cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs`, and in `trust-tasks-dart` both `dart analyze --fatal-infos` and the language-floor `dart format` check.

title: feat(vtc): a by-DID vetter status lookup
body:
Closes #1651 (Keyring VTI-Q3). The spec half merged as [trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#603](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/603); `trust-tasks-rs` 0.21.21 publishes it, and this bumps to it.

## The gap

`vtc/vetting/vetters/list` omits a vetter with no published profile and a vetter whose grant was revoked **identically** — both are absent. So an applicant mid-exchange with a vetter who stopped responding could not tell whether that vetter had been removed or had simply never been listed, and a vetter could not check their own standing at all. The only way to find out was to read the grant credential's status list, which requires already holding it.

## What it answers

By DID: `live`, `revoked`, `expired` or `none`, plus `grantId`, the timestamp that ended or will end the grant, and — for a live grant — `listed`. That last member is what separates "a vetter who chose not to be listed" from "not a vetter", which is Keyring's actual complaint.

| Surface | |
|---|---|
| `/v1/trust-tasks`, DIDComm, TSP | applicants and members, identified callers only |
| `POST /v1/vetting/vetters/show` | the console, admin session |
| `vtc-client::show_vetter` | |

## Decisions worth reviewing

- **The live case reuses `live_grant`** — the same lookup the listing and every grant check already use, so "live here" cannot drift from "live there". Only the non-live answer reads the grant record directly.
- **`revoked` outranks `expired`** where a grant is both. Withdrawal and lapse are different statements: a vetter told `expired` would reasonably ask for a renewal, one told `revoked` would not.
- **`none` does not distinguish a stranger from a member who is not a vetter.** The caller asked about vetting. A test asserts those two answers are identical.
- **`CheckShape` on the response enforces what the schema cannot** — the schema is one object whose required members depend on `status`. A response saying `revoked` while carrying `validUntil` and no `revokedAt` reads as an expiry to a client branching on members rather than status, so that combination is refused rather than trusted.
- **`GrantStatus` is `#[non_exhaustive]`**, so the match needs a catch-all. It *accepts*: an unknown status comes from a newer specification, the schema check has already passed, and inventing a rule for a status this build cannot interpret would refuse a response that is valid under the spec that produced it. The reasoning is in the code.

## Tests

- `a_by_did_lookup_tells_revoked_from_unlisted_from_never_a_vetter` — stranger and non-vetter member both `none` and indistinguishable; granted → `live` with `listed: false`; profile published → `listed: true`; revoked → `revoked` with `revokedAt`, no `listed`, no reason; and the listing confirms she is absent from it, which is the ambiguity being resolved.
- `a_lapsed_grant_reads_expired_and_a_withdrawn_one_still_reads_revoked` — a grant seeded already lapsed reads `expired`; add a newer withdrawn grant and the answer becomes `revoked`, pinning the ordering rule.

Two conformance guards caught this before I did, and both were right: `every_bound_published_uri_has_a_witness` wanted a `checked!` entry built from the wire types the handler emits, and `dispatcher_routes_every_dispatched_uri` wanted the dispatched and declared lists to agree. Both are satisfied rather than waived.

`cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`: clean. `cargo test -p vtc-service -p vta-sdk -p vtc-client`: 2658 passed. OpenAPI snapshot and `admin-ui/src/lib/wire.ts` regenerated and committed; the console's `wire:check` and build pass.

title: build(deps)!: dtg-credentials 0.11
body:
Closes nothing; #1068 stays open.

Bumps the workspace `dtg-credentials` requirement from 0.9.1 to 0.11, which
crosses two releases: 0.10.0 was merged, versioned and never tagged, so
crates.io went straight from 0.9.1 to 0.11.0 and a consumer on 0.9.x takes both
sections at once. Step 2 of what #1068 still needs.

### What the bump crosses

Three compile-time changes, none of which changes a credential on the wire:

- `DTGCredentialError` is `#[non_exhaustive]` and gains nine variants across the
  two releases. **The workspace has no `match` on it at all**, so nothing needed
  a wildcard arm.
- `DTGCommon` gains a public `task_digest_multibase` field. **The workspace has
  no exhaustive `DTGCommon` struct literal**, as the upstream change predicted;
  every construction goes through a `new_*` constructor and `..Default::default()`.
- Three constructors are deprecated, not removed. They still compile, but CI's
  clippy runs `-D warnings`, so every call site moves.

### Call sites moved

All four are test fixtures — the workspace issues no VMC acknowledgement or VWC
in production code today.

| Site | From | To |
|---|---|---|
| `vtc-service/src/members/inbound_vmc.rs` (`pair`) | `new_member_vmc` | `new_member_vmc_for(&grant_wire, "did:key:zMember", …)` |
| `vtc-service/src/routes/relationships.rs` (`member_row`) | `new_member_vmc` | `new_member_vmc_for(&grant_json, did, …)` |
| `vtc-service/src/credentials/witness.rs` (`vwc_for`) | `new_vwc` | `new_vwc_for_session(…, &witness_session(), digest, …)` |
| `vtc-service/src/routes/members/personhood.rs` (`presentation_with_witness`) | `new_vwc` | `new_vwc_for_session(…, &witness_session(), digest, …)` |

The `_for` forms take the party the grant is expected to name, established
independently of the grant, and refuse a mismatch — so each site now passes the
member DID it already had rather than letting the constructor read one out of
the document it is meant to be checked against.

`new_vwc_for_session` reads **both** halves of the citation off the
`witness/session` document — `taskContext` from its `id`, `taskDigestMultibase`
from its task digest — so the two cannot disagree. Both test helpers therefore
gained a `witness_session()` fixture: the opening document, with `threadId`
equal to its own `id`, which is what the constructor requires and refuses
otherwise.

One consequence worth naming. `new_vwc_for_session` takes the edge digest as
REQUIRED, which the specification makes it, so it cannot produce the
"witness with no `digestMultibase`" case `personhood.rs` tests. That case is a
VWC predating the requirement, and the only honest way to hold one is to drop
the member from the wire form, which is how it would arrive — so the helper now
builds the credential and removes `credentialSubject.digestMultibase` for that
one case rather than asking the constructor for something it should refuse.

### One fixture the stricter checks refused

`vti-rooms-dtg`'s `an_expired_nomination_is_refused` built its "stale" nomination with
`validFrom` a minute ago and `validUntil` a **day** ago — a window that closes before it
opens. 0.10.0's `InvalidValidityWindow` caught it at construction.

The fixture was wrong, not the check. A credential whose window never opened is malformed,
not expired, so the test was asserting that `verify` refuses something — just not the thing
its name claims, and the refusal it was getting would have been the same for a credential
with no window at all. The window now opens two days ago and closes one day ago, so it is
an expiry the test can actually be about. `nomination()` gained a `valid_from` parameter so
every call site states both ends rather than one; passing only `validUntil` is exactly what
let this read as expired while being malformed.

No check was loosened. It was the only fixture any of 0.10.0's new refusals caught:
nothing else in the workspace nests past `MAX_JSON_DEPTH` or answers a grant that names
somebody else.

### `cites_task` on the verifier: not yet, and why

#1068's remaining item 3 asks whether `credentials::witness` should now pair a
presented VWC with its session document through `cites_task`. It should
eventually, but it is not a small addition and is deliberately not in this PR.

`cites_task(&self, document)` needs the `witness/session` document itself.
`resolve_binding` has the relationships keyspace and the presented credential
JSON, and neither the VTC nor the presentation carries that document:

- there is no wire slot for it — `extract_vp_claims` projects credentials, and
  a cited Trust Task document is not one;
- the VTC was not a party to the witnessing exchange. A VWC presented at a join
  names a *foreign* exchange by construction (`TaskContextBinding::ForeignExchange`
  is the honest case, not the suspicious one), so the VTC cannot have retained
  the document;
- even `credentials::task_context::resolve`, which does compare a credential's
  `taskContext` against the ceremony it was presented in, compares thread ids —
  it has no document to digest either, and Trust Task documents are not stored.

Adding the check therefore means a wire slot for the presenter to ship the
session document, a decision about what an absent or unattributable session
document resolves to (a task digest attests content, not authenticity — it is
load-bearing only because the credential's *issuer* signed it), a new host
verdict beside `WitnessBinding`, and a default-policy change to branch on it.
That is design work. #1068 stays open for it, alongside item 1 (implement the
witness role) and the `assert`-path gap.

What *is* in this PR is the issuing-side half, which is small and clearly
correct: `a_catalog_built_vwc_carries_the_required_task_context` now also
asserts that the VWC carries the session document's own task digest and that
`cites_task` resolves both halves back to the document it was built from. That
pins the two implementations together the same way the digest round-trip below
it already does.

### Where else `task_digest_multibase` belongs

Checked, and the answer is nowhere yet in this workspace:

- **No production issuing site exists.** `new_vwc*` appears only in the two test
  helpers above; the witness role (#1068 item 1) is unimplemented, so there is
  no VWC-issuing code path that could carry the field.
- **`vtc-service/src/credentials/task_context.rs`** answers a different question
  (which exchange a credential was *presented* in) and is blocked on the same
  missing document.
- **`vta_sdk::protocols::vetting`** carries a `task_context` on the vetting
  statement, and `vetting/session/0.1` does publish a `taskDigestMultibase` —
  it is the vector dtg-credentials 0.11 tests itself against. But that type is
  generated from the Trust Task registry, so the field lands in
  dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf first and reaches here through a `trust-tasks-rs` bump,
  never as a local edit.

### `vti-rooms-dtg` takes the workspace requirement

It carried a literal `dtg-credentials = "0.9.1"` while every other consumer took
`{ workspace = true }`. That is the drift `vti-rooms-wasm`'s manifest comment
argues against in so many words: a chain built by one version and verified by
another is refused as a *broken chain* rather than as a version skew. It now
takes the workspace requirement, so it cannot fall out of step again.

### Why `!`

`vti-rooms-dtg` publishes, and `open_credential` is `pub` and returns
`DTGCredential`. That makes `dtg-credentials`' version part of its public API,
so moving the requirement across a breaking release is a breaking change to the
crate itself — the re-export rule in CLAUDE.md, and the same shape as the
`ApproveScope` skew that rule was written for.

### Verification

`cargo tree -d` shows exactly one `dtg-credentials` in the graph (0.11.0). No
crate's own `version =` field was touched.

### Test results

- `cargo test --workspace --exclude vtc-service --exclude vtc-client --no-fail-fast` —
  **128 targets, 4814 passed, 0 failed.** The first run of this job failed once, in
  `vti-rooms-dtg` (the fixture above); green after the fix.
- `cargo test -p vtc-service -p vtc-client --no-fail-fast` — **67 targets, 1865 passed,
  0 failed.** `VTC_SKIP_ADMIN_UI_BUILD` was not set.
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` — clean.
- `cargo fmt --all -- --check` — clean.

Those runs were made before the rebase onto `a07f83ce`. After it, `cargo fmt --all --
--check` and the VTC job were re-run locally (67 targets, 1865 passed, 0 failed), and CI
ran the whole suite on the rebased head: Test (workspace), Test (VTC), Clippy, Format,
MSRV, cargo-deny and the rest all pass.

title: fix(vtc): answer the auth tasks with the error codes their specs declare
body:
Follows #1649's error-code census, which left the five auth codes.

## What was wrong

`routes/auth.rs` and `routes/recognise.rs` used **no declared error code at all**. Every refusal was a status plus prose, so a client distinguishing "your credential did not hold up" from "this community grants your role nothing here" had to match on English.

## What now carries a code

| Code | Refusal |
|---|---|
| `vtc/auth/admin-session:invalidToken` | the mirrored access token did not verify — signature, audience or expiry |
| `vtc/auth/recognise:credentialInvalid` | the VEC or VMC failed proof verification, fell outside its validity window, or was revoked |
| `vtc/auth/recognise:roleNotMapped` | policy allowed the issuer but mapped the foreign role to no local role |

The last two are worth separating: `roleNotMapped` is an operator's policy decision about roles, `credentialInvalid` is the credential itself. A caller acts differently on each.

**`credentialInvalid` is applied to exactly what the spec describes** — "failed proof verification, was expired, or was revoked via credentialStatus", i.e. `ProofInvalid`, `StatusListFailed`, `ValidityWindow`, plus the zero-window case at mint, which is "was expired" arriving a moment later. `IssuerKeyUnresolved` and `Malformed` stay **uncoded**: they are refusals about a document that could not be checked at all rather than one that was checked and failed, and filing them under this code would misdescribe them. A unit test pins that.

## One thing worth reviewing

Both handlers now return `TaskError` instead of `AppError`. That is not cosmetic: `From<TaskError> for AppError` deliberately **drops** the code (for surfaces that cannot carry one), so a handler returning `AppError` would have constructed each code and thrown it away. The first version of this change did exactly that and looked fine.

## The census

Baseline 11 → 8. The two remaining auth codes are **not** missing tests, and the baseline now records why rather than leaving the next person to re-derive it:

- **`rateLimited`** — declared by the challenge task, but the limiter in front of it is the chain-wide per-IP governor. `governor_error_response` receives a `GovernorError` with no request, so it cannot know which route was refused and cannot name a route-scoped code. Emitting this means giving the limiter route context first.
- **`issuerNotRecognised`** — comes from the trust registry answering "no". Every fixture in the tree wires `registry_client: None`, so the route stops at the registry pre-flight and the gate never runs. Witnessing it means building a registry stub.

I would rather leave those two visible in the baseline with a reason than manufacture a witness that asserts against a mock of our own refusal.

## Tests

- `the_admin_session_task_answers_with_the_invalid_token_code_its_spec_declares` — a junk token and a token minted for another audience, both through the route.
- `the_recognise_task_answers_with_the_codes_its_spec_declares` — the role-mapping and expired-credential refusals, rendered and read back as a client sees them.
- `caller_rejections_stay_403` extended: each mapped variant carries its code, and `Malformed` carries none.

`cargo test -p vtc-service`: 1843 passed, 0 failed. `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`: clean. The census test passes with the new witnesses and the lowered baseline.

title: feat(vtc/vetting/vetters/show): a by-DID vetter status lookup
body:
Adds `vtc/vetting/vetters/show/0.1`. This is the spec half of OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#1651, which came from Keyring's VTI-Q3.

## Why

`vtc/vetting/vetters/list` omits a vetter with no published profile and a vetter whose grant was revoked in exactly the same way: both are simply absent. So:

- an applicant mid-exchange with a vetter who has gone quiet cannot tell whether that vetter was removed or never chose to be listed;
- a vetter cannot check their own standing at all.

The only way to find out today is to read the grant credential's own status list, which requires already holding the credential.

## What it answers

By DID: `live`, `revoked`, `expired` or `none`, plus `grantId`, the timestamp that ended or will end it, and — for a live grant — `listed`, which is what separates "a vetter who chose not to be listed" from "not a vetter".

A **new task** rather than a `status` member on the listing response: adding a member to an existing response is breaking for consumers that reject unknown members, and the two answer different questions — the listing is discovery, this is a lookup about someone you can already name.

## Three judgement calls worth reviewing

1. **`revoked` outranks `expired`** where both hold. Withdrawal and lapse are different statements about the community's trust, and an applicant reads them differently.
2. **`none` does not distinguish a non-member from a member who is not a vetter.** The caller asked about vetting; membership is not theirs to learn here. Conformance also asks that the answer cost the same whatever the status, so timing does not leak what the payload withholds.
3. **The revocation reason is not carried**, including through `ext`, which the Security & Privacy section says explicitly. It is the community's internal record and frequently concerns a third party; the caller needs to know the grant does not hold.

The response is also deliberately *not* evidence: a grant can be revoked a second after the answer is sent, so the spec says a `live` answer must not be treated as durable proof of eligibility — that is what the vetter's credential in `vetting/request` is for.

## Checks

- `npm run validate`: 473 specs, no errors, and no warning against this spec.
- `npm run build`: passes; all three examples validate against the framework envelope.
- Bindings regenerated for **Rust, TypeScript and Go** — the Go drift check in `.github/workflows/go.yml` makes that third one required, though the contributing guide lists only two.
- `cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs`: passes.
- No version bumps and no changelog entries, per RELEASING.md — the Release PR assigns those.

title: feat(vta): advertise TSP on a minted DID when the mediator carries it
body:
Closes #1652 (Keyring VTI-Q11).

## The problem

A persona minted by a TSP-capable VTA advertised only `DIDCommMessaging`, so a Rev 3 client reading its document kept the applicant ↔ vetter leg on DIDComm.

The cause is narrower than it looks: `addTspService` defaulted to `false` at the mint, and **a persona is minted by a caller that sends no such field** — `vta-sdk` skips it on the wire when false. So the answer was always "no", however TSP-capable the VTA and its mediator were.

## The change

`addTspService` becomes three-state, and only the absent case is new:

| Wire | Before | Now |
|---|---|---|
| `true` | `#tsp` (subject to the existing gates) | unchanged |
| `false` | no `#tsp` | unchanged |
| absent | **no `#tsp`** | `#tsp` iff this VTA and its mediator carry TSP |

"Carries TSP" is the check VTA setup already makes for the VTA's own document: `services.tsp` is on, a mediator is configured, and that mediator's DID document advertises `TSPTransport`.

**An unresolvable mediator answers no** — deliberately stricter than setup, which warns and proceeds. There the operator named the mediator deliberately and sees the warning; here nobody asked for `#tsp` at all, so the quiet default must not publish a transport peers cannot reach the DID on.

Every internal caller now passes `Some(false)` explicitly, so no existing path changes behaviour. No SDK change is needed: it already omits the field when false, which is exactly the "absent" case.

## Tests

- `tsp_is_advertised_only_when_the_vta_and_its_mediator_both_carry_it` — drives the decision against **real, resolvable** `did:peer` mediators, one advertising `TSPTransport` and one not, plus the VTA-not-TSP, no-mediator and unresolvable cases. title: Personas advertise TSPTransport when their VTA and mediator carry TSP — Keyring VTI-Q11
body:
From Keyring's VTI-Q11.

A persona minted by a TSP-capable VTA advertises only `DIDCommMessaging`, so a Rev 3 client reading its document keeps the applicant ↔ vetter leg on DIDComm.

**Decision:** a persona advertises `#tsp` (`TSPTransport`) when its VTA is built with TSP (on by default since #1622) **and** the mediator it names advertises `TSPTransport`. That's the same check VTA setup now makes before advertising `#tsp` for the VTA itself. A persona behind a mediator that doesn't carry TSP stays DIDComm-only, so it never advertises a transport its peers can't use.

Scope:
- the persona mint path and its DID template(s);
- `SERVICE_TSP` rendered from the mediator check;
- tests for both cases: the mediator carries TSP, and it doesn't.

Related: the reference client's peer vetting legs are DIDComm-only today (Keyring VTI-Q2). Once a persona advertises `#tsp`, openvtc's vetting inbound path would also need a TSP receive leg before a Rev 3 peer can use it.

title: feat(vta): advertise TSP on a minted DID when the mediator carries it (#1665)
body:
feat(vta): advertise TSP on a minted DID when the mediator carries it (#1665)

A persona minted by a TSP-capable VTA advertised only `DIDCommMessaging`,
so a Rev 3 peer reading its document kept the leg on DIDComm (Keyring
VTI-Q11). The cause: `addTspService` defaulted to `false` at the mint, and a
persona is minted by a caller that sends no such field — the SDK skips it
when false — so the answer was always "no" however TSP-capable the stack was.

`addTspService` becomes three-state. An explicit `true` or `false` is
honoured exactly as before. Absent now means "decide from what this VTA and
its mediator can actually carry": `services.tsp` on, a mediator configured,
and that mediator's own document advertising `TSPTransport` — the same check
VTA setup makes before advertising `#tsp` for the VTA itself.

A mediator that does not resolve answers no, which is deliberately stricter
than setup's warn-and-proceed. There the operator named the mediator and is
told; here nobody asked for `#tsp` at all, so the quiet default must not
publish a transport peers cannot reach.

Every internal caller passes `Some(false)`, so no existing path changes.
