title: fix(auth): consume the challenge before minting, atomically
body:
Closes #1656.

## The bug

`handle_authenticate_with_aal` consumed a single-use challenge as a read-then-write:

1. `get_session(session_id)`
2. refuse unless `state == ChallengeSent`
3. challenge compare, TTL, signer, freshness
4. `check_acl(...)` — **await**
5. `mint_session_tokens(...)` — **await**, signing work
6. `store_session(...)`, then `delete_session(challenge row)`

The check at (2) was the only guard, and the row that invalidates it survived until (6). The window is not sub-millisecond: it spans an ACL lookup and a mint. Two interleaved presentations of the same signed envelope both passed (2), and both minted.

Because sessions coalesce per DID (last write wins, access token pinned by `token_id`), the winner holds the live session **as the holder** and the loser's access token is immediately superseded. So an attacker who captured a correctly-addressed signed envelope and replayed it inside the 5-minute freshness window, racing a genuine sign-in, could take the holder's session and knock out the holder's own token.

Sequential replay was never the issue — it is refused with `SessionStateMismatch`, and affinidi/affinidi-webvh-service#208 added route tests for that at three services.

## The fix

`SessionStore::take_session` — read **and** remove, a claim rather than a look. The handler takes the challenge row before the ACL lookup and the mint, and refuses the caller who did not get it.

**This is not a new pattern.** The same trait already closes exactly this TOCTOU on the refresh path with `take_session_id_by_refresh`, documented as cross-replica safe (Redis `GETDEL`, DynamoDB `DeleteItem ReturnValues=ALL_OLD`, fjall mutex). The authenticate path simply never got the same treatment — an omission, not a design choice.

**Non-breaking, by choice.** The trait method has a default implementation that keeps today's `get_session` + `delete_session`, so every existing backend — including webvh's three services and the in-crate test backends — compiles unchanged and none silently changes behaviour. The default is documented as *not* atomic; `KeyspaceSessionStore` overrides it with the keyspace's atomic `take_raw`, so the VTC and VTA get the real claim immediately.

A challenge row is always uuid-keyed (`handle_challenge` mints a v4), so taking it can never remove the DID-keyed row of an established session.

## Tests

`two_presentations_of_one_challenge_mint_once` interleaves two presentations of the same envelope and asserts exactly one mints. **Revert the ordering and it fails with two successes** — two complete token bundles issued for one challenge. I checked that, so the test discriminates rather than passing either way.

`the_default_take_session_reads_and_removes` pins the non-atomic default's behaviour, since a backend that never overrides depends on it.

`cargo test --workspace`: 6746 passed, 0 failed. `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`: clean.

## Follow-up, not in scope here

Any other single-use row consumed the same way deserves the same look. The refresh path is already correct; nothing else was audited as part of this.

title: handle_authenticate consumes the challenge non-atomically: a replayed sign-in can win a race
body:
Found while answering code-scanning alerts on affinidi/affinidi-webvh-service#208 (the recipient-binding fix, the webvh relay of #1638). The scanner hedged on "if session/challenge consumption is not atomic". It isn't.

## What

`vti_common::auth::handlers::handle_authenticate_with_aal` (`src/auth/handlers/authenticate.rs`) consumes a single-use challenge as a read-then-write, with no compare-and-swap and no lock:

1. `get_session(&input.session_id)`
2. refuse unless `session.state == SessionState::ChallengeSent`
3. constant-time challenge compare, challenge TTL, signer check, freshness
4. `check_acl(&session.did)` — an await
5. `mint_session_tokens(...)` — an await, signing work
6. `store_session(&auth_session)`, then `delete_session(&input.session_id)`

The `ChallengeSent` check at step 2 is the only guard, and the row that would invalidate it is not removed until step 6. The window is not sub-millisecond: it spans an ACL lookup and token minting.

`AuthBackend::SessionStore` offers only `store_session`, `get_session` and `delete_session` (`src/auth/backend.rs:172-178`) — there is no primitive with which a caller could make this atomic.

## Impact

Two sufficiently interleaved presentations of the same signed sign-in both pass step 2 and both mint. Since sessions coalesce per DID (last write wins, access token pinned by `token_id`), the loser's access token is immediately superseded. So an attacker who captured a correctly-addressed signed envelope, and replays it inside the 5-minute freshness window while the holder signs in, can win the race and hold the live session **as the holder**, invalidating the holder's own access token.

Preconditions are narrow: the attacker needs the holder's signed envelope, within the freshness window, and has to interleave with a real sign-in. It is a race, not a straightforward replay — the sequential replay path is correctly refused (`SessionStateMismatch`), and webvh #208 now has tests for that at all three of its routes.

## Suggested fix

Consume the challenge before the expensive work, not after: add a compare-and-delete (or compare-and-swap on `state`) to `SessionStore`, take the row at step 2, and mint only if this caller is the one that took it. A backend without an atomic primitive can serialise per `session_id`.

The same shape applies to any other single-use row consumed this way — the refresh path is worth checking alongside it.

## Not affected

- Sequential replay: refused, and the state check logs it as a replay.
- webvh #208: unrelated to that change; the recipient binding is orthogonal and lands independently.

title: fix(auth): consume the challenge before minting, atomically (#1664)

fix(auth): consume the challenge before minting, atomically (#1664)

`handle_authenticate` read the challenge row, checked it was in
`ChallengeSent`, then looked up the ACL and minted tokens, and only after
all that deleted the row. Those are awaits, and the row stayed alive across
them, so two interleaved presentations of the same signed envelope both
passed the state check and both minted. Sequentially it was correct; under
concurrency the single-use challenge was not single-use (#1656).

Sessions coalesce per DID (last write wins, access token pinned by
`token_id`), so an attacker who captured a correctly-addressed envelope and
replayed it inside the freshness window while the holder signed in could win
the race, hold the session as the holder, and supersede the holder's own
access token.

`SessionStore::take_session` is the claim: exactly one concurrent caller
observes `Some`. The handler now takes the row before the ACL lookup and the
mint, and refuses the loser as it refuses a replay. This is the treatment
`take_session_id_by_refresh` already gives the refresh path — the
authenticate path was an omission, not a different design.

The default implementation keeps today's `get` + `delete`, so every backend
compiles unchanged and none silently changes behaviour; it is documented as
not atomic, and `KeyspaceSessionStore` overrides it with the keyspace's
atomic `take_raw` (Redis GETDEL / DynamoDB DeleteItem ALL_OLD / fjall mutex).

title: spec(messaging/account): opt-in lifetime counters on account/get and account/list
body:
## What

`Account` gains an optional **`stats`** object, so an operator can read an account's lifetime totals from the mediator rather than counting locally from a live traffic feed:

- `messagesReceived` / `messagesSent`, and `bytesReceived` / `bytesSent`
- `receivedByProtocol` / `sentByProtocol` — the same counts split by wire protocol (`didcomm`, `didcommV1`, `tsp`, `other`), which is what makes a protocol mix answerable per account rather than per connection

Every member is optional: a mediator reports what it keeps, and a counter absent from a response was **not kept**, rather than zero. The counters survive restarts, reading them does not reset them, and removing an account discards them.

## Why opt-in

`account/get` and `account/list` each gain an optional request member, `includeStats`, exactly like `includeActivity`. A mediator returns `stats` only when it is `true`, and **MUST NOT** otherwise.

The generated clients reject unknown members, so a mediator that always sent `stats` would break every requester built against the older schema. In the other direction, a requester that sends `includeStats` to an older mediator gets a schema rejection, so the prose says to set it only where the mediator is known to support it.

The change is additive inside version 0.1 of `messaging/account/{get,list}`: every existing document stays valid.

## Also

- Security & Privacy notes for both tasks: the counters disclose volume rather than content, and get the same authorization as the rest of the account view.
- All four client libraries regenerated. `npm run build`, `npm run check-bindings` and `cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs` pass.

title: feat(cli): pnm reaches worlds and the claim-type registry
body:
`persona/facet/{put,list,delete}` and `persona/claim-types/list` had **no method on `VtaClient`** — not merely no CLI verb — so `pnm` could not reach worlds or the claim-type registry at all, while both graphical clients do.

**SDK.** Four new methods on the persona slice, built from `trust_tasks_rs::specs` rather than hand-written bodies, and decoding into the generated `Response`. The older methods on that slice return `Value` because they predate the generated modules; these do not, so a response the specification does not describe is an error at the call rather than a `None` three screens later.

**CLI.** `pnm persona world {list,put,delete}` and `pnm persona claim-types`.

- **Both id lists on a put replace.** Omitting `--face` empties the world rather than leaving it alone — the specification is explicit that a member whose absence meant "keep" would make emptying one impossible. The help says so and points at `world list`.
- **Delete leaves every member where it was.** There is no cascading form; the response's `releasedFaces` is how many faces now belong to no world.
- **The colour's mapping to the specification's tokens is written out, not derived.** Pinned from both sides, because `pnm-cli` does not depend on the generated types and `vta-cli-common` does not know the CLI's enum: `pnm-cli` checks the eight tokens its enum offers, `vta-cli-common` checks those tokens all parse as a `FacetColour`.
- A bad ULID names itself, rather than reporting a pattern failure against whichever of six repeated flags was wrong.

`docs/02-vta/claim-type-registry.md` gains a line pointing at `pnm persona claim-types` — the table to read before wondering why a value came back masked.

CI set run locally: `cargo fmt --all -- --check`, `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`, workspace tests (4817), `-p vtc-service -p vtc-client` (1831).

title: feat(console): contacts, formats, and faces made inside a context
body:
Three parts of the persona surface the console could not reach. Each already had an SDK call in `@openvtc/pnm-core/persona` with nothing importing it.

### People — `persona/contact/{put,get,list,delete}`
What others have told the holder about themselves, on the context card in the identity map. Filed against the persona this context knows, because "who was I when they told me this" is part of the record.

A card is a revision, not an overwrite, so the pane shows the revision number, offers what they said before, and surfaces `hasUnreviewedChange`. What the holder types is sent with no `provenance`: it is their note of what someone said, and claiming one on the peer's behalf would turn a note into an assertion about them.

### Formats — `persona/renderers/list`
A panel in the Released view, beside the disclosure history. The two answer halves of one question — what left, and what shape it left in. "Drops nothing" and "this agent does not offer it" are kept apart, per `dropsOf`'s own warning: rendering the second as the first tells a holder a format is safe when the disclosure is about to be refused.

### Faces made here — `persona/local/profile/{put,delete}`, `persona/local/binding/set`
The existing promote picker gains make, wear and delete. Delete sends `unbind`, since the question the holder answers says the face comes off as it goes; without it the agent refuses while it is worn and delete would work only sometimes. A made face is inline-only and self-asserted — that is the boundary, not a shortcut: a context-local face has nowhere in its wire type to name a pool attribute.

### Not included, deliberately
`persona/disclosure/{preview,present}` looked missing but is not: `background.ts` drives both from a page request through the consent window, by URI rather than through the SDK helpers. A console flow would be a second way to do the same thing.

Ran locally: `npm run lint`, `npm run build`, `npm test`, and every dist guard in `ci.yml` — MV3 single bundle, the admin, seeds and holder-scoped-persona confinement checks, console-carries-persona, and the console single-bundle check.

title: feat(tui): contacts, formats, purge, and faces made inside a community
body:
Everything in `persona/*` the identity pane could not reach, plus §5.8 of the persona design note.

| New | Task | Where |
|---|---|---|
| People | `persona/contact/{put,get,list,delete}` | `p` on a community |
| Formats | `persona/renderers/list` | `f` on Disclosures |
| Who it knows you as | `persona/binding/list` | `k` on a community |
| Forget earlier versions | `persona/attribute/purge-version` | `p` on an attribute |
| Make / wear / delete a face made here | `persona/local/profile/{put,delete}`, `persona/local/binding/set` | in the faces-made-here view |

**People.** Filed against the persona this community knows — "who was I when they told me this" is part of the record, so there is no picker. A card is a revision rather than an overwrite, so the detail shows what they said before and the list marks a change the holder has not looked at. What the holder types is sent with no provenance: it is their note of what someone said.

**Who it knows you as** warns when a community holds more than one of the holder's personas. Anyone reading both rows can see they are the same person, and no other row in the pane says so.

**Forget earlier versions** asks first and cannot be undone. The listing does not say which faces pin an *old* version, so the question names the faces at risk rather than claiming a number it cannot know, and the purge reports how many pins it actually broke.

**Worlds are offered rather than asked for** (§5.8): at four faces with none, the Faces tab says what they are for. The same threshold the browser console uses — below it a world arranges one thing, and an "add a world" step asks the holder to pre-think a taxonomy before they have the members.

**Esc withdraws one layer at a time.** A view holding a form, an armed question or an open record closes that first; dropping the whole view would throw away a half-typed card to answer "not that one".

`openvtc-core` gains `persona::contacts`, `pool::purge_versions`, `binding::{list,set_local}`, `disclosure::renderers` and `lifecycle::{local_face_put,local_face_delete}`.

CI set run locally: fmt, both clippy runs, doc, tests with `--include-ignored` (1510), `--no-default-features` (1491), `-p openvtc --features dev-overrides` (680), bench build.

body:
Release PR for the Dart package `trust_tasks`, the counterpart to the release-plz PR for the
crates and the `release-ts` / `release-go` PRs. **Merging this starts the
release**: the `tag-dart` job in `publish.yml` verifies the package and pushes
`trust-tasks-dart-v0.1.18`, and that tag triggers `publish-dart.yml`, which
publishes to pub.dev over OIDC.

- `trust_tasks`: `0.1.17` → `0.1.18` (`patch`)
- derived from the conventional commits in `trust-tasks-dart-v0.1.17..HEAD` touching `specs`, `trust-tasks-dart`, `scripts/build-dart-bindings.mjs`

Unlike the other three, pub.dev refuses a publish that was not triggered by a tag
push — so the tag is a step in the chain rather than a record of one. If
`RELEASE_PLZ_TOKEN` is unset the tag is pushed by the default token, which does
not trigger workflows; `tag-dart` warns when that happens and the fix is to
re-push the tag from a workstation.

This branch is regenerated from `main` on every push, so do not commit to it —
edits are force-pushed away. See RELEASING.md.

title: feat(console): contacts, formats, and faces made inside a context
body:
feat(console): contacts, formats, and faces made inside a context

Three parts of `persona/*` the console could not reach, each of which had
an SDK call in the wallet half and no surface calling it.

**People.** `persona/contact/*` — what others have told the holder about
themselves, per context, filed against the persona that received it. A
card is a revision, so the pane shows the revision number, offers the
history and says when someone changed something the holder has not looked
at. What the holder types carries no provenance: it is their note of what
was said, not an assertion about the person who said it.

**Formats.** `persona/renderers/list`, beside the disclosure history,
because the two answer halves of one question: what left, and what shape
it left in. A format that drops provenance turns "my employer attested
this" into "they said so", and the panel keeps "drops nothing" and "this
agent does not offer it" apart.

**Faces made here** gains make, wear and delete —
`persona/local/profile/{put,delete}` and `persona/local/binding/set` —
beside the promote it already had. Delete sends `unbind`, because the
question the holder answered says the face comes off as it goes.

`persona/disclosure/{preview,present}` needed nothing: the wallet already
drives them from a page request, through the consent window.

title: feat(specs): add the ExtCritical framework def, and open vetting requirements to ext
body:
Companion to **trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-spec#23**, which adds the criticality marking to the framework text. This is the schema half plus the first specification to use it.

## The problem it fixes

A community publishing an admission mode the join manifest does not enumerate — the parameters of a zero-knowledge vetting scheme, in the case that prompted this — has had two options: put them in an undeclared member of `vetting` and watch them disappear, or wait for a manifest version that names them.

`vetting` is `additionalProperties: true`, so an undeclared member has always **validated**. That is not the same as **arriving**. A generated type carries the members its schema declares and drops the rest, so the member is discarded on the way in — and discarded again on the re-serialization `requirementsDigest` is computed over, so a reader that recomputes the digest from what it parsed gets a value that does not match the one it was sent. An open object and an open type are different things, and only the declared member is both.

## What is here

**`specs/_framework/0.4/framework.schema.json`** — additive over 0.3 on the pattern 0.3's own description sets out: `Ext` and `DigestMultibase` carried forward unchanged, `ExtCritical` new.

Neither rule `ExtCritical` carries is checkable by JSON Schema, and the $def says so rather than implying otherwise: that an entry names a namespace present in the sibling `ext` is checkable only against that sibling, and whether a namespace is load-bearing is not a schema question at all. Both are consumer-side checks.

**`vtc/join-requests/manifest/0.2`** — a draft, so edited in place per SPEC §5.2. `vetting` gains `ext` and `extCritical`; this draft's framework $refs re-pin from 0.2 to 0.4, errata-style, with no change to any payload's effective wire shape.

A new response example shows a criterion carrying its parameters under a namespace it controls and marking that namespace critical — an applicant that ignored it would gather named statements and present them to a criterion whose whole purpose is that it never receives them, so it stops with `unsupportedExtension` instead of applying the wrong way. Its `requirementsDigest` is the real value for the criterion as printed; I verified the routine by recomputing the existing example's published digest first.

## Ordering

The prose links in `spec.md` point only at §4.5.1, which exists today. Nothing here depends on #23 having merged, and no link into `SPEC.md` breaks while it has not — `SPEC.md` is generated from canonical `main`, so the anchor for the new sub-section appears when #23 lands and a follow-up can point at it precisely.

## Checks

- `npm run validate` — 472 specs, 1451 framework links against 154 anchors
- `npm run check-bindings` — 472 specifications across TypeScript, Rust, Go and Dart all agree; 903 error codes match
- `cargo test --workspace` — 927 tests
- `cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs --features "validate,vtc" …manifest::v0_2` — 5 tests, including the new example
- `npm run build` — clean

No version bump and no changelog entry: release-plz owns both.

title: feat(spec): let a producer mark an ext namespace critical
body:
## What

Adds `extCritical` — a sibling array naming `ext` namespaces a consumer must understand or refuse — plus the `unsupportedExtension` error code it rejects with.

## Why

`ext` (§4.5.1) is what lets a specification grow without a version increment, and rule 5 — *a consumer MUST ignore namespaces it does not recognize* — is what makes it safe. It also means a producer cannot distinguish an ignored namespace from an understood one.

That is fine while `ext` carries hints and annotations. It stops being fine as soon as a namespace changes what the document means: a consumer that silently drops it reaches a verdict the producer never asked for, and reaches it invisibly. Today a specification has only two options — put the data in `ext` and accept the silent downgrade, or promote it to a first-class member and bump the version. The second is what the extension point exists to avoid.

The concrete case: a community publishing zero-knowledge vetting parameters in its join manifest. A client that ignores them falls back to the named path and submits under a criterion the community may not accept that way. Nobody involved learns that a downgrade happened.

## The shape

Prior art is uniform — JOSE `crit`, X.509 critical extensions, TLS — so this follows it:

1. `extCritical` is an array of one or more unique namespace strings, allowed only where the specification allows `ext`, and only alongside a sibling `ext`.
2. Every entry must name a namespace actually present in that `ext`; an entry that does not is `malformedRequest`.
3. A consumer that does not recognize a critical namespace must reject with `unsupportedExtension` rather than ignore it. One that does recognize it proceeds exactly as before — criticality obliges a consumer to understand or refuse, never to act.
4. A producer must not mark a namespace whose absence leaves the document correct.
5. A producer should establish support first, through discovery or governance or out of band.

`extCritical` is covered by `proof` exactly as `ext` is, so on a signed document the marking cannot be stripped in transit; on an unsigned one it can, and the text says to sign if that matters.

## Trade-off, stated plainly

Criticality **reports** a downgrade; it does not prevent one. A producer that marks without establishing support has chosen a failed exchange over a silent one — the right trade only where the silent outcome is worse. That is why rules 5 and 6 sit on the producer, and why the error code is distinct: an operator seeing `unsupportedExtension` learns the counterparty understood the task and refused over one namespace, which `malformedRequest` would have hidden.

## Compatibility

Additive. Opting in is per specification and per object level, so no existing document changes meaning, and no consumer acquires work unless a producer marks something. A specification that allows `ext` and not `extCritical` rejects the member under its existing `additionalProperties: false`, and every namespace there stays ignorable.

No version header change: releases are their own commits here (#18), as with #17.

## Downstream

The framework schema `ExtCritical` $def and the first specification to opt in are a companion PR in `dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf`, where `SPEC.md` is generated from this repository.

title: feat(spec): let a producer mark an ext namespace critical (#23)
body:
feat(spec): let a producer mark an ext namespace critical (#23)

`ext` lets a specification grow without a version increment, and rule 5
makes a namespace safe to ignore. That is what makes it useful, and it
is also why a producer cannot tell an ignored namespace from an
understood one. A consumer that drops a namespace the document's
meaning depends on reaches a verdict the producer never asked for, and
reaches it invisibly.

This adds the marking that forecloses that, on the model of JOSE's
`crit`, X.509 critical extensions and TLS: a sibling `extCritical`
array naming namespaces that a consumer must understand or refuse.

- A new sub-section, Marking a Namespace Critical, with six rules: the
  member's shape, that every entry names a namespace present in the
  sibling `ext`, what critical means, the consumer's obligation,
  the producer's obligation not to mark what is merely useful, and the
  SHOULD to establish support before marking.
- A new standard error code, `unsupportedExtension`, distinct from
  `unsupportedType` and `unsupportedVersion`: the consumer understood
  the type and its version and refused over the namespace.
- Rule 5 of the ext section and the ext paragraph of Consumer
  Requirements each carry the exception.

Criticality reports a downgrade rather than preventing one, so the
producer rules are where the weight is: marking a namespace that is
merely useful turns every consumer that has not implemented it into a
failure where it would otherwise have interoperated. The text says so,
and says to establish support first.

Opting in stays per specification and per object level, so no existing
document changes meaning and no consumer has new work unless a producer
marks something.

title: test(vtc): hold the jsonschema resolvers off on the claimSchema path too
body:
#1660 turned off `resolve-http` and `resolve-file` and held the manifest
honest with a test on `/v1/schemas` and one on `validate_instance`. #1657
then added a third caller-supplied schema to the same compiler:
`check_schema`, run when an endorsement type is registered. It makes the same
`validator_for` call, so it carries the same exposure — restoring the features
would have been caught on two paths out of three.

The `file:` case is the decisive one: the referenced file really exists and
really is a valid schema, so the registration would succeed if the resolver
were on. The http case pins that the refusal happens at compile rather than
as an attempted fetch, and an internal `$ref` still registers, because this
removes remote resolution and not `$ref` itself.

Follow-up to #1660 and #1657, agreed with the session that owned #1660.

## Verification

`cargo test -p vtc-service --test endorsements external_ref` — 2 passed, 0 failed (the new test and #1660's `register_schema_refuses_an_external_ref`). `cargo fmt --all` clean. Test-only change: no production code touched.

title: fix(vtc): stop a caller's JSON Schema from fetching a URL or reading a file
body:
Closes the dependency half of #1657, handed over from that PR's author.

## The problem

The workspace pinned `jsonschema = "0.56"` and took its default features, which are `resolve-http`, `resolve-file`, `tls-aws-lc-rs`, `idna`. Every schema the VTC compiles comes from a caller:

- `POST /v1/schemas` — an admin's `credentialSchema` (on `main` today)
- `POST /v1/endorsement-types` — an admin's `claimSchema` (compiled at registration as of #1657)
- issuance — both again, via `validate_instance`

With those resolvers on, an external `$ref` makes the service fetch a URL or read a local file while compiling the schema.

## It reproduces

Not a theoretical gap — I checked both directions before and after the change:

| `jsonschema` features | `POST /v1/schemas` with `{"$ref": "file:///<a real file>"}` |
|---|---|
| default (before) | **201 Created** — the file was read and the schema stored |
| `default-features = false` (after) | **400** — refused at compile |

## The change

One manifest line: `default-features = false, features = ["idna"]`.

- `idna` is kept — it is the `hostname`/`idn-hostname` format check, pure computation, no I/O.
- `tls-aws-lc-rs` goes with `resolve-http`; it exists only to fetch over HTTPS.
- `Cargo.lock` drops `reqwest` and `rustls` from the jsonschema tree.

Nothing in the repo uses an external `$ref` (I grepped for `"$ref": "http(s)://"`), and a schema that needs one belongs inlined. Only `vtc-service` depends on jsonschema, so nothing else in the workspace is affected.

## Tests

One at each compile site, and **each fails if the features come back** — I verified that by re-enabling them, otherwise the tests would prove nothing:

- `vtc-service/src/schemas/validate.rs` — `an_external_ref_is_refused_rather_than_fetched`. The `file:` case is decisive: the target exists and is a valid schema, so it would compile if the resolver were on. Also asserts an ordinary internal `$ref` still resolves — this removes remote resolution, not `$ref`.
- `vtc-service/tests/endorsements.rs` — `register_schema_refuses_an_external_ref`, the same thing through the admin route.

`cargo test --workspace`: 6713 passed, 0 failed. `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`: clean.

## Note for #1657

If this lands first, #1657 wants a rebase, and the same test is worth adding on the `claimSchema` registration path that PR introduces — that path compiles a caller's schema too, so it has the same exposure. No file overlap: this touches `Cargo.toml`, `Cargo.lock`, `schemas/validate.rs` and `tests/endorsements.rs`; #1657 touches the endorsement-type routes.

title: security(vtc)!: enforce the proof and freshness a Trust Task declares (VTI-OPS-020/021/024)
body:
The VTC's Trust Task document dispatcher verified a `proof` whenever one was
present and otherwise took attribution from the transport — including for the
nine dispatched tasks whose own definitions declare `proof` **REQUIRED**. It
applied no acceptance window to `issuedAt`, and the replay record it claimed
for every document was bounded by nothing but the guard's capacity.

That is the second of the two divergences Appendix F.2 records against this
service (trustoverip/dtgwg-vti-spec#35). It is the one the first depends on:
moving the 49 bearer-served tasks into the dispatcher closes nothing while the
dispatcher does not enforce.

`docs/05-design-notes/vtc-trust-task-proof-enforcement.md` has the argument,
the re-derived task census and the migration path.

## What is now enforced, on every transport

In `dispatch_trust_task_core`, before any handler runs, reached identically
from REST, DIDComm and TSP — which is VTI-OPS-021's whole point:

- **VTI-OPS-024** — an acceptance window over `issuedAt`: `max_age` 10 minutes,
  `skew` 60 seconds (SPEC §4.2's own "typically ≤ 60s"), `issuedAt` required.
  A future-dated `issuedAt` and an `expiresAt` at or before it are
  `malformedRequest`, not `expired` (SPEC §7.2 item 13 — neither was ever
  acceptable, so telling the producer to wait would be wrong).
- **VTI-OPS-020 / §7.2 items 5b, 7a, 8, §7.3 17** — the flag-driven rules the
  *specification* declares, via `schema_index::spec_policy_for(..).enforce(..)`:
  `recipient` REQUIRED, `proof` REQUIRED, audience binding, `issuedAt`
  REQUIRED. Read off the generated bindings by URI; there is no list of task
  URIs in this repository to drift from the registry.
- **VTI-OPS-020, the issuer binding** — a present proof must verify under a key
  the document's own `issuer` controls (SPEC §4.7). Previously a valid
  signature by *any* DID satisfied the requirement, establishing only that
  somebody signed something — which is not what `verified_signer` is read as by
  the `rooms/*` arms.
- **VTI-OPS-025…027** — the replay record is unchanged in mechanism but now
  *bounded*. `retain_until` caps a producer-chosen `expiresAt` at
  `issuedAt + max_age + skew`, so a document stamped `expiresAt = now + 10
  years` can no longer pin an id for ten years.

## What is not enforced, and why

**One client does not sign.** `openvtc-core` builds
`join-requests/{submit,status}`, `members/{self-remove,vmc}` and
`members/personhood/assert` with a deliberate "no `proof` is attached",
relying on the authcrypt sender or the TSP sender VID. `pnm-browser-plugin`,
`vtc-client` and `vta-sdk` sign on every channel.

So the one refusal that is gated is *a missing proof where the specification
declares one REQUIRED*: `[trust_tasks] require_declared_proof`, default
`false`. The allowance is narrow and loud —

- it relaxes a **missing** proof only, never an invalid one, never a missing
  `recipient` or `issuedAt`, never the audience-binding rule;
- it applies only where the transport authenticated the sender, so a REST
  document with no proof is refused whatever the setting;
- every waiver logs at `warn!` naming `VTI-OPS-021` and the task URI, so the
  debt is counted rather than assumed away.

A deployment serving only the three signing clients can set it to `true`
today and should.

**Its removal condition is exact**: when `openvtc-core` signs those five
documents, the default flips and the field goes with it. That is a one-line
change here and roughly five call sites there. No upstream specification change
is needed — `openvtc-core` already signs Trust Task documents on its vetting
path with the same `eddsa-jcs-2022` primitive.

**The transport cross-check (§7.2 item 6)** stays in the handlers
(`resolve_holder`), not the spine: a spine-level comparison of in-band `issuer`
against transport-derived sender would refuse the relayer ≠ holder shape this
workspace supports deliberately.

## What the next phase must do

1. `openvtc-core` signs. Flip the default, delete `require_declared_proof`.
   Divergence 2 closes.
2. Bind the 49 bearer-served proof-REQUIRED tasks in `DISPATCHED_URIS` /
   `dispatch_typed`, taking authorization from the verified signer's ACL entry.
   `auth/authenticate/0.1` and `vtc/relationships/publish/0.2` already do this
   and are the model.
3. Keep each bearer route as a documented transitional path with a stated
   removal point; the admin SPA, `cnm` and `vtc-client` need the signed path
   first.
4. Remove them, and close the Appendix F.2 entries.

One thing to carry into step 2: **VTI-OPS-027** requires the accepted-identifier
record to be shared across every binding. `REPLAY_GUARD` is process-local and
covers only the dispatcher, so a task served on both a bearer route and the
dispatcher would have a record on one binding and none on the other.

## Re-derived census, and its drift

Re-derived from `routes/mod.rs` (the single mount site) against
`spec_policy_for`, rather than taken from the register: **95** distinct task
URIs on REST routes, **51** declaring `proof` REQUIRED, of which two already
verify one — so **49** are served on a bearer token, not the 48 recorded. The
difference is exactly `vtc/invitations/deliver/0.1`, bound by #1648 after the
entry was written. `vtc/relationships/persona/0.1` has no published spec policy
in this build. No other drift.

## Why `!`

Three shapes that were accepted are now refused on the wire, on every
transport: a document with no `issuedAt` (or one outside a ten-minute window),
a document missing an in-band `recipient` its specification declares REQUIRED,
and a proof that verifies under a key the `issuer` does not control. Every
known producer already sends what is now required.

Refs #1641

title: chore(deps): take vta-sdk 0.49, trust-tasks-rs 0.21.17, vta-service 0.39
body:
Takes the persona release published from VTI:

| Crate | From | To |
|---|---|---|
| `vta-sdk` | 0.48.0 | 0.49.0 |
| `trust-tasks-rs` | 0.21.3 | 0.21.17 |
| `vta-service` (dev, MockVta) | 0.38.0 | 0.39.0 |

What the line carries: `persona/binding/set` takes an optional `personaDid`, so a face can be worn in a community as the persona already used there without naming it (spec §9.7, VTI #1654); and a credential-backed value is re-derived from its credential wherever it is read, failing closed if the credential has gone (VTI #1653).

**One call site changed.** `persona_binding_set` now takes `Option<&str>`. Each call here knows which persona the community holds, so each names it — omitting it only helps a caller that does not know.

**Why the lockfile moves further than three crates.** Bumping the sdk alone left two `vti-common` and three `vta-sdk` nodes: `vta-service` 0.39 pulls subsystem crates the lockfile still held a line behind, and those ask for `vta-sdk ^0.48`. A split `vti-common` is a build failure rather than untidiness, since it re-exports `vta_sdk::acl::{ActScope, ApproveScope, ContextDirection}` as its own API. A full `cargo update` collapses it to one `vti-common` 0.23.0 and one `vta-sdk` 0.49.0. The `vta-sdk` 0.42.1 that `did-git-sign` 0.4.12 pulls is unchanged and pre-existing; it stays tolerable only because no sdk type crosses that boundary, which is the standing obligation the root manifest's note describes.

CI set run locally: fmt, both clippy runs, doc, tests with `--include-ignored` (1501), `--no-default-features` (1482), `-p openvtc --features dev-overrides` (673), bench build.

title: fix(vtc)!: admin promotion goes through acl/change-role, behind a step-up
body:
Closes #1645. Resolves the divergence recorded in the VTI specification's
divergence register (Appendix F.2) by trustoverip/dtgwg-vti-spec#35 — that
entry can be closed once this merges.

## Security fix: the step-up on admin promotion was bypassable

**This is the part that matters, and it is not a refactor.**

`vtc/members/update/0.1` carried an in-handler `require_fresh_step_up` for
`role: admin`. That gate bounded one *route*. Two other doors reach the same
ACL row and assign the same `admin` role:

- `acl/change-role/0.1` (`PATCH /v1/acl/{did}`) — `update_acl` set
  `entry.role` and stored it. No step-up, no self-promotion refusal, no
  role-change policy, no VEC re-mint, no serialisation.
- `acl/grant/0.1` (`POST /v1/acl`) — `create_acl` wrote a fresh `admin`
  entry. Same: nothing but `validate_vtc_role_assignment`, which only asks
  whether the *caller* is an admin.

So any admin session could confer admin with no second factor by using the
other door, and the admin console's passkey gesture was decoration rather
than a control. All three claims were verified against the code before
anything was changed.

The gate now sits on the **operation**, not on a route.

### How it is enforced

`role_change_via_pipeline` took a `step_up: bool` from its caller. That made
the handler the gate: the host invariant it fed
(`ceremony::invariant::StepUpForAdmin`) could only check that somebody had
said `true`, and a second route reaching the same row simply said nothing.

The pipeline now resolves the elevation itself, from the caller's **live
session** (`acl::elevation::verified`), and two host invariants are applied
in `ceremony::decide` — around the policy, where an operator's policy edit
cannot reach them:

- `StepUpForAdmin` (**VTI-OPS-051**) — an `allow{role: admin}` needs a live
  elevation.
- `SelfPromotion` (**VTI-OPS-050**, new) — nobody promotes themselves,
  however well authenticated. A second factor proves who is at the keyboard,
  never that a second person agreed.

A vetoed decision is rendered back in its own terms rather than as
`denied by policy (step-up-required)`: the step-up veto answers
`403 step_up_required`, which is the signal the console turns into a passkey
prompt, and the self-promotion veto names the command to run instead.

**`policy.enforcement` (#1633) does not apply here, and nothing depends on
it.** That flag is `vta-config`'s; the VTC has no equivalent. Its decision
pipeline always runs — `load_active_compiled` is not optional, and boot
installs the default bundle idempotently — and `decide` applies the host
invariants unconditionally after the policy. There is no configuration in
which these lapse, and none in which an operator can switch them off by
editing `role_change.rego`.

`acl/grant` is the one gate that is not an invariant, stated plainly rather
than hidden: a grant writes an entry rather than moving one, so there is no
transition to hang one on. It calls the same predicate
(`acl::elevation::verified` / `required`) one layer further out, so the two
cannot drift.

It is gated on the *widening*, not the write (`elevation::
widens_admin_authority`). `acl/grant` is "the entry the maintainer should
hold", so it is also how the console edits an admin's **label** — re-granting
at the same role and the same scopes. Demanding a passkey for that would be
theatre. Demanding it for the rewrite that takes an admin from one context to
two, or from a context to none at all (which is how a community-wide
super-admin is spelled), is not: that is authority conferred without the role
ever changing.

## What came with the promotion, so nothing was lost

Everything the `members/update` path did now happens on `acl/change-role`,
and for every caller of the pipeline rather than for one route:

- **Self-promotion refused** — moved from a handler `if` to the invariant.
- **Serialised** — `PROMOTE_LOCK` moved from `routes/members/update.rs` into
  `ceremony::orchestrate`. The window it closes is a property of the
  operation; with the lock on one handler, the second door raced the first.
- **Compare-and-swap under the lock** — the subject's row is re-read inside
  the critical section and re-checked against the caller's `fromRole`, so a
  promotion racing another role write is a `409` rather than an overwrite of
  whatever landed in between. This subsumes the old already-an-admin
  re-check.
- **Role-change policy + role-VEC re-mint** — the `Remint` executor arm,
  including the no-last-admin guard on demotion that `acl/change-role`
  previously skipped entirely.
- **Admin sister record** — without it a promotion produces an admin who
  cannot enrol a passkey, i.e. cannot sign in to the console.
- **`AdminPromoted` audit** — its own variant beside `AclUpdated`, joined to
  the `AuthSteppedUp` row by `authorisingSessionId`.

`RemintOutcome.role_vec` became `Option<VerifiableCredential>`: a role VEC is
re-minted only where there is a **member row** to repoint it on. An ACL-only
subject (an integration or operator DID, which `acl/change-role` legitimately
serves) has no role assertion to re-issue, and minting one anyway would have
made an ACL role change impossible on a VTC with no credential signer.

## A second escalation, found while moving the promotion

`update_acl` never ran `validate_acl_modification` — `create_acl` always has.
The existing `caller_covers_admin_target` guard only fires on an entry that is
*already* admin, so a context admin of `ctx-a` could not demote a peer admin
scoped to `[ctx-a, ctx-b]` (its own doc comment says so) but **could promote a
member** with those scopes into exactly that entry, minting an admin over a
context they do not hold. The check is now run on the resulting entry, decoded
through `ActScope` so "no scopes" is read as *unrestricted* under `admin` and
*nowhere* under every other role rather than conflated. Covered by
`a_context_admin_cannot_promote_across_a_context_it_does_not_hold`.

## `vtc/members/update` answers `adminRoleForbidden`

`role: admin` is refused with the code the specification declares for it,
using `TaskError::declared` and the generated constant, before anything is
read or written — the task's consumer conformance is "return
`adminRoleForbidden` and change nothing". The message names the replacement
endpoint and body verbatim, per the workspace rule that an operator error
suggests the fix.

Census (`trust_tasks/error_code_census.rs`): witness added,
`s::members::update::v0_1::error_codes::ADMIN_ROLE_FORBIDDEN` removed from
the baseline, `UNWITNESSED` 12 → 11.

## The open question: does `acl/grant` of `admin` count as promotion?

**Decided: no — `acl/grant` cannot promote a member, and that is now
structural rather than incidental.**

A VTC member is 1:1 with an ACL row by DID, and `create_acl` already refuses
a grant that would change an existing entry's role, pointing at
`acl/change-role`. So the only member-facing path to `admin` is the ceremony,
which is where the invariants live. What `acl/grant` can do is *create* an
admin from nothing, or *re-grant* an existing admin (which rewrites its
scopes). Creating one always takes the fresh step-up; re-granting takes it
when the rewrite widens what the entry holds. A self-targeted grant that would
mint the caller a *new* admin entry is refused outright.

The case deliberately **not** gated is a re-grant that confers nothing new —
same role, same scopes. That is how the console corrects a label, and it hands
over no authority that was not already there.

## Affected clients — breaking

| Client | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| `admin-ui` `members.tsx::promoteToAdmin` | passkey step-up, then `PATCH /v1/members/{did}` `{role:"admin"}` under `vtc/members/update/0.1` | passkey step-up (unchanged), then `PATCH /v1/acl/{did}` `{fromRole, toRole:"admin"}` under `acl/change-role/0.1`. `fromRole` comes from the rendered row and is a real compare-and-swap. **Updated in this PR.** |
| `admin-ui` `acl.tsx::createAcl` (**Access control → Add entry**) | no step-up — this was the second half of the bypass, reachable from the console itself | steps up when the role is `admin`, and the form says so before you submit. **Updated in this PR.** |
| Any external client promoting via `members/update` | `200` | `400 adminRoleForbidden`, message naming the replacement |
| Any client conferring `admin` via `acl/change-role` or `acl/grant` **without** a step-up | `200`/`201` | `403 step_up_required` — this is the fix |

The step-up ceremony moved out of `members.tsx` into `lib/step-up.ts` so both
console paths run one implementation — the daemon's gate is shared, so the
client's should be too, and a screen that offers an admin-conferring operation
without it can only ever answer `step_up_required`.

Checked and **not** affected: `vtc-client` has no role-change or promote
function at all (`update_member_extensions` hard-codes an extensions-only
body and cannot send a role); `cnm-cli` has no VTC member-role command — its
`--role admin` surfaces are VTA ACL entries and error-message text. No change
needed in either; neither has a step-up helper, so neither could have
completed a promotion.

## Operational note: what an operator with no passkey can still do

A step-up is `auth/passkey/login/{start,finish}/0.2` with `purpose: stepUp`,
so an admin with no enrolled passkey cannot perform one. That was already
true of the `members/update` promotion, so nothing regresses — but it now
also holds for `acl/change-role` and `acl/grant` of `admin`, which is the
point. First-admin provisioning does not go through either (it is `vtc
setup` / the install token / emergency bootstrap), and the offline
break-glass — `vtc --config <config.toml> acl add --did … --role admin`,
direct fjall with the daemon stopped — is untouched.

## A note on ACL narrowing (#1279, #1619, #1642)

On the VTA an entry can hold less than its role, so a role is a ceiling and a
gate reading only the role over-trusts the entry. Two questions follow for any
promotion gate: what happens to a narrowed capability set when the role moves,
and whether a caller can escalate by widening their own set without touching
their role.

Neither arises here, structurally rather than by luck: `VtcAclEntry` has **no**
`capabilities` field and `AuthClaims` carries none, so a VTC entry is exactly
`(role, scopes)` and nothing can disagree with the role because nothing else is
stored. The analogous widening axis is `scopes`, and `validate_acl_modification`
already bounds it (a non-super-admin cannot confer the unrestricted entry; a
context admin is bounded to contexts it holds). What it does *not* bound is how
recently the caller authenticated — which is why the step-up is required on a
**re-grant that widens**, not only on a fresh one. This is recorded in
`acl/elevation.rs` so that if the VTC ever gains per-entry narrowing, the note
says what has to be decided with it.

## Docs

- `docs/03-vtc/bootstrap-runbook.md` — a new **Adding a second admin later**
  section (both paths, the compare-and-swap, why `members/update` is not it,
  and the no-self-promotion rule), and the existing "Access control → Add
  entry" instruction now says it asks for a passkey.
- `docs/05-design-notes/vtc-mvp.md` §10.4 — the superseded-status note records
  the second move and why the first was not enough.

## Tests

- `ceremony::invariant` — self-promotion vetoed even with a step-up; a
  self-*demotion* still passes; step-up veto unchanged.
- `ceremony::orchestrate` — promotion without a live elevation is
  `StepUpRequired`; self-promotion is `Forbidden` and names the fix; a stale
  `current_role` is a `409`; the happy path and the deny-policy path still
  hold.
- `tests/acl_canonical.rs` (named for the requirements they hold) —
  `vti_ops_051_change_role_to_admin_without_a_live_step_up_is_refused`,
  `vti_ops_051_a_lapsed_step_up_does_not_promote`,
  `vti_ops_051_a_live_step_up_promotes_and_runs_the_role_change_pipeline`
  (asserts the ACL move, the re-minted role VEC, and the admin sister
  record), `vti_ops_050_self_promotion_is_refused_on_the_change_role_path`,
  `vti_ops_051_granting_the_admin_role_without_a_step_up_is_refused`,
  `granting_the_admin_role_with_a_step_up_succeeds`,
  `vti_ops_050_granting_yourself_the_admin_role_is_refused`,
  `re_granting_an_admin_at_the_same_scopes_needs_no_step_up` (and that
  widening the same entry *is* refused),
  `a_context_admin_cannot_promote_across_a_context_it_does_not_hold`, plus two
  regressions that a non-admin role change and a non-admin grant need no
  step-up.
- `tests/members_crud.rs` —
  `the_update_task_answers_with_the_admin_role_forbidden_code_its_spec_declares`
  (the census witness; refused even *with* a live elevation, because it is the
  field that is forbidden) and
  `admin_role_forbidden_is_answered_before_the_member_is_looked_up`.
- `tests/passkey_step_up.rs` — `a_step_up_authorises_the_promotion_it_was_run_for`
  retargeted at `acl/change-role`, so the end-to-end WebAuthn ceremony still
  covers the operation it authorises.

title: vtc: admin promotion goes through members/update, which declares adminRoleForbidden; acl/change-role promotes with no step-up (VTI-OPS-110/051)
body:
Tracks the intended resolution of a divergence recorded in the VTI specification's divergence register (Appendix F.2) by trustoverip/dtgwg-vti-spec#35. Found while building #1644, which left `vtc/members/update:adminRoleForbidden` on the unwitnessed baseline in `vtc-service/src/trust_tasks/error_code_census.rs`.

## What the definition says

`specs/vtc/members/update/0.1` in dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf declares `adminRoleForbidden` ("`role` was `admin`. Promotion to admin is a separate, gated flow, not a metadata update."), its payload schema says `role` MUST NOT be `admin`, and its consumer conformance says: if `role` is `admin`, return `adminRoleForbidden` and change nothing.

`specs/acl/change-role/0.1` is the task defined for role transitions. It says maintainers MAY require stronger authentication, such as a passkey step-up, for a transition into an elevated role, and SHOULD forbid self-promotion.

## What vtc-service does

- `routes/members/update.rs::update_member` accepts `role: admin`. It refuses self-promotion, requires `require_fresh_step_up` in the handler, serialises on `PROMOTE_LOCK`, and runs the role-change pipeline (`role_change.rego`, which re-mints the role VEC). `adminRoleForbidden` is never emitted.
- The admin console relies on this path. `admin-ui/src/plugins/members.tsx::promoteToAdmin` runs `auth/passkey/login/{start,finish}/0.2` with `purpose: stepUp`, then sends `PATCH /v1/members/{did}` `{role: "admin"}` under `vtc/members/update/0.1`.
- `routes/acl.rs::update_acl` (`acl/change-role/0.1`) and `create_acl` (`acl/grant/0.1`) both assign `VtcRole::Admin` to any admin caller through `validate_vtc_role_assignment`. Neither requires a step-up or refuses self-promotion, and neither runs the role-change pipeline. **So the step-up on the members/update path does not bound promotion today.** An admin session without a step-up can promote through `acl/change-role` or `acl/grant`.

## Intended resolution

1. Require a fresh step-up on `acl/change-role` (and on `acl/grant` when the role granted is `admin`), as a rule evaluated at the policy gate rather than a check in a handler (VTI-OPS-050/051).
2. Carry over what the members/update path does: refuse self-promotion, serialise against concurrent role writes, and apply the role-change policy and VEC re-mint.
3. Point `promoteToAdmin` in the admin console (and `cnm` / `vtc-client`, if they promote) at `acl/change-role`.
4. Refuse `role: admin` on `vtc/members/update` with `adminRoleForbidden`, and remove it from the census baseline (lower `UNWITNESSED`).
5. Close the Appendix F entry.

Step 1 has to land before step 3. Moving the console first would remove the only gate that promotion has.

title: fix(vtc)!: admin promotion goes through acl/change-role, behind a step-up (#1658)
body:
fix(vtc)!: admin promotion goes through acl/change-role, behind a step-up (#1658)

`vtc/members/update/0.1` carried an in-handler step-up for `role: admin`.
That gate bounded one route. `acl/change-role` and `acl/grant` reach the
same ACL row and assign the same `admin` role, and neither asked for a
step-up, refused self-promotion, or ran the role-change pipeline — so the
gate was walked around by using a different door. The task also *declares*
`adminRoleForbidden` for exactly this: promotion is a separate, gated flow,
not a metadata update.

The gate now sits on the operation. `role_change_via_pipeline` took a
`step_up: bool` from its caller, which made the handler the gate; it now
resolves the elevation from the caller's live session, and two host
invariants are applied around the policy in `ceremony::decide`, where an
operator's policy edit cannot reach them: `StepUpForAdmin` (VTI-OPS-051)
and `SelfPromotion` (VTI-OPS-050, new). The VTC has no `policy.enforcement`
switch and its pipeline always runs, so neither can lapse by configuration.
`acl/grant` of `admin` checks the same predicate directly — it writes an
entry rather than moving one, so there is no transition to hang an invariant
on — and refuses a self-mint.

Everything the members/update path did came with the promotion: the promote
lock moved into the ceremony (the window is a property of the operation, and
with the lock on one handler the second door raced it), the already-an-admin
re-check generalised into a compare-and-swap re-read under that lock, the
role-change policy and role-VEC re-mint, the admin sister record, and the
`AdminPromoted` audit row.

`update_acl` also never ran `validate_acl_modification`. The existing
`caller_covers_admin_target` guard only fires on an entry that is already
admin, so a context admin of ctx-a could not demote a peer scoped to
`[ctx-a, ctx-b]` but could promote a member with those scopes into exactly
that entry. It is checked now, decoded through `ActScope`.

`RemintOutcome.role_vec` is now `Option<VerifiableCredential>`: a role VEC is
re-minted only where there is a member row to repoint it on, so an ACL-only
subject no longer needs a credential signer to change role.

Breaking: a client promoting via `PATCH /v1/members/{did}` `{role:"admin"}`
now gets `400 adminRoleForbidden` naming the replacement, and conferring
`admin` through `acl/change-role` or `acl/grant` without a live elevation
now gets `403 step_up_required`. The admin console is updated here; it was
the only client in the repo that promoted. `vtc-client` and `cnm-cli` have
no promotion path.

Closes #1645. Resolves the divergence register entry in
trustoverip/dtgwg-vti-spec#35 (Appendix F.2).

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

title: fix(vtc): refuse an invalid claimSchema at registration, and name the broken type at issuance
body:
Refs #1649, #1600

#1649 made `vtc/endorsements/issue/0.1` enforce the endorsement type's stored
`claimSchema`, which registration had always stored and nothing had ever read.
That turned a document nobody had validated into a load-bearing one: a type
registered with a `claimSchema` that is not itself valid JSON Schema now fails
**every** issuance against it with a 500, and neither the issuer (whose claim is
fine) nor the operator (who sees "internal error") can tell why.

Both ends are fixed. The schema is checked where it is supplied, and where a
pre-existing broken one is met the answer says the *type* is broken.

## At registration — refused, naming the bad keyword

`POST /v1/endorsement-types` now refuses a `claimSchema` that will not compile,
with the part of the document that is wrong:

```
400 {"error":"claimSchema is not a valid JSON Schema — at /properties/level/type:
     \"intiger\" is not valid under any of the schemas listed in the 'anyOf' keyword.
     Correct the schema and register again; …",
     "code":"malformedRequest"}
```

**No declared code covers it.** `vtc/endorsement-types/register/0.1` declares
exactly three — `invalidUri`, `reserved`, `exists` — and `invalidUri` is "empty
or over 512 bytes", about `typeUri`. So the refusal carries the framework's
standard `malformedRequest` (SPEC §8.3), spelled
`trust_tasks_rs::StandardCode::MalformedRequest.as_str()`, not a literal and not
a new code minted under the task's namespace.

**The census baseline is unchanged (still 12).** The census tracks the codes a
`spec/vtc/*` task *declares*; all five endorsement-type/endorsement codes in
scope were already witnessed by #1649, and `CONSUMER_MINTED` is for codes
namespaced under the task slug, which a framework code is not. `TaskError`'s
doc comment is updated to say the standard-code case is allowed, so the "always
a generated constant" invariant stays honest.

**There is no update or upsert path.** The endorsement-type surface is
register / list / delete only, so register is the one gate.

The check is `crate::schemas::check_schema`, which makes the *same*
`jsonschema::validator_for` call `validate_instance` makes at issuance — so a
schema registration accepts is one issuance can use, and one it refuses is one
issuance would choke on. A separate, stricter gate would only move the failure
to a different pair of inputs. A non-object is refused before the compile:
`claimSchema` is `"type": "object"` in the register payload schema, while JSON
Schema itself accepts the bare booleans as schemas.

## At issuance — a 5xx that names the type, not the claim

A stored schema that will not compile is answered with a 500 whose message
names the type and says what to do:

```
500 {"error":"endorsement type 'https://…/corrupt' has an invalid stored
     claimSchema (at /type: \"intiger\" is not valid …) — the claim was not at
     fault. An admin must delete and re-register the type with a valid JSON
     Schema before it can be issued against."}
```

It carries **no** `code`, and deliberately not `claimSchemaViolation`: that code
means a claim failed a *valid* schema and would send the operator to fix the
claim, which is the one thing that is not wrong. No other declared code fits
either, and a 4xx would blame the caller for server-side state. The type id is
logged at `error!` alongside the compile detail.

## Existing data — one WARN per broken type at boot

`report_invalid_claim_schemas` walks the registry at boot and logs one WARN per
type whose stored `claimSchema` will not compile, naming the type, the bad part
and the fix. Same shape as #1633's unenforced-policy warning: advisory, a read
failure is logged and never stops boot. It was cheap — `all_types` plus the same
`check_schema` — so it is here rather than in the PR body as a reason not to.

## Consumers

- **admin-ui**: `StatementTypesCard` sends only `typeUri` and `description` —
  it never sends `claimSchema`, so its register call cannot be refused where it
  was not before. If it ever does, the card already renders the daemon's message
  verbatim (`errorMessage(register.error)`). No UI code change.
- **`openapi.json` is regenerated, description-only, and it is a correctness
  fix.** `claimSchema`'s doc comment is rendered into the document, and the one
  checked in still said the schema was "reserved for future per-type validation"
  and that issuance "only checks type is registered without consulting the
  schema" — which #1649 made false. The new text is two lines, so the field's
  history moved into an ordinary `//` comment that utoipa does not read.
  `wire.ts` regenerates byte-identical (openapi-typescript drops a description
  sitting beside a `$ref`), and `npm run lint`'s `wire:check` confirms it.
- **vtc-client**: does not touch endorsement types.
- No REST body or status changed, and no `#[utoipa::path]` was touched. The 400
  gains a `code` member exactly as every other declared refusal on this route
  already does.

## Tests

- `check_schema_names_the_part_that_is_not_a_schema`,
  `check_schema_refuses_a_non_object` (unit) — a valid schema compiles; four
  malformed ones each report their JSON Pointer; the four non-object shapes are
  named.
- `a_claim_schema_that_is_not_a_json_schema_is_refused_at_registration` — 400 +
  `malformedRequest` + the bad part in the message, nothing stored, and the same
  URI registers once the schema is a schema. A type with no `claimSchema` is
  unaffected.
- `a_type_with_a_corrupt_stored_claim_schema_names_the_type_not_the_claim` — the
  corrupt row is written straight into the keyspace (the fixed registration path
  cannot produce one), issuance answers 500 naming the type with no error code,
  nothing is issued, and delete-then-re-register restores issuance.
- `all_types_returns_every_row_in_key_order` — the new storage helper.
- `a_claim_failing_the_type_claim_schema_is_the_declared_violation` is unchanged
  and still green: a valid schema still passes a good claim and still refuses a
  bad one with `claimSchemaViolation`.

## Noted, not fixed

`jsonschema`'s default features include `resolve-http` and `resolve-file`, so
compiling a schema with an external `$ref` can make a blocking fetch. That is
pre-existing on the issuance path (`validate_instance` has always done it, for
`credentialSchema` as well as `claimSchema`), reachable by the same admin, and
turning it off is a workspace-wide dependency change — out of scope here, worth
a follow-up.

## Verification

- `cargo test -p vtc-service -p vtc-client --no-fail-fast` — 67 binaries, **1836
  passed, 0 failed** (run on the rebased tree, `VTC_SKIP_ADMIN_UI_BUILD` unset).
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` — clean.
- `cargo fmt --all -- --check` — clean.
- admin-ui `npm run lint` + `npx vitest run` — 21 files, 170 tests, all pass.

body:
### Specifications

- **messaging/account**: Opt-in activity timestamps on account/get and account/list ([#594](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/594))

Account gains optional lastReceivedAt (the last message accepted for it,
  may lag by up to 60 s) and lastAuthenticatedAt (its last completed
  authentication), both Unix epoch seconds. A mediator returns them only
  when the request sets includeActivity: generated clients reject unknown
  members, so a requester that did not ask must never see them.

title: chore(release): 0.11.0
body:
Cuts **0.11.0**, the first release published to crates.io since 0.9.1.

## Why 0.11.0 and not 0.10.0

`Cargo.toml` has said 0.10.0 since #28, and the CHANGELOG has a `[0.10.0] - 2026-09-11` section, but no `v0.10.0` tag was ever pushed, so 0.10.0 never reached crates.io (latest there is 0.9.1). Since then #31 (`feat!`, `taskDigestMultibase`) merged, and its code already carries `#[deprecated(since = "0.11.0")]`. So this releases both as 0.11.0 rather than retroactively tagging 0.10.0.

## Changes

- `Cargo.toml`: `0.10.0` → `0.11.0`
- `CHANGELOG.md`:
  - `[Unreleased]` content moves under `## [0.11.0] - 2026-09-22`, with `[Unreleased]` left empty
  - a lead paragraph and an **Upgrading from 0.9** section for consumers crossing 0.10.0 and 0.11.0 at once: `DTGCredentialError` is `#[non_exhaustive]` (+9 variants), `new_member_vmc` / `new_delegate_vdc` / `new_vwc` deprecated in favour of `new_member_vmc_for` / `new_delegate_vdc_for` / `new_vwc_for_session`, and `DTGCommon::task_digest_multibase` breaks exhaustive struct literals. Ordering: verifiers first (from 0.10.0's stricter checks); 0.11.0 adds none.
  - the `[0.10.0]` section is marked **never published to crates.io**
- `README.md`: the upgrade-ordering table gains a 0.11.0 row ("Any order") and notes that 0.10.0 first ships in 0.11.0

No code changes. The file has no compare links, so none to update.

## affinidi-tdk bump (#30)

Not user-visible: `affinidi-tdk` (0.12 → 0.16) is a **dev-dependency** only (examples and integration tests), so no CHANGELOG entry. The affinidi crates that *are* in the public API (`affinidi-data-integrity` 0.7: `DataIntegrityProof`, `DataIntegrityError` via `#[from]`; `affinidi-secrets-resolver` 0.5: `&Secret` in `sign`) are unchanged since 0.9.1.

## Verification (local, on this commit)

- `cargo fmt --check`: clean
- `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings`, `--all-features` and `--no-default-features`: clean
- `cargo test --all-features`: 186 passed, 0 failed
- `cargo test --no-default-features`: 170 passed, 0 failed
- `cargo doc --no-deps`, both feature sets: builds
- `cargo publish --dry-run --locked`: packaged 23 files (561.9 KiB, 140.0 KiB compressed), verify build OK, upload aborted (dry run)

Pre-existing, not addressed here: `RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings" cargo doc --no-default-features` fails on intra-doc links to `DTGCredential::sign` / `verify_proof_with_public_key`, which only exist behind `affinidi-signing`. docs.rs builds default features, and CI does not run rustdoc, so it does not block the release.

## Publishing (after merge — not done in this PR)

Earlier release tags (`v0.9.0`, `v0.9.1`) are **annotated, not signed**, on the merge commit, with a `vX.Y.Z — <summary>` message. To match:

```sh
git fetch origin
MERGE_SHA=$(git rev-parse origin/main)   # confirm this is the squash-merge of this PR
git tag -a v0.11.0 "$MERGE_SHA" -m "v0.11.0 — taskDigestMultibase; first publish of 0.10.0's issue-time validation"
git push origin v0.11.0
```

(Use `git tag -s` instead of `-a` if you want it signed; earlier tags were not.) The tag push triggers `.github/workflows/publish.yml`, which checks tag == `Cargo.toml` version, skips if 0.11.0 is already on crates.io, then publishes via Trusted Publishing in the `crates-io` environment.
